statements.quote: The Lebombo bone, a baboon fibula found by \citeauthor{lebomboboneoriginal} in Border Cave in the Lebombo Mountains on the South Africa-Eswatini border, and dated to approximately 42,000 to 43,000 years ago (c.
41,000 BCE), represents the earliest known instance of “outsourcing mathematical thought to physical objects”.
Featuring 29 distinct notches, the artifact is widely interpreted as a tally stick or lunar calendar, probably used to track the moon's phases or menstrual cycles.
As a foundational example of “spatial abstraction,” it serves as a prehistoric precursor to modern computation by mapping abstract numbers onto a physical medium.
It can be thought of as the earliest surviving external mathematical memory of early humans.
\citealternativetitle{wolfbonephoto} (CC BY-SA 3.0, \citeauthor{wolfbonephoto}): the wolf radius from Dolní Věstonice with 55 notches in two groups of 30 and 25, dated to roughly 27,000 years ago

The **Dolní Věstonice bone**, commonly called the **wolf bone** (Czech: *vlčí radius*, “Věstonice notch-stick”), is the radius of a wolf, found in 1936 by **\citeauthor{wolfbone}** at the Upper Paleolithic site of Dolní Věstonice in Moravia, Czech Republic, at the base of Mount Děvín.
That site is one of the richest Gravettian settlements known (c.
27,000 to 20,000 BC), famous for the Venus of Dolní Věstonice, one of the oldest fired clay figurines in the world.

The 18 cm long bone carries **55 notches** carved in two groups of 30 and 25, separated by two longer marks, and is dated to roughly **27,000 years ago**; a fragment of the head of an ivory Venus figurine lay right next to it.
The marks are interpreted as tally marks: some researchers read them as a record of lunar months.

What makes the bone remarkable is the *independence* of its invention: the same impulse to “outsource counting to a physical object” shows up, without contact, in south-east Africa (Lebombo, ~43,000 years ago), central Europe (Dolní Věstonice, ~27,000) and again in central Africa (Ishango, ~20,000).
Counting devices appear to be a repeatedly convergent human invention rather than a single invention that spread.

\marginfig{ishango.jpg}{The \citealternativetitle{ishangobonephoto} is one of the earliest known attempts of outsourcing mathematical thought to physical objects, a baboon fibula carved with grouped notches that may encode prime numbers, lunar months, or a tally of goods.}
The **Ishango bone** is a Paleolithic artifact discovered in 1950 by Belgian geologist \citeauthor{ishangobone} in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Dated to approximately **c.
18,000 BCE**, this baboon fibula predates the Sumerian and Babylonian mathematical records by roughly 15,000 years.

It features three columns of grouped notches that exhibit curious mathematical properties, such as a column of prime numbers (11, 13, 17, 19) and groups that sum to 60 or 48, though it is not clear whether the prime numbers are intentional of coincidental.
Researchers have long debated whether the artifact served as a simple tally, a **lunar calendar** as suggested by \citeauthor{marshackishango}, or a more complex mathematical tool.
De Heinzelin's original 1957 publication, \citetitle{ishangobone}, introduced the bone to the scientific community, sparking decades of inquiry into the “mathematical Out of Africa” theory.

Modern scholars like \citeauthor{ishango12} continue to investigate its potential use as a primitive “slide rule” or evidence of a base-12 counting system, marking it as a critical precursor to later mechanical calculation aids.
It could also have been a counting system, where quantities of something have been represented by notches in the bone.
It is not clear exactly what it was used for, though.
Ultimately, the Ishango bone represents the most significant archaeological indicator of prehistoric mathematical reasoning, and thus is a *very* early precursor to modern computers and AI systems.

Long before silicon chips, the 13th-century Majorcan mystic \citeauthor{arsmagna} attempted to mechanize thought itself.
In his seminal work \citealternativetitle{arsmagna}, he designed a system of rotating, concentric paper circles inscribed with letters representing fundamental philosophical and theological concepts.
By turning these wheels, one could generate every logically possible combination of ideas.
While it looks like a curious mix of mysticism and combinatorics, it is the first documented attempt to create a universal logical language that generates new knowledge through mechanical operations.
Llull believed that systematically combining symbols could “calculate” truth, a direct ancestor of the symbol-manipulation view of intelligence.
A Transformer's billions of vector operations are the same principle at an unimaginable scale.
A complete guide on how to use the Llullian **Volvelle** as intended by Llull can be found in (\cite[Bonner, 2007]{artandlogicofllull}).

Medieval scholar Ramon Llull had quite an interesting life, and has done many things beyond his combinatorial wheels.\sidenote{One of the earliest novels in medieval Europe after antiquity, *Blanquerna* (\citetitle{blanquerna}), was by him: it tells the rise of a monk through the ranks of the church to the papacy.

He is also the only person whose writings were condemned as heretical by one pope (Gregory XI., in 1376) \cite[yet whose legacy was later explicitly honoured by another]{arsmagnavolvelle}, Pius IX., roughly five centuries later.} His intellectual range, theology, novel-writing, and combinatorial logic together, is a useful reminder that the boundary between "mystic" and "logician" was much thinner in the 13th century than it is now.
Eight centuries later, a \citeyear{zhao2025thinkingmachine} paper \cite{zhao2025thinkingmachine} directly reconstructed Llull's thinking machine for the age of large language models.

By mining three compositional axes, Theme, Domain, and Method, from conference papers and combining them via templates inspired by Llull's combinatorial wheels, the authors built a pipeline that generates diverse, grounded research ideas automatically.

This modern incarnation demonstrates that Llull's fundamental insight, that new knowledge can be produced through systematic symbolic recombination, remains productive even in the era of deep learning.
The work of \citeauthor{arsmagna} inspired \citeauthor{leibniz1686calculus} with the philosophical conviction that human reason itself is a form of computation.
In his \citeyear{leibniz1686calculus} work \citetitle{leibniz1686calculus}, Leibniz proposed a universal logical language that would reduce all human reasoning to a series of calculations.
If controversies were to arise, there would be no more need of disputation between two philosophers than between two accountants.
For it would suffice to take their pencils in their hands, to sit down to their slates, and to say to each other: Let us calculate!

Leibniz's vision was revolutionary: he sought to mechanize thought by creating a symbolic system where every concept was represented by a unique number, allowing complex arguments to be resolved with the same algebraic certainty as a math problem.
This “Mathesis Universalis” represents the true birth of the mechanical philosophy that underpins AI.
Crucially, Leibniz also formalized the binary system, reducing all mathematical logic to the interplay of 0 and 1, providing the literal alphabet for the digital age.
It shifted the quest for intelligence from the mystical to the mathematical, providing the logical foundation that would eventually be realized in \citealternativetitle{turing1950computing}.

statements.quote: Louis Lapicque, 1866-1952 (\cite[Lapicque]{lapicque_portrait})
The mathematical birth of the neuron model predates McCulloch and Pitts by 36 years.

In \citeyear{lapicque1907}, French neuroscientist \citeauthor{lapicque1907} published \citealternativetitle{lapicque1907}, the paper that introduced what we now call the **integrate-and-fire** neuron.

Working at the Sorbonne, Lapicque replaced the messy biophysics of the nerve membrane with the simplest possible electrical analogue: a parallel capacitor-resistor circuit representing the membrane's capacitance and leakage resistance, charged by an input current until its voltage crosses a fixed threshold, at which point a “spike” is emitted and the capacitor discharges back to rest.
In modern notation, the non-leaky form he wrote down is

With this model Lapicque computed the firing frequency of a nerve fiber resistively coupled to a stimulating electrode held at fixed voltage, a calculation that \citeauthor{abbott1999lapicque}, writing in \citeyear{abbott1999lapicque} \cite{abbott1999lapicque}, calls a “remarkable achievement” given that it was made long before the mechanisms responsible for action-potential generation were known.

The achievement, Abbott argues, “stresses that, in neural modeling, studies of function do not necessarily require an understanding of mechanism”: significant progress is possible if a phenomenon is adequately described, even if its biophysical basis cannot yet be modeled.

He further notes that the model's enduring utility comes from the **separation of time scales** between the extremely rapid action potential and the slower processes, synaptic integration, bursting, and adaptation, so that today one avoids recomputing the voltage trajectory during a spike and concentrates instead on the computation-relevant dynamics.

Even with Hodgkin and Huxley's 1952 conductance-based models available, the simple integrate-and-fire cell remains adequate for many purposes and has been used in simulations of networks containing hundreds of thousands of neurons; Abbott observed at the close of the twentieth century that “the utility of this model, devised early in the 20th century, is likely to last well into the 21st” \cite{abbott1999lapicque}.
So strictly speaking, the often-cited McCulloch-Pitts cell of 1943 is *not* the first artificial neuron; it is the first **logical** one.
Lapicque's integrate-and-fire came first, and is still the workhorse of modern spiking networks.
Long before digital computers existed, physicists \citeauthor{lenz1920} and his student \citeauthor{ising1925} introduced what is now recognized as the first recurrent neural network architecture .

The Ising model describes a lattice of nodes (spins) with feedback connections, where each node influences its neighbors, and the system settles into an equilibrium state in response to input conditions.
While it was designed to model ferromagnetism, not computation, its mathematical structure is identical to that of later associative memory networks.

In \citeyear{amari1972}, \citeauthor{amari1972} made this recurrent architecture adaptive , enabling it to learn to associate input patterns with output patterns by changing its connection weights, creating the first published learning recurrent neural network.
Ten years later, the basic equations of Amari's network were republished and its storage capacity analyzed under the name “Hopfield Network.”
Logician and psychologist Walter Pitts (\cite[Pitts, 1954]{walter_pitts_photo})
The mathematical birth of Artificial Intelligence did not start with silicon or vacuum tubes, but with the realization that nervous activity could be described as a logical calculus.

Strictly speaking, the first formal neuron model was \citeauthor{lapicque1907}'s integrate-and-fire cell of \citeyear{lapicque1907} (see the aside above); the work of \citeauthor{mccullochpitts1943} that follows is the first **logical** neuron, which is what most histories of AI mean when they speak of “the first artificial neuron.” But the standard story treats 1943 as a sudden founding.

\cite[Abraham's archival study]{abraham2002physio} shows something more interesting: the paper grew out of a specific Chicago milieu: Rashevsky's mathematical biophysics, McCulloch's cortical neurophysiology, Pitts's symbolic logic, and a philosophical program that ran from Northrop's axiomatic biology to von Domarus's psychiatry.

Pitts's own first paper, “Some observations on the simple neuron circuit” (1942), had appeared in Rashevsky's *Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics*, the same journal where \citeauthor{steadystates}'s steady-state theory of nerve nets was being worked out; the 1943 paper itself cites no neurophysiologist at all (\cite{pittsfirstpaper, steadystates, mccullochpitts1943, abraham2002physio}).
Warren Sturgis McCulloch was born on 16 November 1898 in Orange, New Jersey, into a family of Scottish descent.

His mother, Mary Hughes Bradley, was devoutly Episcopalian and hoped he would enter the ministry; at the Carteret Academy he memorised poetry and set up a basement laboratory for what he later called “endless experiments, some with happy, others with catastrophic results.” In 1917 he entered Haverford College, a Quaker liberal-arts college near Philadelphia, where the philosopher Rufus M.
Jones encouraged his interest in mathematics and philosophy.
He moved to Yale for the Navy's officers' training programme (he never saw active service) and took a philosophy major with psychology; at Columbia he took an M.A.

in psychology with a thesis on “dynamic symmetry,” Jay Hambidge's claim that the golden-section rectangle is the most pleasing proportion, which McCulloch tested on fellow students with picture cards.
In 1924 he married Ruth “Rook” Metzger; they bought a run-down farm in Old Lyme, Connecticut, which became first a children's summer camp and then a working farm.
From 1932 he worked at Rockland State Hospital, where he met Eilhard von Domarus and began to treat psychiatric illness as a logical disturbance.
Six years in Dusser de Barenne's laboratory at Yale followed; in 1941 he moved to the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute, where he met Jerome Lettvin and Walter Pitts.
He chaired the Macy conferences, moved to MIT's Research Laboratory of Electronics in 1952, and died in Old Lyme on 24 September 1969, leaving his body to Yale.
Ralph Gerard's obituary called him a “rebel genius” (\cite[Abraham, 2016]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
The question he said drove him, “What is a number, that a man may know it, and a man, that he may know a number?”, he later dated to a conversation with a teacher at Haverford in 1917.

Abraham treats that origin story with caution: McCulloch was an intellectual showman who constructed his autobiography over decades, and the anecdote is best read as a retrospective framing of the epistemological question, not as a verbatim memory (\cite{mcculloch1965embodiments, abraham2016rebelgenius}).
The paper's intellectual home was the mathematical-biophysics group at the University of Chicago, even though the byline names the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute.
The reason the paper exists at all was a Russian theoretical physicist named Nicolas Rashevsky (1899-1972).

Rashevsky arrived in Chicago in 1934 and set out to build a mathematical biology on the model of mathematical physics: begin with deliberately idealized systems, the biological equivalents of the physicist's “material point” and “ideal fluid”, and approach real organisms asymptotically.
In 1939 he founded the *Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics*, initially a supplement to *Psychometrika*, and around him gathered Alston S.
Landahl, and the young Walter Pitts.
Their nerve-net models were written in differential equations, with continuous excitation and inhibition.
McCulloch and Pitts published in that Bulletin, and their move was a discrete turn within it.
Where Rashevsky modeled the graded electrical state of the membrane, they took the all-or-none law literally and replaced the differential equations with propositional logic.
McCulloch later said that they were able to publish “thanks to Rashevsky's defense of logical and mathematical ideas in biology” (\cite[Abraham, 2002]{abraham2002physio}).

The contrast is the point: the 1943 paper was not Rashevsky's biophysics dressed in logic, but a logical turn inside the space Rashevsky had opened (\cite{rashevsky1936psychometrika, abraham2002physio}).
McCulloch's half of the collaboration was empirical.

At Yale he spent six years in the laboratory of the Dutch physiologist Johannes Gregorius Dusser de Barenne (1885-1940), who mapped functional connections in the cerebral cortex by applying small squares of paper soaked in strychnine (“chemical neuronography”) instead of the usual electrical stimulation.

McCulloch co-authored more than twenty papers with him, and the lab's program was exactly what McCulloch meant by “experimental epistemology”: a physiological theory of knowledge, not a philosophical one.

When Dusser died in 1940, McCulloch moved to the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute in Chicago, invited by Percival Bailey, and it was there, as professor of psychiatry, that he met Pitts (\cite{abraham2002physio, abraham2003mcculloch}).
McCulloch's question was epistemological before it was computational.

In the 1920s he set out to invent “a kind of least psychic event, or ‘psychon’” with four properties: it either happens or does not; it happens only if its bound cause has happened, so that it implies its temporal antecedent; it proposes this to subsequent psychons; and psychons compound into the equivalents of more complicated propositions.
Around 1929 he realized that the all-or-none impulse of a neuron fit the description.
The 1943 paper says it outright: “a psychon can be no less than the activity of a single neuron” (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}).
The logical neuron is therefore not a metaphor for the mind; it is McCulloch's candidate for the atom of experience (\cite{mcculloch1965embodiments, abraham2002physio}).
The psychiatric route into the paper is easy to miss.
In 1932 McCulloch was training at Rockland State Hospital, where he met the German-born psychiatrist Eilhard von Domarus (1893-1958).
Von Domarus had written a Yale dissertation under F.

Northrop, *The Logical Structure of Mind* (\cite[Von Domarus, 1930]{domarus1930logicalstructure}), with McCulloch's help, and in 1939 he presented “The specific laws of logic in schizophrenia” (\cite[Von Domarus, 1944]{domarus1944specificlaws}), arguing that delusional thought follows its own inferential rules.

Northrop, a philosopher of science at Yale, held that every empirical science matures from an inductive, descriptive stage into a deductive, axiomatic one; biology, he thought, was making that transition through J.
Woodger's *The Axiomatic Method in Biology* (\cite{woodger1937axiomatic}) and Rashevsky's mathematical biophysics.
McCulloch moved in that circle (he also attended Clark Hull's Wednesday-evening seminar at Yale in 1936), and the result is a paper that treats mental illness as a logical disturbance.

Its final section lists tinnitus, paraesthesias, hallucinations, delusions, confusion and disorientation as what happens when the net is altered, and concludes that “diseased mentality can be understood without loss of scope or rigor, in the scientific terms of neurophysiology” (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}; \cite{northrop1931sciencefirstprinciples, abraham2002physio}).
Walter Pitts grew up in a tough family in Prohibition-era Detroit.
His father, a boiler-maker, wanted him out of school and at work; Pitts taught himself Greek, Latin, logic and mathematics in the public library instead.
At twelve he read all three volumes of *Principia Mathematica*, found mistakes in it, and wrote to Bertrand Russell; Russell replied and invited him to Cambridge, but Pitts was too young to go.
At fifteen he ran away from home, headed for Chicago to hear Russell lecture, and never saw his family again.
He was homeless, self-taught and without a degree when he met McCulloch \cite{gefter2015pitts}.

Neil Smalheiser, who collected reminiscences of Pitts, calls him a “shadowy folk hero” of the brain-as-computer idea, a man who helped change several fields and was then largely forgotten \cite{smalheiser2000pitts}.
What they discovered in their first conversation was a shared hero: Gottfried Leibniz, whose “alphabet of human thought” promised to encode concepts as symbols and combine them by logical rules.
McCulloch was trying to build a Leibnizian calculus for the brain; Pitts knew the logic needed to make it work (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).
Warren McCulloch came from a well-to-do East Coast family of lawyers, doctors, theologians and engineers.
He studied mathematics at Haverford, philosophy and psychology at Yale, and medicine at Columbia.

Tara Abraham's biography calls him an “intellectual showman” who adopted many identities: philosopher, poet, neurologist, neuropsychiatrist, cybernetician, mentor, engineer \cite{abraham2016rebelgenius}.

Gefter's portrait describes him as a “confident, gray-eyed, wild-bearded, chain-smoking philosopher-poet who lived on whiskey and ice cream and never went to bed before 4 a.m.” He wrote poetry, hosted bohemian evenings at his farm in Old Lyme, where he also designed buildings and a dam, and posted a sign on the door of his MIT lab reading “Experimental Epistemology.” When he met Pitts, he invited the homeless teenager to live with his family in Hinsdale.

The house was a bohemian salon of Chicago intellectuals, poetry, radical politics and Spanish Civil War songs; late at night, after the household had gone to bed, the two worked on a logical model of the brain \cite{gefter2015pitts}.
“Experimental Epistemology” was not a joke.
McCulloch wanted to know what it means to know, and he treated the brain as the place where that question could be answered experimentally.
Raised in a family of theologians and trained in philosophy before medicine, he never saw the mind as a merely technical problem.

His essays were collected in *Embodiments of Mind* (1965), and one of them asks the question that drove him: “What is a number, that a man may know it, and a man, that he may know a number?” \cite{mcculloch1965embodiments}.

Abraham's study of his years at the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute argues that the 1943 paper grew out of this project (out of a mathematical treatment of biological problems, not out of a plan to build a thinking machine) and that his identities as neuropsychiatrist and cybernetician were inseparable \cite{abraham2003mcculloch, abraham2016rebelgenius}.

His 1945 paper “A Heterarchy of Values Determined by the Topology of Nervous Nets” made the point that value is not a hierarchy: depending on the state of the network, A can be preferred to B, B to C, and C to A \cite{mcculloch1945heterarchy}.
Pitts supplied the mathematics McCulloch lacked: modular arithmetic for the loops, and the propositional calculus for the logic.

Their 1943 paper gave the field its first logical neuron and, in McCulloch's words, let him say “for the first time in the history of science, we know how we know” \cite{gefter2015pitts, mccullochpitts1943, abraham2002physio}.
McCulloch called Pitts his “bootlegged collaborator” and wrote of him, “Would I had him with me always.” Pitts called McCulloch's house home for the rest of his life.
Both men wrote poetry; a poem of Pitts's, “On Quantity of Information,” survives in McCulloch's papers.
The paper's influence ran wider than the perceptron.

Wiener was so impressed that he promised Pitts a PhD at MIT even though Pitts had never finished high school; in 1954 Fortune named Pitts one of the twenty most talented scientists under forty, alongside Claude Shannon and James Watson \cite{gefter2015pitts}.

Inside the group his authority was absolute: McCulloch wrote that none of them would publish a paper without Pitts's corrections and approval, and Lettvin called him “the genius of our group” (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).
Pitts had struggled with depression for years.

He described it to McCulloch as a “melancholy apathy” that made “the positive value seem to disappear from the world,” and traced it partly to an “excessively logical education” that left him unable to believe in induction: “one cannot prove,” he wrote, “that the sun should rise tomorrow.” His dissertation was an attempt to make the logical brain statistical: since genes cannot specify the brain's trillions of synapses, he reasoned, the brain might start as a random net and let experience alter thresholds until order emerged (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).

Two blows deepened the depression: a break with Norbert Wiener, who had been a father figure, and the frog's-eye experiments, which showed that the retina already extracts contrast, curvature and movement before the brain gets involved, evidence that the brain was not the clean logical machine he had modeled.
The experiments became “What the Frog's Eye Tells the Frog's Brain” (1959), by Lettvin, Maturana, McCulloch and Pitts (\cite{lettvin1959frog}).

The byline is misleading: the year of single-fibre recording was Lettvin's and Maturana's work, and McCulloch and Pitts joined the paper, in Lettvin's recollection, largely out of respect (\cite[Abraham, 2016, pp.
163-164]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).

The break with Wiener has been traced, in secondhand accounts, to a story his wife told him about Pitts and Lettvin; Wiener never asked them, and never spoke to Pitts again (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).
He began drinking heavily, refused to sign the paperwork for his doctorate on probabilistic three-dimensional neural networks, burned the manuscript and his notes, and withdrew from nearly everyone.
McCulloch died four months later, in September 1969 \cite{gefter2015pitts, smalheiser2000pitts}.
The paper runs in two directions.
Given a net, one can read off the propositions its activity realizes; given a logical expression, one can build a net that realizes it.
*Nets without circles* compute Boolean functions of the afferents.

*Nets with circles* can hold a state, and McCulloch and Pitts argued that such a net, furnished with a tape and scanners, can compute exactly the numbers a Turing machine can, and that some of them it can compute without tape or scanners.
The bibliography is a giveaway.

The paper cites Carnap's *Logical Syntax of Language* (\cite{carnap1938logicalsyntax}), Hilbert and Ackermann's *Grundzüge der theoretischen Logik* (\cite{hilbert1928entscheidung}), and Russell and Whitehead's *Principia Mathematica* (\cite{russell1910principia}), and no neurophysiologist at all (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}).
The physiology is in the assumptions; the argument is in the logic.
The same calculus then carries the paper into psychiatry: if the net is the mind, a changed net changes the facts.

Tinnitus, paraesthesias, hallucinations, delusions, confusion and disorientation are, in the paper's words, what happens when “our nets are undefined”, and the psychiatrist is told that “diseased mentality can be understood without loss of scope or rigor, in the scientific terms of neurophysiology” (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}).
McCulloch and Pitts's “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity” appeared in the *Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics* 5 (1943), 115-133, not in a physiology journal.

statements.quote: The \citealternativetitle{wienerajedrecista}, a chess playing machine first demonstrated in 1914, invented by Leonardo Torres Quevedo.

Before the term “Artificial Intelligence” existed, the Spanish engineer \citeauthor{torres1914} built the first working AI system: **El Ajedrecista**, an electromechanical chess endgame player capable of automatically checkmating a human opponent with king and rook against king \cite{torres1914}.
Back then, chess was considered an activity restricted to the realm of intelligent creatures.

Torres Quevedo wanted to redefine what we mean by “thinking,” demonstrating that machines could make choices from a complex set of relational possibilities without human intervention \cite{ieeespectrum2023chess}.

The machine's sensing system used a chessboard where each of the 64 squares consisted of three metallic pieces separated by insulating material: a circular central piece connected to the positive terminal and two triangular side pieces connected to horizontal and vertical conductors.
The black king's silver mesh base closed two electrical circuits upon placement, driving sliding bars to positions encoding its coordinates; four additional bars tracked the white pieces similarly.

The decision logic, implemented via battery-driven relays in a tree structure, partitioned the board into three zones (left: a-c files; center: d-e files; right: f-h files) and selected one of six operations based on the relative positions of the pieces, whether the black king shared a zone with the rook, the vertical distance between pieces, and the parity of horizontal separation \cite{torres1914}.

Actuation was achieved through eight electro-mechanical actuators using a disc-and-pawl mechanism: when an electromagnet released the pawl, one full disc rotation executed a mechanical “microprogram” for a specific piece movement.
In the upgraded 1920 version, electromagnets concealed beneath an ordinary chessboard moved the white pieces, and a gramophone announced *jaque al rey* (check) or *mate* (checkmate).
If the opponent made three illegal moves, the machine shut down \cite{ieeespectrum2023chess}.
While the algorithm was suboptimal, it guaranteed checkmate in fewer than 63 moves against any defense \cite{ieeespectrum2023chess}.

The machine was still considered impressive decades later when AI pioneer Norbert Wiener played against it at the 1951 Paris conference on calculating machines and human thought \cite{torres1914} \cite{ieeespectrum2023chess}.

Before the chess machine, the same inventor had already been building **analog calculating machines** (*máquinas algébricas*) from 1895, using floating-point arithmetic to compute the roots of polynomials up to the eighth degree, complex ones included, to a thousandth of a unit, an early rival to the purely mechanical path that ran from Babbage to the digital computer (\cite[Thomas, 2008]{thomas2008torres}).
\citealternativetitle{mechanicalturkimage}, shown here in Joseph Racknitz's 1789 reconstruction, wrong about the details, right that a person sat inside.
Above, we met the first *practical* chess machine (1914).
A century and a half before it, an earlier automaton had already captivated the world, and fooled it, for 84 years.
In **1770** the Hungarian inventor **Wolfgang von Kempelen** unveiled the **Mechanical Turk**, a life-sized figure that appeared to play a strong game of chess by itself.

It was, in fact, the most elaborate con in the history of the field: a hidden human grandmaster sat inside the cabinet, moving the pieces by levers and magnets, and the "memory" that let it beat any single challenger again and again was simply the size of a human brain.

Yet it toured for 84 years, won most of its games, including, it was claimed, against **Napoleon Bonaparte** and **Benjamin Franklin**, and was not destroyed by fire until **1854** (\cite[Mechanical Turk, Wikipedia]{mechanicalturk}).
The Turk matters for the history of AI for the opposite reason to its trick.

It is the first machine the public was asked to *believe* could reason, and its test (can it hold its own in a real contest against a real person, over and over?) is the ancestor of the challenge-based test that would, a century and a half later, be formalized as the **Turing test**.

The Turk could even *chat*: between games it answered questions from the crowd on a letterboard, in English, French, and German, on its age, its "life," and how it worked, a talking head, the direct descendant of Roger Bacon's brazen head.

When the mechanism was finally explained in detail in 1857, the lesson stuck: *to tell a machine that thinks from a person hidden in a box, you need a test that is hard to fake*, the founding question of machine intelligence (\cite[Mechanical Turk, Wikipedia]{mechanicalturk}).
Babbage's encounter with the Turk is the missing link in that story.
In **1819** he played the machine twice and lost both matches.
He suspected the cabinet hid a person, but he did not write the exposé that some of his contemporaries did.
The encounter stayed with him.
In **1864** he recorded in his diary that he had chosen, as a test for his "mechanical notation," "the contrivance of a machine that should be able to play a game of purely intellectual skill ...

chess." There is no mechanical link between the Turk and the Analytical Engine (one was a hoax, the other a real design), but the hoax showed what a machine that *appeared* to think could do to the imagination of the person who would build the first programmable computer (\cite[Standage, 2002]{standage2002turk}).
I was too lazy to calculate by hand.
\citealternativetitle{zusez1}, the first fully automatic programmable Computer, completed in 1938
\citeauthor{zusebook}, a civil engineer tired of manual arithmetic, spent 1936 to 1945 building the first binary computers in his parents' Berlin living room.

His Z-series evolved from the mechanical **Z1**, which used sliding metal plates but suffered from frequent jams, to the **Z3** (1941), the world's first functional, programmable, and fully automatic digital computer.
By switching from mechanical parts to 2,000 electromagnetic telephone relays, Zuse proved that binary electricity was the future of calculation.

He even pioneered the first high-level programming language, **Plankalkül**, while hiding his **Z4** model in the Alps to survive WWII, eventually launching the world's first commercial computer company (\citetitle{zusebook}, p.

Zuse did not directly work on modern AI systems, but together with people like Aiken, based on earlier ideas of Leibniz, Babbage, Llull, and, in parts, of Aristotle, he helped to create the *hardware* AI can run on.

statements.quote: \citealternativetitle{img_walter_tortoise} (\citeauthor{img_walter_tortoise}, \citeyear{img_walter_tortoise}): one of W.
Grey Walter's *Machina speculatrix* tortoises, with its photocell "eyes" and vacuum-tube brain.
Starting in 1948, the British neurophysiologist **W.

Grey Walter** (1910-1977, born in Kansas City, Missouri) built small wheeled machines whose "brains" were simple vacuum-tube circuits: the circuits sensed the environment with photocells and drove the two wheel motors.
Walter gave them the taxonomic name ***Machina speculatrix***, "machine that looks".
The circuits could be arranged so that a machine moved toward, or away from, a light mounted on a sister machine.

The behavior looked purposive, and was often complex and unpredictable, so much so that Walter said it "might be accepted as evidence of some degree of self-awareness" (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
He described the tortoises in a May 1950 *Scientific American* article, "An Imitation of Life", and in *The Living Brain* (1953).

Nilsson calls the *Machina speculatrix* "the beginning of a long line of increasingly sophisticated 'behaving machines'", and Rodney Brooks's behavior-based robotics of the 1980s explicitly drew on the same approach: controlling an animal-like body with simple situation-specific circuits, without internal representations or reasoning (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
Built by **Marvin Minsky** and **Dean Edmonds** in 1951, the **SNARC** (Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator) was the world's first physical artificial neural network.

Between the 1943 neuron papers and the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, a loose, deliberately cross-disciplinary group of mathematicians, neurophysiologists, engineers and anthropologists briefly gave the emerging field a different name: **\citealternativetitle{wiener1948cybernetics}**.
The word is Greek: κυβερνήτης, *kybernētēs*, "the steersman".
Steer a ship and you are running a feedback loop, turning the rudder in response to the effect it already had.

\citeauthor{wiener1948cybernetics} and his circle coined it in the summer of 1947 for "control and communication in the animal and the machine", the one logic shared by a thermostat, a gun's fire-control, and a nervous system \cite{wiener1948cybernetics}.
The word was not Wiener's invention.

The French mathematician and physicist \citeauthor{ampere1843cybernetique}, better remembered for the *ampere* and for the right-hand rule of electromagnetism, proposed, in his unfinished *\citealternativetitle{ampere1843cybernetique}*, a classification of human knowledge in which he imagined two new political sciences, one of which he called **cybernétique**, after the same Greek root κυβερνήτης.
The volume appeared only in \citeyear{ampere1843cybernetique}, seven years after his death in 1836.

Ampère's *cybernétique* was the science of *how* a government steers the state, the science of public administration by means of feedback, the study of how a minister's orders propagate through the bureaucracy and how the resulting reports loop back to update policy.

It was a political science, not a science of machines; but the underlying picture was exactly the one Wiener would later draw on the board at the Macy conferences: a chain of command is a feedback loop, a bureaucracy is a control system, and a nervous system is a more elaborate version of the same thing.
The vocabulary waited more than a century for its subject matter to catch up.

When Wiener finally used it in 1947, he knew he was reaching back to Ampère's term, and he kept the French ending, **cybernetics**, not **governology**, in part because Ampère had already done the work of naming the concept, leaving only the science to be done.
The **Macy Conferences** (1946-1953), ten meetings funded by the Josiah Macy Jr.

Foundation and chaired by **McCulloch**, gave the field its first regular meeting place; their stated aim was "a general science of the workings of the human mind" \cite{macyconferences} \cite{heims1991cyberneticsgroup}.
In Britain the **Ratio Club** did the same thing over dinner in Cambridge \cite{ratioclub}.

Its two founding papers both date to 1943: McCulloch-Pitts (above), and **Arturo Rosenblueth, Norbert Wiener and Julian Bigelow's** *Behavior, Purpose and Teleology*, which modelled purposeful action as negative feedback and asked what "purpose" even means when a machine acts \cite{behaviorpurpose1943}.
Abraham and Heims both describe the Macy conferences as a social experiment as much as a scientific one.
McCulloch was its architect and showman; Frank Fremont-Smith called the cybernetics group “the wildest” of his conference groups.

The shared vocabulary (feedback, purpose, information, Gestalt) was deliberately ambiguous, a strategy Leah Ceccarelli calls strategic ambiguity: it let mathematicians, anthropologists and psychiatrists talk to one another, but it also made agreement hard.

McCulloch recalled that when the word “Gestalt” came up, “five members of the group thought the other twenty were misusing it.” Robert Morison said he had the odd impression of being able to follow almost every sentence without understanding the paragraphs.
By the last meeting in 1953 there was no unified science, only a set of rival programmes.

Andrew Pickering's contrast is useful: the British cyberneticians around Ashby, Grey Walter and Pask were more playful and anti-disciplinary, while the American group around McCulloch and Wiener wanted a disciplined science with predictive laws (\cite{abraham2016rebelgenius, heims1991cyberneticsgroup, macyconferences}).
McCulloch left Illinois for MIT's Research Laboratory of Electronics in 1952, and the move changed what kind of scientist he was.

The most under-rated of the group, the psychiatrist \citeauthor{ashbyintrocybernetics1956}, built a machine to prove his ideas.

His **Homeostat** (1948) wired four scrapped Royal-Air-Force bomb-control units into a maze of feedback; dropped into any state, it mechanically hunted its way back to equilibrium, a "self-organizing" machine that appeared to act with purpose \cite{ashbyhomeostat1948} \cite{ashbydesigndbrain1952}.
\citeauthor{wienerhumaneuse1950} called the emergence of purposeful behaviour in it "one of the great philosophical contributions of the present day" \cite{wienerhumaneuse1950}.

From the same insight came the **Law of Requisite Variety** (1956): a controller can cancel the variety (number of possible states) thrown at it only with its own variety: "only variety can destroy variety" \cite{ashbyintrocybernetics1956}.

Conant and Ashby sharpened this in 1970 into the **Good Regulator Theorem**: every good regulator of a system must be a *model of that system* \cite{conantashby1970}, a prediction that a controller must resemble the thing it controls, made decades before deep learning rediscovered it.
Ashby kept a private notebook of ideas for 44 years: 25 volumes, 7,189 pages, now digitized as the W.
Ross Ashby Digital Archive.

He took correspondence courses in "Effective English and Personal Efficiency" before daring to write his first book, warning: "My fear is now that I may become conspicuous, for a book of mine is in the press." And in 1946 \citeauthor{turing1937} wrote to him suggesting he use the Automatic Computing Engine for his experiments instead of building his own machine.

statements.quote: Before the term “Artificial Intelligence” even existed, **Alan Turing** laid the philosophical groundwork in \citeyear{turing1950computing} with his paper *\citetitle{turing1950computing}*.
I propose to consider the question, 'Can machines think?'
Turing argued that defining “thinking” was too ambiguous.

Instead, he proposed the **Imitation Game** (now known as the Turing Test), an *operationalization*: a behavioral test designed to let the question “Can machines think?” be settled empirically rather than by philosophical argument \cite{hnfturing2020}.
A computer would be considered intelligent if it could converse indistinguishably from a human.
This shifted the goal of AI from replicating biological mechanics to replicating observable behavior.
It is worth being clear, however, about what the test is and what it has come to mean.

The test was never adopted as a formal scientific standard for measuring intelligence, and in modern AI research it is widely regarded as outdated: it probes the ability to *imitate* human conversation, which can be carried by surface fluency, small talk, and brief deceptions (the three classical objections of \citeauthor{levesque2014bestbehaviour} (\citeyear{levesque2014bestbehaviour}): **deception**: the machine must fabricate a human identity, which is not itself a component of intelligence; **conversation**: small talk and parlor tricks can carry a machine to a pass without real reasoning; and **evaluation**: human judges disagree and err), rather than by understanding, reasoning, or world knowledge.
Its historical role is real (it shaped the field's first decades), but contemporary AI evaluation has largely moved to capability-specific benchmarks rather than open-ended mimicry.
A detail in the paper is easy to miss.
In Turing's sample dialogue the computer is asked to add 34,957 and 70,764 and answers **105,621**; the correct sum is **105,721**.
Turing, a mathematician, almost certainly put the error there on purpose.

Elsewhere in the paper he had suggested that a machine could be programmed to "deliberately introduce mistakes in a manner calculated to confuse the interrogator." A perfect calculator gives itself away; a machine that slips is easier to mistake for a person.

The trick has a modern afterlife: **Eugene Goostman** (2014) was said to have passed a version of the test by playing a thirteen-year-old with English as a second language, and Google's **Duplex** (2018) inserted "umms" and "ahhs" into its speech.
In both cases the imitation of fallibility did the work that understanding was supposed to do (\cite[Turing, 1950]{turing1950computing}).

The term “Artificial Intelligence” was coined in the 31 August 1955 proposal for the \citealternativetitle{darthmouthartificialintelligence}, when **John McCarthy**, along with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon, submitted it.

The workshop itself took place in 1956, founded on the conjecture that “every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it,” marking the official birth of the field.
The founding story is tidier than the event.

Crevier, drawing on interviews with the participants, records that the summer project deeply disappointed its organizer: people came for different periods, no consensus emerged on what the field was or where it was going, and most participants returned to their own approaches.

Herbert Simon later estimated that “Dartmouth got only half a dozen people active that weren't before.” Even the name was contested (Samuel thought “artificial” sounded phony, while Newell and Simon kept calling their work “complex information processing” for years), but McCarthy got “artificial intelligence” adopted, and with the label gave the discipline its public identity \cite{crevier1993ai}.

statements.quote: The Dartmouth workshop catalyzed the first wave of AI programs.
**Allen Newell**, **John Cliff Shaw**, and **Herbert A.
Simon** presented the **Logic Theorist** (LT), a program that could prove symbolic logic theorems by searching a space of possible proof steps.

LT successfully proved 38 of the first 52 theorems in the second chapter of Whitehead and Russell's *\citetitle{russell1910principia}* \cite{newell1956logictheorist}, and even discovered a proof for one theorem that was shorter than the one in the original text.

Newell and Simon submitted that proof to the *Journal of Symbolic Logic* with the program listed as a co-author; the editor rejected it on the grounds that proving a theorem in the outmoded system of *Principia* was no accomplishment \cite{crevier1993ai}.

This was the first program to deliberately separate human problem-solving into manipulable symbolic representations, establishing the “physical symbol system” hypothesis that would dominate AI for decades.
Around the same time, **Arthur Samuel** at IBM developed a **checker-playing program** that learned through self-play using what we now recognize as **reinforcement learning**.

The program evaluated board positions through a weighted sum of features (piece advantage, center control, etc.) and adjusted these weights based on game outcomes, improving over time until it could play at an intermediate level, better than its own creator \cite{samuel1959checkers}.
Samuel's work demonstrated that a machine could improve its performance through experience, a foundational principle of modern machine learning.

Building on the Logic Theorist, Newell and Simon released the **General Problem Solver (GPS)** in 1957, designed to mimic the problem-solving protocols of the human brain through “means-ends analysis” \cite{newell1957gps}.
statements.section: The Symbolic Path: Newell and Simon's General Problem Solver

statements.quote: GPS could solve a range of well-defined tasks, from proving logical theorems to solving puzzles, by recursively decomposing the difference between the current state and the goal state into subgoals.

statements.quote: Two programs from the years after Dartmouth showed that the Logic Theorist's search machinery could be pointed at more than logic.

At IBM, **Herbert Gelernter**'s **Geometry Theorem Prover** (1959) proved theorems in Euclidean geometry by working backward from the goal, and, its real innovation, by consulting a coordinate description of the diagram to prune the search: what would have been a million candidate steps for a two-step proof collapsed to twenty-five, and the program could handle proofs up to ten steps.
The program was the first demonstration of what AI would call **model referencing**, the ancestor of every system that reasons against an internal model of its problem \cite{crevier1993ai}.
At MIT, **James Slagle**'s **SAINT** (1961) applied the same goal-directed search to symbolic integration.

Tested on eighty-six problems, many of them from MIT freshman calculus exams, it solved eighty-four, and it was probably the first program to search an **and/or tree**: a goal that splits into subgoals that must *all* be solved, versus alternatives of which only one need be.
Joel Moses later extended SAINT into SIN, which grew into the computer-algebra system MACSYMA \cite{crevier1993ai}.
A \citeyear{poirier2025neat} historical study \cite{poirier2025neat} shows that the Symbolic AI program was never unified to begin with.
From the 1960s through the 1990s, knowledge-representation researchers sorted themselves into two camps that Poirier traces back to a methodological, then an aesthetic, opposition.
The **logicists** (“neats”) gathered around **McCarthy at Stanford** and traced their intellectual lineage to \citeauthor{frege1879}; Frege himself died in 1925 and was never at Stanford.
They pursued McCarthy's program of expressing everyday knowledge in formal, declarative logic and drawing conclusions by predicate calculus.

The **proceduralists** (“scruffies”) gathered around Minsky at MIT and were willing to tolerate paradox, hand-coded heuristics, and incomplete representations in exchange for systems that actually worked on messy problems.
Patrick Hayes, interviewed by Poirier, summarizes the split bluntly: the classical line-up was Minsky versus McCarthy, and he adds that this is very much an oversimplification.
Minsky's 1974 paper “A Framework for Representing Knowledge,” which introduced **frames** as stereotyped data structures, was the scruffy camp's counter-move to pure logic.

By the 1990s most knowledge architects concluded both approaches were necessary, but by then the field had spent two decades unable to deliver commonsense reasoning, and the resulting loss of confidence, not the Perceptrons book alone, is what tipped AI into its first winter.

The neat/scruffy split is also why the Minsky who co-authored the devastating critique of perceptrons was *not*, in this earlier frame, an enemy of neural networks; he was the champion of the *procedural* wing of symbolic AI against McCarthy's *logicist* wing.

statements.quote: \citealternativetitle{img_widrow_adaline} (Public Domain): \citeauthor{widrow1960adaline} with the ADALINE machine, 1963.
While Rosenblatt was modeling the brain, a second tradition was building neural nets as *control instruments*.
\citeauthor{widrow1960adaline}, an electrical engineer who had just joined Stanford after a Ph.D.
in control theory at MIT, wanted neural networks for what he called **adaptive control**: a controller whose own parameters adjust themselves to the plant it regulates.

His **ADALINE** (ADaptive LInear NEtwork) was a single neural element whose adjustable weights were implemented as switchable resistor circuits, and he and one of his students, **Marcian "Ted" Hoff Jr.** (who would a decade later invent the first microprocessor at Intel) built a "memistor" for the weights: a graphite rod on which a thin layer of copper could be electroplated or stripped off, varying its resistance.
The training procedure they developed, the **Widrow-Hoff least-mean-squares (LMS) algorithm** \cite{widrow1960adaline}, is the direct ancestor of the delta rule.
A stack of ADALINEs, a **MADALINE**, was trained by Stanford Ph.D.
student William Ridgway (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
Most of the work was simulation on an IBM 1620; the hardware was the argument that the idea was real.

The first publicly-documented working **multilayer feedforward pattern recognizer with adaptive weights** is \citeauthor{roberts1960perceptron}'s (\citeyear{roberts1960perceptron}) "Pattern Recognition with an Adaptive Network", a 1960 technical report from the **Aerospace Corporation** in El Segundo, California, the same \citeauthor{roberts1960perceptron} who, five years later, would draw the engineering sketch for **ARPANET** and earn a place in the canonical photograph of the ARPA principals.
statements.section: Roberts 1960: The First Multilayer Pattern Recognizer

statements.quote: Roberts's report describes a small *two-layer* adaptive network (a *fixed* feature-extraction layer built of random feature detectors, followed by a *trained* classification layer built of adjustable threshold units) trained on hand-printed letters, and demonstrates that the network learns the classification task end-to-end.
statements.section: Roberts 1960: The First Multilayer Pattern Recognizer

statements.quote: The training procedure was a perceptron-style error-correction rule, but the *architecture* (a non-trainable feature front-end feeding a trainable classifier) is the template that every modern convolutional network still uses, with the random-feature front-end replaced by learned convolutional filters.
statements.section: Roberts 1960: The First Multilayer Pattern Recognizer

statements.quote: The historical weight is two-fold.
statements.section: Roberts 1960: The First Multilayer Pattern Recognizer

statements.quote: First, Roberts's report is the earliest known working *multi-layer* neural-network system: the *x*, *y* retinal coordinates of an image go through a bank of feature detectors (the *first* layer), then through a bank of threshold units with adjustable weights (the *second* layer), and the network as a whole is trained by adjusting only the second layer's weights.
statements.section: Roberts 1960: The First Multilayer Pattern Recognizer

statements.quote: The pattern of *fixed* front-end, *trained* back-end is what the modern convolutional net inherits; the *fully* trainable version came later, with Ivakhnenko's GMDH (1965) and the modern backprop-trained ConvNets of the 1990s.
statements.section: Roberts 1960: The First Multilayer Pattern Recognizer

statements.quote: Second, the report is a small, clean, working example of a *deep* system solving a real visual task at a moment when the field's leading lights were still arguing about whether one layer could solve XOR.

statements.quote: First, it anticipates **AutoML** and **neural architecture search**: the modern recognition that the *operators* the model uses are themselves a variable to be optimised, and that a search over operator space can outperform hand-designed operators once compute is available.

statements.quote: Second, it anticipates the **genetic-programming** line of Koza in the 1980s and 1990s, in which the program *text* itself is the chromosome; Uhr and Vossler's composite operators are a small step away from Koza's full LISP programs, and the evolutionary loop is essentially the same.

statements.quote: Third, and most strikingly for this course, it anticipates the modern **LLM-tool-discovery** line: where a modern agent learns to *use* tools (a calculator, a search engine, a code interpreter) as primitive operations whose compositions the model learns to drive, Uhr and Vossler's system learned to *use* feature operators as primitive operations whose compositions the program learned to drive.

statements.quote: The same structural pattern (*a learner that picks which operator to invoke on which input, with the operators themselves partly plastic*) shows up in three fields (AutoML, GP, agents) sixty years apart, because it is genuinely the right way to delegate work that the programmer does not want to specify by hand.

statements.quote: The thesis's closing survey is a snapshot of how distributed the early-1960s scene already was.

At the Aeronutronic/Ford group someone was building an adaptive neuron, the **MIND** element, on a square-loop magnetic core whose magnetic state encoded connection strength, analog weights in physical hardware.

There were working groups on the limits of **majority logic** (the circuits a fully self-organized perceptron reduces to, Joseph notes), on **front-end feature extraction** (translating raw patterns into a form a classifier can use, the focus of Von Foerster's group at Illinois and of Sebestyen at Litton), and on military applications of the machinery.

And at Stanford, **\citeauthor{widrow1960adaline}** and his student were analyzing the same adaptive systems with the tools of **servo theory**, the \citeyear{widrow1960adaline} *ADALINE* and LMS (delta-rule) line \cite{widrow1960adaline} that eventually leads, through backpropagation, to deep learning.

Joseph's closing note is quietly proud and a little defensive: the field was attracting capable people from many directions, and although Cornell had benefited from all that outside activity, there was no reason to change the direction of the Cornell program in any fundamental way \cite{joseph1961perceptron}.

At the same time, at Sandia Laboratories, **Woodrow Bledsoe** and **Iben Browning** were winning character-recognition work with a rival idea, the **N-tuple method**: project a character onto a 10×15 mosaic of photocells, sample 75 randomly chosen *pairs* of cells, and let the tally of which pairs light up vote for the letter, a statistical template scheme with no learned weights at all that rivaled the perceptron for a decade (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
The same decade produced the most ambitious neural hardware after the Mark I: the **MINOS** systems at the Stanford Research Institute.
(The name comes from Greek mythology: Minos, king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa, who after his death became one of the three judges of the underworld.) Charles A.

Rosen, who was trying to etch microscopic vacuum tubes onto a solid-state substrate, had hired Frank Rosenblatt as a consultant, and Rosenblatt stayed in close contact with SRI because he hoped Brain's new magnetic weight devices could replace the Mark I's motor-driven potentiometers.
Alfred "Ted" Brain's team then built a small network, MINOS, rather than simulating it, because on the IBM 1620 a simulation cycle took 21 microseconds and random-access memory held 60,000 digits.
Army Signal Corps from 1958 to 1967, the MINOS line aimed at a concrete military job: automatic recognition of symbols on maps.

In MINOS II each input image was replicated 100 times through a 10×10 array of plastic lenses, each copy passed through its own optical feature mask, and the resulting 100 binary features fed 63 neural elements with 100 variable *magnetic* weights each; the 63 binary outputs addressed one of 64 equally distant prototype points in a 63-dimensional space, each prototype encoding one symbol category (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).

By the mid-1960s the group, by then called the **Learning Machines Group**, had moved to **MINOS III**: the network's front end had grown to an array of 1,024 lenses, and the net now ran alongside an SDS 910, one of the first computers built with silicon transistors.

Its most successful application, reading hand-printed FORTRAN coding sheets (led by John Munson, Peter Hart, and Richard Duda), achieved just over 98 percent accuracy on a large sample of material the system had never been trained on, and anticipated a design pattern that would dominate for a century: the net ranked the candidate letters for each character with a confidence score, and a **dynamic-programming** pass then chose, among all possible strings, the one with the highest total confidence that was also *legal FORTRAN*.
The neural net proposed, the language vetoed, and search combined the two, the same division of labor a modern OCR pipeline still runs.
The Learning Machines Group ultimately became the SRI Artificial Intelligence Center.
In parallel with the Anglophone debate over the limitations of single-layer perceptrons, deep learning was being developed independently in the Soviet Union.
In \citeyear{ivakhnenko1965}, \citeauthorlastnameand{ivakhnenko1965} published the first general, working learning algorithms for deep multi-layer perceptrons with arbitrarily many hidden layers.

Their method, known as the **Group Method of Data Handling (GMDH)**, incrementally grew and trained layers using regression analysis, pruning superfluous units via regularization on a separate validation set.
By \citeyear{ivakhnenko1971}, Ivakhnenko described a deep learning network with **8 layers**, trained when compute was millions of times more expensive than today.
Their networks learned hierarchical, distributed internal representations of incoming data, two decades before the term “connectionism” became fashionable in the 1980s.

The work remained highly cited and popular well into the new millennium, especially in Eastern Europe, and is surveyed in \citeauthor{schmidhuber2022deep}'s annotated history alongside the Anglophone deep-learning lineage.

A year after Ivakhnenko's GMDH, the Moscow Institute for Information Transmission Problems (IITP, the Soviet Academy of Sciences' centre for cybernetics) produced a different *kind* of Soviet machine-vision contribution.

statements.quote: \citeauthor{bongard1966pattern} (\citeyear{bongard1966pattern}), working alone at IITP, with no team, no GPU, no internet, published a thin monograph, \citetitle{bongard1966pattern}, that introduced what the field now calls the **Bongard problems**: visual analogy puzzles of the form "*here are six pictures that share a feature, here are six that share a different feature, which feature* differentiates them", and demonstrated a small program that learned to *solve* them.
statements.section: Bongard 1966: Learning Visual Concepts from Examples

statements.quote: The program's input was a set of line drawings; its output was the *rule* that distinguished the positive from the negative examples; the test of competence was whether the program could recover the rule on a held-out problem without being told it.
statements.section: Bongard 1966: Learning Visual Concepts from Examples

statements.quote: \citeauthor{bongard1966pattern}'s system used a hand-engineered vocabulary of shape features (closure, intersection, parallel-line counts, eccentricity) and a learned linear classifier to weight the features; the *learning* was a perceptron-style error-correction rule over the classifier weights.
statements.section: Bongard 1966: Learning Visual Concepts from Examples

statements.quote: The system was, in modern vocabulary, a **weakly-supervised shape-analogy learner**: given only labels of which examples were positive and which were negative, it had to discover the visual concept that separated them.
statements.section: Bongard 1966: Learning Visual Concepts from Examples

statements.quote: The work is striking for two reasons.
statements.section: Bongard 1966: Learning Visual Concepts from Examples

statements.quote: First, \citeauthor{bongard1966pattern}'s 1966 system is the earliest known example of *programmatic visual-concept learning from examples*, and the structural template it established (a fixed feature front-end, a learned classifier on top, an analogy-test for competence) is what every modern few-shot vision system (matching networks, prototypical networks, CLIP) still uses.
statements.section: Bongard 1966: Learning Visual Concepts from Examples

statements.quote: Second, the **Bongard problems** themselves became a famous benchmark in AI: the original IITP monograph, translated into English in 1970, laid out a collection of 100 problems that became the canonical "Bongard-100" benchmark used to evaluate AI visual-reasoning systems in the 2010s.

statements.quote: Two years after Ivakhnenko's layer-by-layer approach (so around 1967), \citeauthor{adaptivepattern} proposed training multi-layer perceptrons with many layers in end-to-end fashion using stochastic gradient descent (SGD).

His student Saito implemented this in a **five-layer MLP with two modifiable layers**, which learned internal representations to classify non-linearly separable pattern classes, demonstrating that hidden units could discover useful features without explicit human engineering.
This was achieved when compute was billions of times more expensive than today, and predates the popularization of backpropagation by nearly two decades.
In 1967, Shunichi Amari made a foundational contribution to the theory of adaptive pattern classifiers in \citetitle{adaptivepattern}.
His work addressed the problem of determining the optimal weight vector of linear pattern classifiers under general, potentially non-separable pattern distributions.

Amari proposed a “probabilistic-descent method,” in which a correction vector is associated with each misclassified pattern such that, on average, the correction moves the discriminant function toward the optimum, even though any individual trial may worsen it.

He proved that the weight vector converges to the optimal solution and revealed an important tradeoff between the speed and accuracy of convergence: a larger learning constant accelerates convergence but reduces final accuracy, while a smaller one improves accuracy at the cost of slower learning.

He further generalized the theory to multicategory classifiers, piecewise-linear discriminant functions, and general nonlinear classifiers, and even introduced an adaptive scheme for learning the learning rule itself.
\citealternativetitle{img_warren_weaver} (Public Domain, \citeauthor{img_warren_weaver}, \citeyear{img_warren_weaver}): seven years before his 1947 letter proposing machine translation.

Machine translation was one of the first uses proposed for computers beyond numerical calculation: word dictionaries could be stored in memory, and a machine could look up English equivalents for foreign words.

In 1947, the mathematician and science administrator **Warren Weaver** wrote to **Norbert Wiener** asking whether a digital computer might translate between natural languages; Wiener, who had spent the war predicting where aircraft would be, was unconvinced: the boundaries of words in different languages, he replied, are "too vague" and their connotations "too extensive" for any quasi-mechanical scheme to hope on.
The New York Times got there first in print: on May 31, 1949, it reported that a new "electric brain" under construction at the National Bureau of Standards laboratory (Harry D.

Huskey's team at the University of California's Institute of Numerical Analysis) would be "capable not only of performing complex mathematical problems but even of translating foreign languages," by holding the 60,000 words of the Webster Collegiate Dictionary with equivalents in as many as three foreign languages.
The machine had not yet translated anything, and the next day's editorial doubted it could: how would it know whether French "pont" meant "bridge" or "deck"?

By July 1949, Weaver had elaborated the idea into a memorandum, "Translation", which he sent to some 200 colleagues, and which is generally credited with initiating the field of **machine translation (MT)** (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
The first demonstration came faster than the skeptics expected.

On January 7, 1954, a collaboration between **IBM** and **Georgetown University**, running on the IBM 701, translated short Russian sentences into English for a press audience (\cite{georgetown_ibm_1954}): a woman who "didn't understand a word of the language of the Soviets" punched *Mi pyeryedayem mislyi posryedstvom ryechyi*, and the machine printed "We transmit thoughts by means of speech" at two and a half lines per second.
The funding surge that followed ran for a decade before crashing against the wall **Yehoshua Bar-Hillel** had already identified: a translating machine needs *world knowledge*.

His example was a child who finds his toy box, "the box was in the pen", and a machine that knows only the two dictionary senses of *pen* cannot tell a writing instrument from a playpen, unless it also knows the relative sizes of pens, toy boxes, and pens.

He concluded that fully automatic high-quality translation was infeasible "not only in the near future but altogether", and called the prospect of equipping computers with the required encyclopedic knowledge "utterly chimerical" (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).

The field's first winter was bureaucratic rather than mathematical: the US **ALPAC** report concluded that there was "no immediate or predictable prospect of useful machine translation", and large-scale funding vanished, leaving what MT's historian W.
John Hutchins called the **"quiet decade"** (1967-1976).
The American exception was **Systran**, built by **Petr Toma**, a Hungarian-born scientist from the Georgetown team: he founded Latsec in La Jolla in 1968, took a U.S.

Air Force contract, and tested the system at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in 1969, where it "continues to provide Russian-English translations", its promoters claimed, for the Air Force's Foreign Technology Division to this day.

By Margaret Boden's reckoning, Systran's intelligibility rose from 45% (1976) to 78% (1978), against 98-99% for human translators, and post-editing a page of its output took twenty minutes where a human translation took an hour.
Machine translation, in other words, never died: it learned to survive as a tool for post-editors, until statistics and then neural networks carried it across the finish line.

The Pāṇinian line of structural linguistics reaches its otherworldly culmination in a single short book, \citetitle{tesniere1959deps} (\citeyear{tesniere1959deps}), written by the French linguist \citeauthor{tesniere1959deps} (\citeyear{tesniere1959deps}) and published posthumously five years after his death.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: Tesnière's central claim is that the basic unit of syntactic description is not the **phrase** (as in Pāṇini's phrase-structure rules and in Chomsky's later constituent-structure trees) but the **dependency relation**: a directed link from a *governor* word to a *dependent* word.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: A sentence is, on this view, a **stemma**: a tree of word-to-word dependencies, with the main verb at the root and each word hanging directly off the word whose meaning it modifies, with no intermediate phrasal nodes.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: A simple sentence like "the cat sat on the mat" is one verb (*sat*) with three dependents (*the cat*, its subject; *on the mat*, its prepositional complement), each of which carries its own dependents (*the* on *cat*, *the* on *mat*).
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: What is striking about Tesnière's framework is how much modern NLP silently inherits from it.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: Constituent-structure trees dominated the syntactic theory of the 1960s-80s and underlie most formal grammars, but the dependency view turned out to be a better match for the kinds of *local* relations that matter in practice (who is the subject of which verb, which noun does a pronoun refer to, which preposition links which argument), and modern dependency parsers now dominate the field.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The Stanford, Universal Dependencies, spaCy, and Stanza parsers all produce exactly Tesnière's dependency trees, with typed governor→dependent relations like `nsubj`, `dobj`, `amod`, `prep`; Universal Dependencies' 200+ typologically diverse languages are precisely the kind of cross-linguistic coverage Tesnière would have wanted.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The two are also formally equivalent in a precise sense: a constituent-structure tree can be derived from a dependency tree (by collapsing chains of head-dependent relations into phrasal nodes), and a *projective* dependency tree can be derived from a constituent-structure tree (by reading off the head of each constituent).
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The difference is not in *what can be expressed*; it is in *what is taken as primitive*, and on that question, the modern NLP field has voted for Tesnière.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The deeper lesson is methodological.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: Tesnière's book appeared in 1959, only two years after Chomsky's *Syntactic Structures* (1957) and before Chomsky's constituent-structure frame had become dominant in generative linguistics, but the dependency idea was not new with him; it had been sketched by the Sanskrit grammarians, by the Roman *modistae*, and by Lucien Tesnière's own predecessors.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The reason the framework is taking *forty years* to mature in NLP is partly that the computational tools needed to parse at scale (transition-based parsers, neural parsers, large dependency-banks) only became available in the 2000s, and partly that the *training data* (sentences annotated with dependency relations) only became widely available in 2014 with the Universal Dependencies project.
statements.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

statements.quote: The progress curve of dependency parsing looks, on the chart, much like the progress curve of every other old AI idea: the framework existed for decades; the right *representation* and *learning algorithm* took decades more; the moment it became usable, every system quietly switched to it.

However, Racter was not the first instance of computer-generated text.

Earlier examples include **Christopher Strachey's** \citetitle{strachey1952} (\citeyear{strachey1952}), which ran on the Manchester Mark I computer and used templates to produce randomized romantic letters, arguably the earliest known computer-generated literary text.

A later example is **Theo Lutz** (1932-2010), a German computer scientist, student of the philosopher-cyberneticist **Max Bense**, and one of the pioneers of what is now called *digital poetry* \cite{lutzobituary}.

His \citetitle{lutz1959} (\citeyear{lutz1959}) ran on a Zuse Z22 at the TH Stuttgart computer center and recombined words from Kafka's *The Castle* according to probabilistic rules, producing what he explicitly called “stochastic texts”:
Nicht jeder Blick ist nah.
Ein Schloss ist frei und jeder Bauer ist fern.
A castle is free and every farmer is far.

Remarkably, Lutz even sketched how such a program could learn: by raising the transition probabilities between subject and predicate whenever a generated sentence was judged “meaningful”, \cite[“the machine has 'learned' in a certain way”]{lutz1959}, preferring certain word combinations over time, essentially a trainable n-gram-style language model proposed in 1959.

These experiments predate Racter by decades and sit at the intersection of combinatorics and language that traces back through \cite[Shannon's]{shannon1948communication} information-theoretic treatment of English as a stochastic process.

statements.quote: Traditional methods for finding optimal flight paths relied on complex differential equations (**Euler-Lagrange**) that were nearly impossible to solve for real-world missions.
They often failed to satisfy “two-point boundary conditions”, meaning you couldn't easily force the math to start at Point A and end exactly at Point B.
\citeauthor{kelley} proposed a **“Direct Method”** (Steepest Descent):
**Start with a guess:** Pick any flight path that hits the start and end points.
**Find the Gradient:** Calculate the direction of steepest improvement (e.g., less time/fuel).
**Stepwise Update:** Shift the path slightly in that direction.
**Iterate:** Repeat until the path converges to the mathematical optimum.
This paper is a foundational application of **Gradient Descent**, the engine of modern AI:
This paper is now recognized as a direct **precursor of backpropagation**.

Kelley's method backpropagated derivative information through standard Jacobian matrix calculations from one “stage” to the previous one, anticipating the core logic of the algorithm that would later be generalized by \citeauthor{linnainmaa1970} in \citeyear{linnainmaa1970} and eventually become the foundation of all modern deep learning.
See also the related early 1960s work of Stuart Dreyfus and Arthur E.
Bryson in control theory.
While AI research suffered through funding winters, the physical substrate of computing was undergoing an explosion.
\citealternativetitle{mooreslaw} describes the observation made by Gordon Moore that the number of transistors in a dense integrated circuit doubles about every two years.
This relentless exponential growth meant that while algorithms remained largely unchanged for decades, the machinery running them became millions of times more powerful.

This “free” improvement in performance is the engine behind \citetitle{sutton2019bitter}: methods that scale with computation (like neural networks) were destined to eventually overtake methods that relied on human cleverness, simply because the hardware kept getting faster.
While the popularization of backpropagation is often credited to the 1980s, its mathematical genesis lies in the 1970 master's thesis of \citeauthor{linnainmaa1970}.
He developed the “automatic differentiation” method, specifically the *reverse mode*, originally to efficiently manage rounding errors in complex computer calculations.
Without explicitly intending it for neural networks, Linnainmaa created the highly efficient algorithm required to calculate gradients in nested functions.
This work serves as the invisible mathematical backbone of modern Deep Learning, allowing error signals to be propagated backward through billions of parameters with minimal computational overhead.
Long before neural networks, a different kind of computing was pushing the hardware forward: the computers that flew.

statements.quote: During the lunar descent of Apollo 11 the AGC began throwing **1201 and 1202 program alarms**: the docking radar was flooding it with interrupt requests and eating about 15% of the machine's resources.
Instead of aborting, the computer's **restart software** gracefully shed the overload, kept the guidance functions alive, and let Armstrong land \cite{tomayko1988spaceflight}.
Sixty years on this is still the textbook example of **fault-tolerant real-time computing**, a property modern autonomous and ML systems quietly depend on.
Computer synchronization proved to be the most difficult task in producing the Shuttle's avionics.
