blocks.quote: The history of AI is not a straight line leading inevitably to the Large Language Model. It is a convergence of ideas from unrelated fields that were never intended to meet. Statistical methods developed by astronomers to map the stars now weigh the next word in a sequence. For example, GPU architectures designed for video games provide the parallel computation required for neural networks, which was never intended for AI use but worked out in the end in favour of it. This document traces the lineage that produced modern LLMs, and tries to check out all paths that lead to it (and where else they lead to). If you want to *see* this convergence, [The Atlas](atlas.php) places every person, place, institution and event of this history as a dot on an interactive globe, with the threads between them.
The Abstraction of Labor: From Wheels to Thought
blocks.section: The Abstraction of Labor: From Wheels to Thought

blocks.quote: We can solve any problem by introducing an extra level of indirection. Any problem in computer science can be solved by adding another layer of abstraction [except, maybe, having too many abstractions].
blocks.section: The Abstraction of Labor: From Wheels to Thought

blocks.quote: The history of machines is fundamentally a history of **abstraction**, where human effort is “drawn away” (\cite[from latin **abstrahere**]{kleinetymology}, p. 4) from the direct task. This began roughly 3.3 million years ago with the \citealternativetitle{lomekwi}, the first stone tools created by ancestors of humans, that later led to the invention of the wheel, which abstracted the friction of the terrain by placing a rotating interface between the load and the ground. This concept of mechanical mediation was radically advanced by **Heron of Alexandria**, whose “automata” and steam-powered *aeolipile* demonstrated that task sequences could be outsourced to the physical logic of a machine (\citeauthor{livingdolls}, p. 16). One of his machines was a cart whose route was preset by a pinned barrel, an early programmable robot by (\cite[Noel Sharkey]{sharkey2007hero}). By introducing these layers, humans stopped performing the action and began managing the mechanism that performs it.
blocks.section: The Abstraction of Labor: From Wheels to Thought

blocks.quote: This trajectory eventually crossed from the physical to the cognitive. As identified by **David Wheeler**, “any problem in computer science can be solved by another layer of abstraction”. Just as the wheel abstracts movement, modern computation abstracts thought, treating reasoning as a formal calculus that can be executed by a machine. Thus, the machine serves as the ultimate “extra level of indirection,” distancing the human from the raw labor of both hand and mind.
blocks.section: The Abstraction of Labor: From Wheels to Thought

blocks.quote: Early Math
blocks.section: Early Math

blocks.quote: Prehistoric Math
blocks.section: Prehistoric Math

blocks.quote: The Lebombo Bone
blocks.section: The Lebombo Bone

blocks.quote: The Lebombo bone, a baboon fibula found by \citeauthor{lebomboboneoriginal} in Border Cave in the Lebombo Mountains on the South Africa-Eswatini border, and dated to approximately 42,000 to 43,000 years ago (c. 41,000 BCE), represents the earliest known instance of “outsourcing mathematical thought to physical objects”. Featuring 29 distinct notches, the artifact is widely interpreted as a tally stick or lunar calendar, probably used to track the moon's phases or menstrual cycles. As a foundational example of “spatial abstraction,” it serves as a prehistoric precursor to modern computation by mapping abstract numbers onto a physical medium.
blocks.section: The Lebombo Bone

blocks.quote: It can be thought of as the earliest surviving external mathematical memory of early humans.
blocks.section: The Lebombo Bone

blocks.quote: The Dolní Věstonice Bone (Wolf Bone)
blocks.section: The Dolní Věstonice Bone (Wolf Bone)

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{wolfbonephoto} (CC BY-SA 3.0, \citeauthor{wolfbonephoto}): the wolf radius from Dolní Věstonice with 55 notches in two groups of 30 and 25, dated to roughly 27,000 years ago
blocks.section: The Dolní Věstonice Bone (Wolf Bone)

blocks.quote: The **Dolní Věstonice bone**, commonly called the **wolf bone** (Czech: *vlčí radius*, “Věstonice notch-stick”), is the radius of a wolf, found in 1936 by **\citeauthor{wolfbone}** at the Upper Paleolithic site of Dolní Věstonice in Moravia, Czech Republic, at the base of Mount Děvín. That site is one of the richest Gravettian settlements known (c. 27,000 to 20,000 BC), famous for the Venus of Dolní Věstonice, one of the oldest fired clay figurines in the world. The 18 cm long bone carries **55 notches** carved in two groups of 30 and 25, separated by two longer marks, and is dated to roughly **27,000 years ago**; a fragment of the head of an ivory Venus figurine lay right next to it. The marks are interpreted as tally marks: some researchers read them as a record of lunar months. What makes the bone remarkable is the *independence* of its invention: the same impulse to “outsource counting to a physical object” shows up, without contact, in south-east Africa (Lebombo, ~43,000 years ago), central Europe (Dolní Věstonice, ~27,000) and again in central Africa (Ishango, ~20,000). Counting devices appear to be a repeatedly convergent human invention rather than a single invention that spread.
blocks.section: The Dolní Věstonice Bone (Wolf Bone)

blocks.quote: The Ishango Bone
blocks.section: The Ishango Bone

blocks.quote: \marginfig{ishango.jpg}{The \citealternativetitle{ishangobonephoto} is one of the earliest known attempts of outsourcing mathematical thought to physical objects, a baboon fibula carved with grouped notches that may encode prime numbers, lunar months, or a tally of goods.}
blocks.section: The Ishango Bone

blocks.quote: The **Ishango bone** is a Paleolithic artifact discovered in 1950 by Belgian geologist \citeauthor{ishangobone} in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Dated to approximately **c. 18,000 BCE**, this baboon fibula predates the Sumerian and Babylonian mathematical records by roughly 15,000 years. It features three columns of grouped notches that exhibit curious mathematical properties, such as a column of prime numbers (11, 13, 17, 19) and groups that sum to 60 or 48, though it is not clear whether the prime numbers are intentional of coincidental.
blocks.section: The Ishango Bone

blocks.quote: Researchers have long debated whether the artifact served as a simple tally, a **lunar calendar** as suggested by \citeauthor{marshackishango}, or a more complex mathematical tool. De Heinzelin's original 1957 publication, \citetitle{ishangobone}, introduced the bone to the scientific community, sparking decades of inquiry into the “mathematical Out of Africa” theory. Modern scholars like \citeauthor{ishango12} continue to investigate its potential use as a primitive “slide rule” or evidence of a base-12 counting system, marking it as a critical precursor to later mechanical calculation aids. It could also have been a counting system, where quantities of something have been represented by notches in the bone. It is not clear exactly what it was used for, though.
blocks.section: The Ishango Bone

blocks.quote: Ultimately, the Ishango bone represents the most significant archaeological indicator of prehistoric mathematical reasoning, and thus is a *very* early precursor to modern computers and AI systems.
blocks.section: The Ishango Bone

blocks.quote: The Number System You Program In
blocks.section: The Number System You Program In

blocks.quote: The digits a machine works with today are not self-evident: they are the accumulation of four separate inventions, each of which once seemed strange. And they are the single most load-bearing fact about "how numbers work" that any programmer relies on:
blocks.section: The Number System You Program In

blocks.quote: Put together, these four moves are the entire arithmetic of the modern machine. An `int` is Babylonian place value on a base-2 (binary) wheel; a `float` is Stevin's decimal with a binary exponent; zero and negative numbers make the number line *complete* so that subtraction and division always have an answer. When a compiler evaluates `float x = 0.1`, it is running a notational technology that took four civilizations and thirty-five centuries to assemble.
blocks.section: The Number System You Program In

blocks.quote: Pingala: the binary before Leibniz
blocks.section: Pingala: the binary before Leibniz

blocks.quote: One more "first" belongs in this chain. The Indian prosodist **Pingala** (c. 3rd to 1st century BCE), working out a system for counting Sanskrit poetic metres, used a device that corresponds exactly to a binary number system, and his combinatorics of metres is an elementary version of the binomial theorem \cite{historyofmath_wikipedia}. In other words, the alphabet of 0 and 1 was being written (literally, in the counting of Sanskrit poetic feet) some two millennia before \citeauthor{leibniz1686calculus} formalized binary notation for the digital age below.
blocks.section: Pingala: the binary before Leibniz

blocks.quote: The Salamis Tablet and the Abacus
blocks.section: The Salamis Tablet and the Abacus

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{salamictablet} from ca. 300 BC, the earliest known surviving counting board
blocks.section: The Salamis Tablet and the Abacus

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{earliestabacusphoto} contains the earliest known depiction of an Abacus
blocks.section: The Salamis Tablet and the Abacus

blocks.quote: The **Salamis Tablet** (c. 300 BC), discovered in 1846 and preserved at the **Epigraphical Museum in Athens**, is the oldest surviving counting board. It utilized a marble slab with etched lines and pebbles, **calculi**, to execute arithmetic through physical manipulation.
blocks.section: The Salamis Tablet and the Abacus

blocks.quote: As noted by \citeauthor{salminictablesource} (\citetitle{salminictablesource}, 1899, p. 393f), this device confirms that modern computation began by reducing thought to a formal calculus executed via a physical interface.
blocks.section: The Salamis Tablet and the Abacus

blocks.quote: The Roots of Formal Logic
blocks.section: The Roots of Formal Logic

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{aristotleandplato} by \citeauthor{aristotleandplato} (\citeyear{aristotleandplato})
blocks.section: The Roots of Formal Logic

blocks.quote: While \citeauthor{aristotleanalytics} is the father of formal logic, his work was the culmination of a tradition beginning with **Zeno of Elea** (c. 460 BC). Zeno is often regarded as the first “logician” for his use of *reductio ad absurdum* to defend his paradoxes. This analytical foundation was further refined by the dialectic methods of **Socrates** and the categorization of ideas by **Plato** (see \citetitle{bochenski}, p. 26f). Aristotle wrote about Syllogisms extensively in \citetitle{aristotleanalytics}, *25b 27* - *26a 2*.
blocks.section: The Roots of Formal Logic

blocks.quote: Aristotle synthesized these influences to create the **Syllogism**, the first system to decouple an argument's structure from its content:
blocks.section: The Roots of Formal Logic

blocks.quote: Or, with concrete details:
blocks.section: The Roots of Formal Logic

blocks.quote: By proving that truth could be derived through the mechanical application of formal rules, Aristotle provided the blueprint for everything from medieval scholasticism to modern computation.
blocks.section: The Roots of Formal Logic

blocks.quote: This transition from philosophical dialogue to a rigid logical calculus paved the way for thinkers to treat thought as a form of algebra. The very word *mathematics* comes from the Greek *μάθημα* (mathema), "that which is learned", and was coined by the Pythagoreans, the first school to study the subject *for its own sake*, not for surveying or taxes \cite{historyofmath_wikipedia}.
blocks.section: The Roots of Formal Logic

blocks.quote: The oldest grammar: Pāṇini (c. 5th to 4th century BCE)
blocks.section: The oldest grammar: Pāṇini (c. 5th to 4th century BCE)

blocks.quote: Western logic was not the only formal science of the ancient world, nor was it the first, if language counts. On the other side of the same landmass, the Sanskrit grammarian \citeauthor{panini_ashtadhyayi} had, around the time of Aristotle or earlier, built the first fully *generative* formal system in history: his **\citealternativetitle{panini_ashtadhyayi}** ("eight chapters") \cite{panini_ashtadhyayi} specifies the entire Sanskrit language with a compact notation of **metarules**, **transformations** and **recursion**, a machinery startlingly close to modern mathematical and later programming-language notation, written down some 2,400 years ago \cite{historyofmath_wikipedia}. Where Aristotle captured *reasoning*, Pāṇini captured *speech*: given his rules, every acceptable sentence is generated and every deviant one rejected: the same logical contract a compiler holds with a programming language.
blocks.section: The oldest grammar: Pāṇini (c. 5th to 4th century BCE)

blocks.quote: That twin founding matters for the story of AI, because it shows the *symbol-manipulation* view of mind was never exclusively Greek. The "if-then" rule-books of the 1970s expert systems, and the recursive grammars that dominated the first decades of computational linguistics, are the direct heirs of Pāṇini's eight chapters; and the grammar the Transformer silently learns while predicting the next token is, in a sense, the same ambition achieved statistically. For the full arc of language-as-formal-system, see the [Language](language) chapter.
blocks.section: The oldest grammar: Pāṇini (c. 5th to 4th century BCE)

blocks.quote: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{antikytheraimage}. A handheld orrery of at least 30 meshing bronze gears recovered from a 1st-century BCE shipwreck, older than any geared technology that would follow it by more than a millennium.
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{antikytherasciam} is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery, often described as the world's oldest known analog computer. It was used to predict astronomical positions and eclipses for calendar and astrological purposes decades in advance. It could also track the four-year cycle of athletic games, including the ancient Olympic Games.
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{pygmalionimage}: the sculptor worshipping the statue Aphrodite will bring to life.
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: Long before anyone wrote a line of code, the Greeks had a myth about the *creation* of an artificial being: the sculptor **Pygmalion** carved an ivory statue so perfect that he fell in love with it, and the goddess **Aphrodite** granted his wish: the statue *came to life* and became his wife \cite[Pygmalion (mythology), Wikipedia]{pygmalionmyth}. It is the oldest and purest expression of the wish that runs through the entire field: that an artefact we build should not merely *compute* but *live*: that the model should become the thing.
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: The myth is the ancestor of every later “the crafted thing gains a soul” story, from the golem (one of the most persistent [AI myths](myths)) to the automata of the Renaissance, and it is why the modern goal of an agent that perceives, decides, and acts in the world is so often phrased as *bringing a machine to life*.
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{zhanghengseismoscopeimage}: the eight-dragon seismoscope of 132 CE.
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: Not every ancestor of AI was meant to *think* or *speak*. In **132 CE**, the Chinese astronomer and engineer **Zhang Heng** built a **seismoscope**: a bronze vessel with eight dragon-headed spouts, each holding a ball poised above a waiting toad. When an earthquake struck far away, the single dragon on the side of the tremor dropped its ball into a toad's mouth, *indicating the direction* of a quake the observer could not feel \cite[Zhang Heng, Wikipedia]{zhanghengseismoscope}. It is the oldest known working **sensor**: a physical system that converts a distant, invisible event (a seismic wave) into a local, readable signal (a ball, falling, in a chosen direction).
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: Sensing is the first half of perception, and perception is the precondition for anything that *acts* in the world. Zhang Heng's bronze vessel, a “peripheral” of 132 CE, is the ancient root of the same idea that today lets a robot detect an obstacle, or a model ingest a signal from its environment, before it can do anything at all.
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: Before there were logic engines, there were *talking heads*. The **brazen head**, a bust of brass or bronze said to sit on the workbench of a medieval scholar, is the oldest known legend of a machine that *answers questions*, and it is a remarkably early sketch of the conversational machine we now call a chatbot.
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{brazenheadimage}. An Elizabethan woodcut from Robert Greene's *Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay* (c. 1590): while Friars Bacon and Bungay sleep, their head speaks, “Time is. Time was. Time is past.”
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: The first written account of such a device is in the chronicle of **William of Malmesbury** (c. 1125), who collected the rumors about the polymath **Pope Sylvester II**: from a stolen book of secrets, Sylvester cast the head of a statue that “would not speak until spoken to, but then answered any yes/no question put to it.” For the next two centuries the same figure re-attached itself to whoever was then the most famous *magus*: **Robert Grosseteste**, **Albertus Magnus**, and above all **Roger Bacon**, who was said to have spent seven years building a head so he could tell whether Britain could be made impregnable by a wall of brass (like the Norse wisdom-head of **Mímir** or the bronze guardian **Talos** of Crete, the brazen head is a *repository of knowledge* that you simply query) (\cite[Brazen head, Wikipedia]{brazenheadwiki}).
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: Read today, the legend is almost uncomfortably close to the architecture of a modern question-answering system. The head is a **passive oracle**: it initiates nothing, and *you* pose the query, the exact turn-taking contract of a chatbot. In its earliest, most disciplined form it is a **binary classifier**, answering only *yes* or *no*. And the most famous version, the Roger Bacon head, is **stateful**: asked its questions in sequence it returns *Time is* (the moment is ripe), *Time was*, then *Time is past* (the moment has gone, the work is lost), so its output depends not just on the question but on the *state of the world*. That is the seed of a model whose answer depends on context, and of a monitoring system that watches a process and *signals the moment a critical threshold is crossed*.
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: The legend also anticipated the *limits* we now attach to intelligent machines. In every telling the builders **miss the decisive instant** (through fatigue or neglect) and the head **explodes, collapses, or is scrapped as useless**. The great 17th-century physician and essayist \citeauthor{brownepseudodoxia} (\citeyear{brownepseudodoxia}) later rationalized the whole episode as a misreading of **alchemy**: the “copper head” was simply the vessel of the Great Work, and “Time is” the moment to seize before the work is irrecoverably lost. The head, modern scholars note, became “a metonymy for the *hubris* of Renaissance intellectuals”, the fantasy of an all-knowing machine that can only be undone by the overreach of the people who built it (\cite[Brazen head, Wikipedia]{brazenheadwiki}).
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: The story never really died. In Dublin, a pub founded in 1198 still trades under the sign of the brazen head, one of the oldest in Ireland; and in 1837 the Viennese magician **Joseffy** built a real mechanical descendant, the singing, jaw-clicking **Skull of Balsamo**, a copper skull that “answered” by clicking its teeth, the last great *mechanical* brazen head before electronics (\cite[Brazen head, Wikipedia]{brazenheadwiki}).
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{brazenheadpubimage}, est. 1198, one of the oldest pubs in Ireland.
blocks.section: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computing

blocks.quote: The idea that logical thought can be mechanically calculated
blocks.section: The idea that logical thought can be mechanically calculated

blocks.quote: The earliest attempt: Ramon Llull
blocks.section: The earliest attempt: Ramon Llull

blocks.quote: Based on earlier ideas (ie. \citetitle{tractatusdespheara}, for displaying astronomical data and inspired by the early-arabic astrological Zairja, as described by \citeauthor{volvelles}), the volvelle by \citeauthor{arsmagnavolvelle}, released in \citeyear{arsmagnavolvelle} was perhaps the first attempt to create combinations of ideas mechanically, and therefore, a precursor to the idea of artificial intelligence, where a physical device can calculate answers through logical means
blocks.section: The earliest attempt: Ramon Llull

blocks.quote: Long before silicon chips, the 13th-century Majorcan mystic \citeauthor{arsmagna} attempted to mechanize thought itself. In his seminal work \citealternativetitle{arsmagna}, he designed a system of rotating, concentric paper circles inscribed with letters representing fundamental philosophical and theological concepts. By turning these wheels, one could generate every logically possible combination of ideas.
blocks.section: The earliest attempt: Ramon Llull

blocks.quote: While it looks like a curious mix of mysticism and combinatorics, it is the first documented attempt to create a universal logical language that generates new knowledge through mechanical operations. Llull believed that systematically combining symbols could “calculate” truth, a direct ancestor of the symbol-manipulation view of intelligence. A Transformer's billions of vector operations are the same principle at an unimaginable scale.
blocks.section: The earliest attempt: Ramon Llull

blocks.quote: A complete guide on how to use the Llullian **Volvelle** as intended by Llull can be found in (\cite[Bonner, 2007]{artandlogicofllull}).
blocks.section: The earliest attempt: Ramon Llull

blocks.quote: Medieval scholar Ramon Llull had quite an interesting life, and has done many things beyond his combinatorial wheels.\sidenote{One of the earliest novels in medieval Europe after antiquity, *Blanquerna* (\citetitle{blanquerna}), was by him: it tells the rise of a monk through the ranks of the church to the papacy. He is also the only person whose writings were condemned as heretical by one pope (Gregory XI., in 1376) \cite[yet whose legacy was later explicitly honoured by another]{arsmagnavolvelle}, Pius IX., roughly five centuries later.} His intellectual range, theology, novel-writing, and combinatorial logic together, is a useful reminder that the boundary between "mystic" and "logician" was much thinner in the 13th century than it is now.
blocks.section: The earliest attempt: Ramon Llull

blocks.quote: Eight centuries later, a \citeyear{zhao2025thinkingmachine} paper \cite{zhao2025thinkingmachine} directly reconstructed Llull's thinking machine for the age of large language models. By mining three compositional axes, Theme, Domain, and Method, from conference papers and combining them via templates inspired by Llull's combinatorial wheels, the authors built a pipeline that generates diverse, grounded research ideas automatically. This modern incarnation demonstrates that Llull's fundamental insight, that new knowledge can be produced through systematic symbolic recombination, remains productive even in the era of deep learning.
blocks.section: The earliest attempt: Ramon Llull

blocks.quote: The work of \citeauthor{arsmagna} inspired \citeauthor{leibniz1686calculus} with the philosophical conviction that human reason itself is a form of computation. In his \citeyear{leibniz1686calculus} work \citetitle{leibniz1686calculus}, Leibniz proposed a universal logical language that would reduce all human reasoning to a series of calculations.
blocks.section: The earliest attempt: Ramon Llull

blocks.quote: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
blocks.section: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz

blocks.quote: If controversies were to arise, there would be no more need of disputation between two philosophers than between two accountants. For it would suffice to take their pencils in their hands, to sit down to their slates, and to say to each other: Let us calculate! (Calculemus!)
blocks.section: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz

blocks.quote: Let us calculate! (Calculemus!)
blocks.section: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{leibnizcc}, begun in 1673 and completed in 1694, was the first calculator able to perform all four arithmetic operations
blocks.section: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz

blocks.quote: Leibniz's vision was revolutionary: he sought to mechanize thought by creating a symbolic system where every concept was represented by a unique number, allowing complex arguments to be resolved with the same algebraic certainty as a math problem. This “Mathesis Universalis” represents the true birth of the mechanical philosophy that underpins AI. Crucially, Leibniz also formalized the binary system, reducing all mathematical logic to the interplay of 0 and 1, providing the literal alphabet for the digital age. It shifted the quest for intelligence from the mystical to the mathematical, providing the logical foundation that would eventually be realized in \citealternativetitle{turing1950computing}.
blocks.section: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz

blocks.quote: The Physical Manifestation: Babbage's Analytical Engine
blocks.section: The Physical Manifestation: Babbage's Analytical Engine

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{babbage}
blocks.section: The Physical Manifestation: Babbage's Analytical Engine

blocks.quote: The transition from Leibniz's theoretical calculus to physical machinery found its most ambitious expression in the work of **Charles Babbage**. Moving beyond his earlier Difference Engine, Babbage conceived of the **Analytical Engine** (c. 1837), a machine that mirrored the architecture of modern computers nearly a century before the electronic age.
blocks.section: The Physical Manifestation: Babbage's Analytical Engine

blocks.quote: The Engine was designed to be powered by steam and constructed from brass and iron. Most importantly, it separated the “Store” (memory) from the “Mill” (the central processing unit). Babbage realized that for a machine to be truly universal, it needed to be programmable via punched cards, a technique borrowed from the Jacquard loom. This allowed the machine to perform different tasks without physical reconfiguration, effectively decoupling the hardware from the logical “software” it executed.
blocks.section: The Physical Manifestation: Babbage's Analytical Engine

blocks.quote: Ada Lovelace: The First Software Architect
blocks.section: Ada Lovelace: The First Software Architect

blocks.quote: While Babbage focused on the mechanical engineering, **Ada Lovelace** provided the conceptual breakthrough that transformed the Engine from a calculator into a computer. In her 1843 “Notes,” she recognized that the Engine's ability to manipulate symbols according to rules meant it could process anything from music to scientific logic.
blocks.section: Ada Lovelace: The First Software Architect

blocks.quote: Lovelace authored what is recognized as the first complex algorithm intended for a machine: a method for calculating **Bernoulli numbers**. She broke the calculation down into a series of iterative steps, anticipating the concept of the “loop”.
blocks.section: Ada Lovelace: The First Software Architect

blocks.quote: Lovelace's genius lay in her understanding of the “Science of Operations.” She saw that the hardware was merely a vessel for the logic, famously stating that the Analytical Engine “weaves algebraic patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves” (\citetitle{lovelacequote}).
blocks.section: Ada Lovelace: The First Software Architect

blocks.quote: The Algebra of Reason: George Boole's Binary Breakthrough
blocks.section: The Algebra of Reason: George Boole's Binary Breakthrough

blocks.quote: \citeauthor{bool1854} achieved what Leibniz had only dreamed of: a formal calculus of the mind. In \citetitle{bool1854}, he reduced Aristotelian logic to algebraic equations, treating truth and falsity as binary variables. This is why `true`/`false` types are still called **booleans**.
blocks.section: The Algebra of Reason: George Boole's Binary Breakthrough

blocks.quote: The foundation of AI rests upon the *Neuron Doctrine*, established by the Spanish neuroanatomist \citeauthor{cajaltextura}. Working in the late 19th century, he used specialized staining techniques to prove that the brain was composed of discrete, individual cells rather than a continuous web, thereby establishing the **Neuron Doctrine**; the **Reticular Theory** was the opposing view, defended by Golgi (\cite{neuron_doctrine_wiki}).\sidenote{Cajal shared the 1906 *Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine* with his former antagonist Camillo Golgi, who had invented the silver-staining technique Cajal used and who continued to defend the Reticular Theory almost to the end of his life. Their joint ceremony in Stockholm is one of the great "discoverer-vs-inventor" confrontations in the history of science: both men used the same method, looked at the same slides, and saw almost opposite things. The cell doctrine won, and that victory is the precondition for every "artificial neuron" ever written down.} His discovery that neurons are the fundamental signaling units of the nervous system is what eventually let us even imagine building one.
blocks.section: The Algebra of Reason: George Boole's Binary Breakthrough

blocks.quote: This shift provided the physical blueprint that would later be digitized into the first artificial neural models.
blocks.section: The Algebra of Reason: George Boole's Binary Breakthrough

blocks.quote: Frege & Russell: The Longing for Determinism
blocks.section: Frege & Russell: The Longing for Determinism

blocks.quote: With \citeauthor{frege1879} and his *Begriffsschrift* (1879), the project of distilling natural language through the sieve of formal logic began: the book introduced **first-order predicate logic** (quantifiers, variables, predicates and functions), the formalism that later became the backbone of symbolic AI and of Prolog; \citetitle{uebersinnundbedeutung} (1892) is a later paper on sense and reference. **Sinn** is the *mode of presentation*, **Bedeutung** the object presented: “Morning Star” and “Evening Star” have different senses but the same reference, the planet Venus (\cite{uebersinnundbedeutung}; \cite{frege1879}; \cite{kowalski1974prolog}). He created the foundation of analytic philosophy: the conviction that thinking is the manipulation of logical symbols. He wrote that logic in a deliberately two-dimensional notation, a vertical **judgement stroke** at the left, a horizontal **content stroke**, quantifier “dimples” cut into the line, and negation as a small vertical tick, a notation that looks more like a circuit diagram than like algebra (\cite{frege1879}).
blocks.section: Frege & Russell: The Longing for Determinism

blocks.quote: A page from \citeauthor{frege1879}'s *Begriffsschrift* (1879). Public domain; scan via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:One_page_from_Frege%27s_Begriffsschrift.png).
blocks.section: Frege & Russell: The Longing for Determinism

blocks.quote: This “Symbolic AI” dominated the field for nearly forty years. It was believed that if we provided the machine with enough “if-then” rules and logical predicates, intelligence would emerge. LLMs are the radical antithesis to this dream: they prove that “sense” (in \citeauthor{uebersinnundbedeutung}'s Meaning) can be simulated through statistical association without ever explicitly defining a single logical rule.
blocks.section: Frege & Russell: The Longing for Determinism

blocks.quote: The earliest roots of modern AI
blocks.section: The earliest roots of modern AI

blocks.quote: The formalization of Neurons
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Louis Lapicque, 1866-1952 (\cite[Lapicque]{lapicque_portrait})
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: The mathematical birth of the neuron model predates McCulloch and Pitts by 36 years. In \citeyear{lapicque1907}, French neuroscientist \citeauthor{lapicque1907} published \citealternativetitle{lapicque1907}, the paper that introduced what we now call the **integrate-and-fire** neuron. Working at the Sorbonne, Lapicque replaced the messy biophysics of the nerve membrane with the simplest possible electrical analogue: a parallel capacitor-resistor circuit representing the membrane's capacitance and leakage resistance, charged by an input current until its voltage crosses a fixed threshold, at which point a “spike” is emitted and the capacitor discharges back to rest. In modern notation, the non-leaky form he wrote down is
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: With this model Lapicque computed the firing frequency of a nerve fiber resistively coupled to a stimulating electrode held at fixed voltage, a calculation that \citeauthor{abbott1999lapicque}, writing in \citeyear{abbott1999lapicque} \cite{abbott1999lapicque}, calls a “remarkable achievement” given that it was made long before the mechanisms responsible for action-potential generation were known. The achievement, Abbott argues, “stresses that, in neural modeling, studies of function do not necessarily require an understanding of mechanism”: significant progress is possible if a phenomenon is adequately described, even if its biophysical basis cannot yet be modeled. He further notes that the model's enduring utility comes from the **separation of time scales** between the extremely rapid action potential and the slower processes, synaptic integration, bursting, and adaptation, so that today one avoids recomputing the voltage trajectory during a spike and concentrates instead on the computation-relevant dynamics.
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Even with Hodgkin and Huxley's 1952 conductance-based models available, the simple integrate-and-fire cell remains adequate for many purposes and has been used in simulations of networks containing hundreds of thousands of neurons; Abbott observed at the close of the twentieth century that “the utility of this model, devised early in the 20th century, is likely to last well into the 21st” \cite{abbott1999lapicque}. So strictly speaking, the often-cited McCulloch-Pitts cell of 1943 is *not* the first artificial neuron; it is the first **logical** one. Lapicque's integrate-and-fire came first, and is still the workhorse of modern spiking networks.
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Long before digital computers existed, physicists \citeauthor{lenz1920} and his student \citeauthor{ising1925} introduced what is now recognized as the first recurrent neural network architecture . The Ising model describes a lattice of nodes (spins) with feedback connections, where each node influences its neighbors, and the system settles into an equilibrium state in response to input conditions. While it was designed to model ferromagnetism, not computation, its mathematical structure is identical to that of later associative memory networks. In \citeyear{amari1972}, \citeauthor{amari1972} made this recurrent architecture adaptive , enabling it to learn to associate input patterns with output patterns by changing its connection weights, creating the first published learning recurrent neural network. Ten years later, the basic equations of Amari's network were republished and its storage capacity analyzed under the name “Hopfield Network.”
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Logician and psychologist Walter Pitts (\cite[Pitts, 1954]{walter_pitts_photo})
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: The mathematical birth of Artificial Intelligence did not start with silicon or vacuum tubes, but with the realization that nervous activity could be described as a logical calculus. Strictly speaking, the first formal neuron model was \citeauthor{lapicque1907}'s integrate-and-fire cell of \citeyear{lapicque1907} (see the aside above); the work of \citeauthor{mccullochpitts1943} that follows is the first **logical** neuron, which is what most histories of AI mean when they speak of “the first artificial neuron.” But the standard story treats 1943 as a sudden founding. \cite[Abraham's archival study]{abraham2002physio} shows something more interesting: the paper grew out of a specific Chicago milieu: Rashevsky's mathematical biophysics, McCulloch's cortical neurophysiology, Pitts's symbolic logic, and a philosophical program that ran from Northrop's axiomatic biology to von Domarus's psychiatry. Pitts's own first paper, “Some observations on the simple neuron circuit” (1942), had appeared in Rashevsky's *Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics*, the same journal where \citeauthor{steadystates}'s steady-state theory of nerve nets was being worked out; the 1943 paper itself cites no neurophysiologist at all (\cite{pittsfirstpaper, steadystates, mccullochpitts1943, abraham2002physio}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Warren Sturgis McCulloch was born on 16 November 1898 in Orange, New Jersey, into a family of Scottish descent. His mother, Mary Hughes Bradley, was devoutly Episcopalian and hoped he would enter the ministry; at the Carteret Academy he memorised poetry and set up a basement laboratory for what he later called “endless experiments, some with happy, others with catastrophic results.” In 1917 he entered Haverford College, a Quaker liberal-arts college near Philadelphia, where the philosopher Rufus M. Jones encouraged his interest in mathematics and philosophy. He moved to Yale for the Navy's officers' training programme (he never saw active service) and took a philosophy major with psychology; at Columbia he took an M.A. in psychology with a thesis on “dynamic symmetry,” Jay Hambidge's claim that the golden-section rectangle is the most pleasing proportion, which McCulloch tested on fellow students with picture cards.
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: In 1924 he married Ruth “Rook” Metzger; they bought a run-down farm in Old Lyme, Connecticut, which became first a children's summer camp and then a working farm. From 1932 he worked at Rockland State Hospital, where he met Eilhard von Domarus and began to treat psychiatric illness as a logical disturbance. Six years in Dusser de Barenne's laboratory at Yale followed; in 1941 he moved to the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute, where he met Jerome Lettvin and Walter Pitts. He chaired the Macy conferences, moved to MIT's Research Laboratory of Electronics in 1952, and died in Old Lyme on 24 September 1969, leaving his body to Yale. Ralph Gerard's obituary called him a “rebel genius” (\cite[Abraham, 2016]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: The question he said drove him, “What is a number, that a man may know it, and a man, that he may know a number?”, he later dated to a conversation with a teacher at Haverford in 1917. Abraham treats that origin story with caution: McCulloch was an intellectual showman who constructed his autobiography over decades, and the anecdote is best read as a retrospective framing of the epistemological question, not as a verbatim memory (\cite{mcculloch1965embodiments, abraham2016rebelgenius}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: The paper's intellectual home was the mathematical-biophysics group at the University of Chicago, even though the byline names the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute. The reason the paper exists at all was a Russian theoretical physicist named Nicolas Rashevsky (1899-1972). Rashevsky arrived in Chicago in 1934 and set out to build a mathematical biology on the model of mathematical physics: begin with deliberately idealized systems, the biological equivalents of the physicist's “material point” and “ideal fluid”, and approach real organisms asymptotically. In 1939 he founded the *Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics*, initially a supplement to *Psychometrika*, and around him gathered Alston S. Householder, Herbert D. Landahl, and the young Walter Pitts. Their nerve-net models were written in differential equations, with continuous excitation and inhibition.
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: McCulloch and Pitts published in that Bulletin, and their move was a discrete turn within it. Where Rashevsky modeled the graded electrical state of the membrane, they took the all-or-none law literally and replaced the differential equations with propositional logic. McCulloch later said that they were able to publish “thanks to Rashevsky's defense of logical and mathematical ideas in biology” (\cite[Abraham, 2002]{abraham2002physio}). The contrast is the point: the 1943 paper was not Rashevsky's biophysics dressed in logic, but a logical turn inside the space Rashevsky had opened (\cite{rashevsky1936psychometrika, abraham2002physio}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: McCulloch's half of the collaboration was empirical. At Yale he spent six years in the laboratory of the Dutch physiologist Johannes Gregorius Dusser de Barenne (1885-1940), who mapped functional connections in the cerebral cortex by applying small squares of paper soaked in strychnine (“chemical neuronography”) instead of the usual electrical stimulation. McCulloch co-authored more than twenty papers with him, and the lab's program was exactly what McCulloch meant by “experimental epistemology”: a physiological theory of knowledge, not a philosophical one. When Dusser died in 1940, McCulloch moved to the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute in Chicago, invited by Percival Bailey, and it was there, as professor of psychiatry, that he met Pitts (\cite{abraham2002physio, abraham2003mcculloch}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: McCulloch's question was epistemological before it was computational. In the 1920s he set out to invent “a kind of least psychic event, or ‘psychon’” with four properties: it either happens or does not; it happens only if its bound cause has happened, so that it implies its temporal antecedent; it proposes this to subsequent psychons; and psychons compound into the equivalents of more complicated propositions. Around 1929 he realized that the all-or-none impulse of a neuron fit the description. The 1943 paper says it outright: “a psychon can be no less than the activity of a single neuron” (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}). The logical neuron is therefore not a metaphor for the mind; it is McCulloch's candidate for the atom of experience (\cite{mcculloch1965embodiments, abraham2002physio}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: The psychiatric route into the paper is easy to miss. In 1932 McCulloch was training at Rockland State Hospital, where he met the German-born psychiatrist Eilhard von Domarus (1893-1958).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Von Domarus had written a Yale dissertation under F. S. C. Northrop, *The Logical Structure of Mind* (\cite[Von Domarus, 1930]{domarus1930logicalstructure}), with McCulloch's help, and in 1939 he presented “The specific laws of logic in schizophrenia” (\cite[Von Domarus, 1944]{domarus1944specificlaws}), arguing that delusional thought follows its own inferential rules. Northrop, a philosopher of science at Yale, held that every empirical science matures from an inductive, descriptive stage into a deductive, axiomatic one; biology, he thought, was making that transition through J. H. Woodger's *The Axiomatic Method in Biology* (\cite{woodger1937axiomatic}) and Rashevsky's mathematical biophysics.
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: McCulloch moved in that circle (he also attended Clark Hull's Wednesday-evening seminar at Yale in 1936), and the result is a paper that treats mental illness as a logical disturbance. Its final section lists tinnitus, paraesthesias, hallucinations, delusions, confusion and disorientation as what happens when the net is altered, and concludes that “diseased mentality can be understood without loss of scope or rigor, in the scientific terms of neurophysiology” (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}; \cite{northrop1931sciencefirstprinciples, abraham2002physio}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Walter Pitts grew up in a tough family in Prohibition-era Detroit. His father, a boiler-maker, wanted him out of school and at work; Pitts taught himself Greek, Latin, logic and mathematics in the public library instead. At twelve he read all three volumes of *Principia Mathematica*, found mistakes in it, and wrote to Bertrand Russell; Russell replied and invited him to Cambridge, but Pitts was too young to go. At fifteen he ran away from home, headed for Chicago to hear Russell lecture, and never saw his family again. He was homeless, self-taught and without a degree when he met McCulloch \cite{gefter2015pitts}. Neil Smalheiser, who collected reminiscences of Pitts, calls him a “shadowy folk hero” of the brain-as-computer idea, a man who helped change several fields and was then largely forgotten \cite{smalheiser2000pitts}.
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: What they discovered in their first conversation was a shared hero: Gottfried Leibniz, whose “alphabet of human thought” promised to encode concepts as symbols and combine them by logical rules. McCulloch was trying to build a Leibnizian calculus for the brain; Pitts knew the logic needed to make it work (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Warren McCulloch came from a well-to-do East Coast family of lawyers, doctors, theologians and engineers. He studied mathematics at Haverford, philosophy and psychology at Yale, and medicine at Columbia. Tara Abraham's biography calls him an “intellectual showman” who adopted many identities: philosopher, poet, neurologist, neuropsychiatrist, cybernetician, mentor, engineer \cite{abraham2016rebelgenius}. Gefter's portrait describes him as a “confident, gray-eyed, wild-bearded, chain-smoking philosopher-poet who lived on whiskey and ice cream and never went to bed before 4 a.m.” He wrote poetry, hosted bohemian evenings at his farm in Old Lyme, where he also designed buildings and a dam, and posted a sign on the door of his MIT lab reading “Experimental Epistemology.” When he met Pitts, he invited the homeless teenager to live with his family in Hinsdale. The house was a bohemian salon of Chicago intellectuals, poetry, radical politics and Spanish Civil War songs; late at night, after the household had gone to bed, the two worked on a logical model of the brain \cite{gefter2015pitts}.
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: “Experimental Epistemology” was not a joke. McCulloch wanted to know what it means to know, and he treated the brain as the place where that question could be answered experimentally. Raised in a family of theologians and trained in philosophy before medicine, he never saw the mind as a merely technical problem. His essays were collected in *Embodiments of Mind* (1965), and one of them asks the question that drove him: “What is a number, that a man may know it, and a man, that he may know a number?” \cite{mcculloch1965embodiments}. Abraham's study of his years at the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute argues that the 1943 paper grew out of this project (out of a mathematical treatment of biological problems, not out of a plan to build a thinking machine) and that his identities as neuropsychiatrist and cybernetician were inseparable \cite{abraham2003mcculloch, abraham2016rebelgenius}. His 1945 paper “A Heterarchy of Values Determined by the Topology of Nervous Nets” made the point that value is not a hierarchy: depending on the state of the network, A can be preferred to B, B to C, and C to A \cite{mcculloch1945heterarchy}.
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Pitts supplied the mathematics McCulloch lacked: modular arithmetic for the loops, and the propositional calculus for the logic. Their 1943 paper gave the field its first logical neuron and, in McCulloch's words, let him say “for the first time in the history of science, we know how we know” \cite{gefter2015pitts, mccullochpitts1943, abraham2002physio}. McCulloch called Pitts his “bootlegged collaborator” and wrote of him, “Would I had him with me always.” Pitts called McCulloch's house home for the rest of his life. Both men wrote poetry; a poem of Pitts's, “On Quantity of Information,” survives in McCulloch's papers.
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: The paper's influence ran wider than the perceptron. Wiener was so impressed that he promised Pitts a PhD at MIT even though Pitts had never finished high school; in 1954 Fortune named Pitts one of the twenty most talented scientists under forty, alongside Claude Shannon and James Watson \cite{gefter2015pitts}. Inside the group his authority was absolute: McCulloch wrote that none of them would publish a paper without Pitts's corrections and approval, and Lettvin called him “the genius of our group” (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Pitts had struggled with depression for years. He described it to McCulloch as a “melancholy apathy” that made “the positive value seem to disappear from the world,” and traced it partly to an “excessively logical education” that left him unable to believe in induction: “one cannot prove,” he wrote, “that the sun should rise tomorrow.” His dissertation was an attempt to make the logical brain statistical: since genes cannot specify the brain's trillions of synapses, he reasoned, the brain might start as a random net and let experience alter thresholds until order emerged (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: Two blows deepened the depression: a break with Norbert Wiener, who had been a father figure, and the frog's-eye experiments, which showed that the retina already extracts contrast, curvature and movement before the brain gets involved, evidence that the brain was not the clean logical machine he had modeled. The experiments became “What the Frog's Eye Tells the Frog's Brain” (1959), by Lettvin, Maturana, McCulloch and Pitts (\cite{lettvin1959frog}). The byline is misleading: the year of single-fibre recording was Lettvin's and Maturana's work, and McCulloch and Pitts joined the paper, in Lettvin's recollection, largely out of respect (\cite[Abraham, 2016, pp. 163-164]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: The break with Wiener has been traced, in secondhand accounts, to a story his wife told him about Pitts and Lettvin; Wiener never asked them, and never spoke to Pitts again (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}). He began drinking heavily, refused to sign the paperwork for his doctorate on probabilistic three-dimensional neural networks, burned the manuscript and his notes, and withdrew from nearly everyone. He died in 1969, at 46. McCulloch died four months later, in September 1969 \cite{gefter2015pitts, smalheiser2000pitts}.
blocks.section: The formalization of Neurons

blocks.quote: What the 1943 paper actually says
blocks.section: What the 1943 paper actually says

blocks.quote: The paper runs in two directions. Given a net, one can read off the propositions its activity realizes; given a logical expression, one can build a net that realizes it. *Nets without circles* compute Boolean functions of the afferents. *Nets with circles* can hold a state, and McCulloch and Pitts argued that such a net, furnished with a tape and scanners, can compute exactly the numbers a Turing machine can, and that some of them it can compute without tape or scanners.
blocks.section: What the 1943 paper actually says

blocks.quote: The bibliography is a giveaway. The paper cites Carnap's *Logical Syntax of Language* (\cite{carnap1938logicalsyntax}), Hilbert and Ackermann's *Grundzüge der theoretischen Logik* (\cite{hilbert1928entscheidung}), and Russell and Whitehead's *Principia Mathematica* (\cite{russell1910principia}), and no neurophysiologist at all (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}). The physiology is in the assumptions; the argument is in the logic. The same calculus then carries the paper into psychiatry: if the net is the mind, a changed net changes the facts. Tinnitus, paraesthesias, hallucinations, delusions, confusion and disorientation are, in the paper's words, what happens when “our nets are undefined”, and the psychiatrist is told that “diseased mentality can be understood without loss of scope or rigor, in the scientific terms of neurophysiology” (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}).
blocks.section: What the 1943 paper actually says

blocks.quote: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: McCulloch and Pitts's “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity” appeared in the *Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics* 5 (1943), 115-133, not in a physiology journal. A companion note in the same volume, by Landahl, McCulloch and Pitts, worked out a statistical consequence of the calculus for nerve nets (\cite{landahl1943statistical}). It was not an instant hit: Marvin Minsky read it as an undergraduate and understood, by his own account, as much of it as he could, and its notation was later criticized as a fusion of Hilbert's and Carnap's symbols (\cite[Abraham, 2002]{abraham2002physio}).
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: Von Neumann had met Pitts through Wiener's Teleological Society, the small wartime group around Wiener and von Neumann (McCulloch, Pitts, Rosenblueth, Bigelow and others) that met at Princeton in early January 1945 and became a precursor of the Macy conferences (\cite{masani1990cybernetical, montagnini2017princeton}). In 1945 his EDVAC report, the first published description of the stored-program computer, cited exactly one paper, “A Logical Calculus”, and proposed building the machine from McCulloch-Pitts-style logic gates, with Pitts's loops as the memory that would hold a program: “An element which stimulates itself will hold a stimulus indefinitely,” he wrote, echoing Pitts. At the 1948 Hixon Symposium, von Neumann gave the McCulloch-Pitts nets their first wide audience and called their theorems “probably the most significant result obtained with the axiomatic method up to now”: “anything that can be exhaustively and unambiguously described ... is ipso facto realizable by a suitable finite neural network” (\cite[Von Neumann, 1951]{vonneumann1951automata}). The relay is worth naming: Pitts, the runaway logician, is the hinge between McCulloch's physiology and von Neumann's computer: he supplied the loops that became memory (\cite{gefter2015pitts, vonneumann, abraham2002physio}). The 1947 follow-up, “How We Know Universals,” applied the calculus to auditory and visual perception and pushed toward invariant representations (\cite{pitts1947universals}).
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: Pitts and McCulloch's 1947 follow-up proposed that the visual cortex extracts an invariant by averaging over a group of transformations (dilations, translations) so that the form “triangle” survives changes in size and position. McCulloch presented the programme at the Hixon Symposium in September 1948 as “Why the Mind Is in the Head,” and the reaction was hostile. Karl Lashley objected that the theory explained a behaviour “that never occurs in the intact organism”; Wolfgang Köhler called its histological assumptions ad hoc and accused McCulloch of using psychological terms “in a diluted sense”; John Eccles said McCulloch's imagination and verbal imagery ran away with the argument. McCulloch's reply, recalled by Seymour Papert, was: “Don't bite my finger: look where I am pointing.”
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: The decisive blow came from inside McCulloch's own laboratory. Donald MacKay built a square that could be expanded, shrunk at any speed, or fed back into the subject's own brain waves; by McCulloch's account it should have destroyed the ability to perceive form, and it did not. Lashley's histological evidence pointed the same way. McCulloch took falsification seriously: “To insist on an error is to insist that there is something to be tested.” The episode is a useful corrective to the usual founder story: the 1943 neuron was a permanent contribution, but McCulloch's own theory of universals was wrong, and he knew it (\cite{pitts1947universals, abraham2016rebelgenius}).
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: Read together, the connections form a circuit: Lettvin introduced Pitts to McCulloch; Rashevsky gave them a journal; Dusser de Barenne gave McCulloch the cortical laboratory; Northrop and von Domarus gave him the philosophical and psychiatric question; Wiener supplied the bridge to von Neumann, first through the Teleological Society and then through the EDVAC; and von Neumann turned the loops into memory and, at Hixon, into a general theory of automata (\cite{abraham2002physio, gefter2015pitts, masani1990cybernetical}).
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: \marginfig{warrenmcculloch_afflictor.jpg}{The 22 September 1948 *Brooklyn Daily Eagle* clipping that reported McCulloch's warning to the Caltech cerebral-mechanisms symposium. Scan: \citealternativetitle{afflictor2014mcculloch}. License not stated by the source.}
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: The *Brooklyn Daily Eagle* reported the same Caltech symposium on 22 September 1948 under the headline “Warns Machines May Some Day Take Over the World.” McCulloch told the audience that machines with “complex mechanical minds” might one day explore the planets without human direction, and that when they became complex enough they “may also become neurotic if badgered by frustration in solving problems.” The dispatch is a useful corrective to the founder story: the same McCulloch who argued that mind is computation also warned, in public, that a sufficiently complex machine might become neurotic under frustration, an early sighting of the worry that machine goals could diverge from ours \cite{afflictor2014mcculloch}.
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: Von Neumann saw the catch early. After “the great positive contribution of Turing-cum-Pitts-and-McCulloch is assimilated,” he wrote to Wiener, “the situation is rather worse than better than before”: the paper had shown, “in absolute and hopeless generality,” that any behaviour could be produced by some neural mechanism, and therefore that a general mechanism gave no clue about the details of the actual neural mechanism. The universality that made the model powerful also made it unfalsifiable as neuroscience, one reason it made “barely a ripple among brain scientists” while it quietly became the blueprint for computing (\cite[Gefter, 2015]{gefter2015pitts}).
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: This breakthrough allowed the brain to be viewed not just as a mysterious organ, but as a computational engine. Parallel to this, \citeauthor{wiener1948cybernetics} defined the field of **\citealternativetitle{wiener1948cybernetics}** in \citeyear{wiener1948cybernetics}. Wiener recognized that both machines and living organisms operate on principles of feedback loops and information transmission. This synthesis of biology, logic, and engineering provided the fertile soil from which modern AI would eventually grow. The full cast of these **cyberneticians** is covered in its own section below.
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: For the anatomical precondition, see [the neuron doctrine](untold_history_ii.php) and [the all-or-none law](mirror_in_machine.php); for McCulloch's philosophical program, see [Philosophy](philosophy.php).
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: This was the conceptual shift from “calculating machines” to the idea that cognition itself might be formalized (see the work of \citeauthor{piccini} for more details).
blocks.section: From a biophysics journal to the Hixon Symposium

blocks.quote: The First Practical AI (1914)
blocks.section: The First Practical AI (1914)

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{wienerajedrecista}, a chess playing machine first demonstrated in 1914, invented by Leonardo Torres Quevedo.
blocks.section: The First Practical AI (1914)

blocks.quote: Before the term “Artificial Intelligence” existed, the Spanish engineer \citeauthor{torres1914} built the first working AI system: **El Ajedrecista**, an electromechanical chess endgame player capable of automatically checkmating a human opponent with king and rook against king \cite{torres1914}. Back then, chess was considered an activity restricted to the realm of intelligent creatures. Torres Quevedo wanted to redefine what we mean by “thinking,” demonstrating that machines could make choices from a complex set of relational possibilities without human intervention \cite{ieeespectrum2023chess}.
blocks.section: The First Practical AI (1914)

blocks.quote: The machine's sensing system used a chessboard where each of the 64 squares consisted of three metallic pieces separated by insulating material: a circular central piece connected to the positive terminal and two triangular side pieces connected to horizontal and vertical conductors. The black king's silver mesh base closed two electrical circuits upon placement, driving sliding bars to positions encoding its coordinates; four additional bars tracked the white pieces similarly. The decision logic, implemented via battery-driven relays in a tree structure, partitioned the board into three zones (left: a-c files; center: d-e files; right: f-h files) and selected one of six operations based on the relative positions of the pieces, whether the black king shared a zone with the rook, the vertical distance between pieces, and the parity of horizontal separation \cite{torres1914}. Actuation was achieved through eight electro-mechanical actuators using a disc-and-pawl mechanism: when an electromagnet released the pawl, one full disc rotation executed a mechanical “microprogram” for a specific piece movement. In the upgraded 1920 version, electromagnets concealed beneath an ordinary chessboard moved the white pieces, and a gramophone announced *jaque al rey* (check) or *mate* (checkmate). If the opponent made three illegal moves, the machine shut down \cite{ieeespectrum2023chess}.
blocks.section: The First Practical AI (1914)

blocks.quote: While the algorithm was suboptimal, it guaranteed checkmate in fewer than 63 moves against any defense \cite{ieeespectrum2023chess}. The machine was still considered impressive decades later when AI pioneer Norbert Wiener played against it at the 1951 Paris conference on calculating machines and human thought \cite{torres1914} \cite{ieeespectrum2023chess}.
blocks.section: The First Practical AI (1914)

blocks.quote: Before the chess machine, the same inventor had already been building **analog calculating machines** (*máquinas algébricas*) from 1895, using floating-point arithmetic to compute the roots of polynomials up to the eighth degree, complex ones included, to a thousandth of a unit, an early rival to the purely mechanical path that ran from Babbage to the digital computer (\cite[Thomas, 2008]{thomas2008torres}).
blocks.section: The First Practical AI (1914)

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{mechanicalturkimage}, shown here in Joseph Racknitz's 1789 reconstruction, wrong about the details, right that a person sat inside.
blocks.section: The First Practical AI (1914)

blocks.quote: Above, we met the first *practical* chess machine (1914). A century and a half before it, an earlier automaton had already captivated the world, and fooled it, for 84 years. In **1770** the Hungarian inventor **Wolfgang von Kempelen** unveiled the **Mechanical Turk**, a life-sized figure that appeared to play a strong game of chess by itself. It was, in fact, the most elaborate con in the history of the field: a hidden human grandmaster sat inside the cabinet, moving the pieces by levers and magnets, and the "memory" that let it beat any single challenger again and again was simply the size of a human brain. Yet it toured for 84 years, won most of its games, including, it was claimed, against **Napoleon Bonaparte** and **Benjamin Franklin**, and was not destroyed by fire until **1854** (\cite[Mechanical Turk, Wikipedia]{mechanicalturk}).
blocks.section: The First Practical AI (1914)

blocks.quote: The Turk matters for the history of AI for the opposite reason to its trick. It is the first machine the public was asked to *believe* could reason, and its test (can it hold its own in a real contest against a real person, over and over?) is the ancestor of the challenge-based test that would, a century and a half later, be formalized as the **Turing test**. The Turk could even *chat*: between games it answered questions from the crowd on a letterboard, in English, French, and German, on its age, its "life," and how it worked, a talking head, the direct descendant of Roger Bacon's brazen head. When the mechanism was finally explained in detail in 1857, the lesson stuck: *to tell a machine that thinks from a person hidden in a box, you need a test that is hard to fake*, the founding question of machine intelligence (\cite[Mechanical Turk, Wikipedia]{mechanicalturk}).
blocks.section: The First Practical AI (1914)

blocks.quote: Babbage's encounter with the Turk is the missing link in that story. In **1819** he played the machine twice and lost both matches. He suspected the cabinet hid a person, but he did not write the exposé that some of his contemporaries did. The encounter stayed with him. In **1864** he recorded in his diary that he had chosen, as a test for his "mechanical notation," "the contrivance of a machine that should be able to play a game of purely intellectual skill ... chess." There is no mechanical link between the Turk and the Analytical Engine (one was a hoax, the other a real design), but the hoax showed what a machine that *appeared* to think could do to the imagination of the person who would build the first programmable computer (\cite[Standage, 2002]{standage2002turk}).
blocks.section: The First Practical AI (1914)

blocks.section: Konrad Zuse: The Engineer

blocks.quote: I was too lazy to calculate by hand.
blocks.section: Konrad Zuse: The Engineer

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{zusez1}, the first fully automatic programmable Computer, completed in 1938
blocks.section: Konrad Zuse: The Engineer

blocks.quote: \citeauthor{zusebook}, a civil engineer tired of manual arithmetic, spent 1936 to 1945 building the first binary computers in his parents' Berlin living room. His Z-series evolved from the mechanical **Z1**, which used sliding metal plates but suffered from frequent jams, to the **Z3** (1941), the world's first functional, programmable, and fully automatic digital computer. By switching from mechanical parts to 2,000 electromagnetic telephone relays, Zuse proved that binary electricity was the future of calculation. He even pioneered the first high-level programming language, **Plankalkül**, while hiding his **Z4** model in the Alps to survive WWII, eventually launching the world's first commercial computer company (\citetitle{zusebook}, p. 72ff, 156ff).
blocks.section: Konrad Zuse: The Engineer

blocks.quote: Zuse did not directly work on modern AI systems, but together with people like Aiken, based on earlier ideas of Leibniz, Babbage, Llull, and, in parts, of Aristotle, he helped to create the *hardware* AI can run on.
blocks.section: Konrad Zuse: The Engineer

blocks.quote: Alan Turing: Theory and the Universal Machine (1936-1950)
blocks.section: Alan Turing: Theory and the Universal Machine (1936-1950)

blocks.quote: \citetitle{turingimage}, c. 1930
blocks.section: Alan Turing: Theory and the Universal Machine (1936-1950)

blocks.quote: \citeauthor{turing1937} provided the mathematical proof for what a computer *could* do.
blocks.section: Alan Turing: Theory and the Universal Machine (1936-1950)

blocks.quote: In 1937, a 21-year-old MIT graduate student named Claude Elwood Shannon submitted his master's thesis, \cite[*A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits*]{shannon1937switching}, which demonstrated that the two-valued Boolean algebra developed by \citeauthor{bool1854} in 1854 could serve as a theoretical foundation for the design of electrical switching circuits. Shannon recognized that the binary states of electrical relay switches, open or closed, on or off, were isomorphic to the truth values of Boolean logic: true and false, 1 and 0. Any arrangement of series and parallel switches could be described by a Boolean expression, and conversely, any Boolean expression could be physically realized as a circuit of relays. His thesis laid the foundations for all digital computing and digital circuits. The utilization of the binary properties of electrical switches to perform logic functions is the basic concept that underlies all electronic digital computer designs, from the earliest relay computers to the GPU clusters training today's large language models.
blocks.section: Alan Turing: Theory and the Universal Machine (1936-1950)

blocks.quote: Howard Aiken & The Harvard Mark I (1944)
blocks.section: Howard Aiken & The Harvard Mark I (1944)

blocks.quote: Howard Aiken. Photo: \citeauthor{aikenphoto}, \citeyear{aikenphoto}. Public domain.
blocks.section: Howard Aiken & The Harvard Mark I (1944)

blocks.quote: Inspired by Babbage's Analytical Engine, **Howard Aiken** designed a program-controlled relay calculator that Harvard and IBM agreed to build on 31 March 1939. IBM built it at its Endicott plant and called it the **Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator (ASCC)**; Harvard called it the **Mark I**. The machine was 16 metres long, weighed 4.3 tonnes, and contained about 3,500 relays and 800 kilometres of wire. Its memory held 72 decimal numbers of 23 digits, plus 60 constants; instructions were punched into paper tape, and output came through punched cards and typewriters. It could do three additions per second; a multiplication took six seconds (\cite[HNF, 2019]{hnfmarki2019}).
blocks.section: Howard Aiken & The Harvard Mark I (1944)

blocks.quote: The Mark I was formally handed over on **7 August 1944**, and the press coverage was immediate: the *New York Times* ran a two-column story about a machine that would solve in hours problems too long to attempt, and a newsreel showed sailors climbing through the "Giant Calculator" while a woman in Navy uniform operated it: **Grace Hopper**, then a reserve officer and later a rear admiral. The machine stood at Harvard but belonged to the US Navy, and Aiken and Hopper were both reserve officers. Before the public dedication, on 29 March 1944, **John von Neumann** had already used it for calculations for the secret atomic-bomb project; from August it ran mostly weapons problems (\cite[HNF, 2019]{hnfmarki2019}).
blocks.section: Howard Aiken & The Harvard Mark I (1944)

blocks.quote: Its place in the genealogy is precise. If relay machines count, the Mark I was the first American digital computer; nobody in the United States knew about Zuse's Z3, which had been running in Berlin since 1941. Zuse learned of Aiken's machine during the war from a photograph (the daughter of his accountant worked as a secretary in German intelligence and had seen it), but the photograph showed little more than the words "Sequence Controlled Calculator" (\cite[HNF, 2019]{hnfmarki2019}). The Mark I itself worked into the 1950s and was partly dismantled in 1959; a control unit is now in the Heinz Nixdorf MuseumsForum in Paderborn (\cite[HNF, 2019]{hnfmarki2019}).
blocks.section: Howard Aiken & The Harvard Mark I (1944)

blocks.quote: John von Neumann & The Stored-Program Concept (1945)
blocks.section: John von Neumann & The Stored-Program Concept (1945)

blocks.quote: Before von Neumann, computers like the ENIAC had to be physically rewired to change tasks. His \citetitle{vonneumann} proposed the **Von Neumann Architecture**.
blocks.section: John von Neumann & The Stored-Program Concept (1945)

blocks.quote: One of his **Big Ideas** for **Computing**: Data and instructions are stored in the same memory. This allowed the computer to be “reprogrammed” via software rather than hardware switches.
blocks.section: John von Neumann & The Stored-Program Concept (1945)

blocks.quote: IBM 702: IBM's First Business Computer (1953)
blocks.section: IBM 702: IBM's First Business Computer (1953)

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{ibm702image}
blocks.section: IBM 702: IBM's First Business Computer (1953)

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{ibm702} (\citeyear{ibm702}) was IBM's first commercial electronic computer aimed at business data processing, and a direct response to Remington Rand's UNIVAC. UNIVAC I (1951) was the first general-purpose computer designed for business, and LEO I (1951) the first commercially available business computer (\cite{univac1951}). It was notable for adapting the new **magnetic-core memory** technology for random-access applications, and it weighed roughly 24,645 pounds. The memory was character-oriented and initially Williams-tube based, later retrofitted to core, with capacities ranging from 2,000 to 10,000 characters \cite{ibm702}.
blocks.section: IBM 702: IBM's First Business Computer (1953)

blocks.quote: Elektro the Moto-Man: the robot as theatre (1939)
blocks.section: Elektro the Moto-Man: the robot as theatre (1939)

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{img_elektro_sparko} (\citeauthor{img_elektro_sparko}, \citeyear{img_elektro_sparko}): replicas of Westinghouse's Elektro and his robot dog Sparko at the Senator John Heinz History Center. \citeauthor{img_elektro_sparko} released the photograph into the public domain.
blocks.section: Elektro the Moto-Man: the robot as theatre (1939)

blocks.quote: Before cybernetics gave machines a feedback loop, the robot most of the public had actually seen was a **performer**. **Elektro the Moto-Man** was built by J. M. Barnett, Jack Weeks Sr., Harold Gorsuch and other engineers at Westinghouse's Mansfield, Ohio, plant. It stood 2.1 metres tall, weighed 118 kilograms, and was advertised as having a "brain" of 48 electrical relays.
blocks.section: Elektro the Moto-Man: the robot as theatre (1939)

blocks.quote: At the 1939 New York World's Fair it performed twenty-six tricks: it appeared to walk, talked, counted, sang, smoked a cigarette, and, after 1941, blew up balloons. Its vocabulary was about 700 words, all prerecorded; its "voice commands" were timed syllabic codes flashed to a photoelectric tube rather than understood speech; and its famous walk was a staged shuffle on wheels along a track, with one knee bent and the other leg dragging (\cite[Marsh, 2018]{marsh2018elektro}).
blocks.section: Elektro the Moto-Man: the robot as theatre (1939)

blocks.quote: Elektro is the perfect foil for what comes next. It looked like a thinking machine, but it had no model of the world, no feedback loop and no learning: every gesture was a scripted sequence triggered by a code. Grey Walter's tortoises, a decade later, were far less human and far more interesting: they actually sensed the world and changed their behaviour in response. The contrast is the history of AI in miniature: the convincing body came first, the control loop came second. Elektro also gave the mechanical servant a public face, alongside **Sparko**, the robot dog added to the Westinghouse show in 1940, which could sit, bark, wag its tail and beg (\cite[Marsh, 2018]{marsh2018elektro}).
blocks.section: Elektro the Moto-Man: the robot as theatre (1939)

blocks.quote: The Electric Tortoise: Machina speculatrix (1948)
blocks.section: The Electric Tortoise: Machina speculatrix (1948)

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{img_walter_tortoise} (\citeauthor{img_walter_tortoise}, \citeyear{img_walter_tortoise}): one of W. Grey Walter's *Machina speculatrix* tortoises, with its photocell "eyes" and vacuum-tube brain.
blocks.section: The Electric Tortoise: Machina speculatrix (1948)

blocks.quote: Starting in 1948, the British neurophysiologist **W. Grey Walter** (1910-1977, born in Kansas City, Missouri) built small wheeled machines whose "brains" were simple vacuum-tube circuits: the circuits sensed the environment with photocells and drove the two wheel motors. Walter gave them the taxonomic name ***Machina speculatrix***, "machine that looks".
blocks.section: The Electric Tortoise: Machina speculatrix (1948)

blocks.quote: The circuits could be arranged so that a machine moved toward, or away from, a light mounted on a sister machine. The behavior looked purposive, and was often complex and unpredictable, so much so that Walter said it "might be accepted as evidence of some degree of self-awareness" (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
blocks.section: The Electric Tortoise: Machina speculatrix (1948)

blocks.quote: He described the tortoises in a May 1950 *Scientific American* article, "An Imitation of Life", and in *The Living Brain* (1953). Nilsson calls the *Machina speculatrix* "the beginning of a long line of increasingly sophisticated 'behaving machines'", and Rodney Brooks's behavior-based robotics of the 1980s explicitly drew on the same approach: controlling an animal-like body with simple situation-specific circuits, without internal representations or reasoning (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
