blocks.section: The Electric Tortoise: Machina speculatrix (1948)

blocks.quote: The SNARC: The First Physical Neural Network (1951)
blocks.section: The SNARC: The First Physical Neural Network (1951)

blocks.quote: Built by **Marvin Minsky** and **Dean Edmonds** in 1951, the **SNARC** (Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator) was the world's first physical artificial neural network. Inspired directly by the theoretical logic calculus of \citeauthorlastnameand{mccullochpitts1943} (\citeyear{mccullochpitts1943}), the SNARC translated abstract mathematical neurons into stochastic, learning hardware. It consisted of a randomly connected network of 40 artificial neurons constructed from vacuum tubes, salvaged B-24 bomber gyropilots, and magnetic clutches, designed to simulate a rat learning to navigate a virtual maze.
blocks.section: The SNARC: The First Physical Neural Network (1951)

blocks.quote: Rather than relying on explicit programming, the machine learned via mechanical reinforcement. When the network made a random but “correct” move, a reinforcement signal engaged the clutches to turn potentiometers, physically altering the electrical resistance of the active connections. This increased the probability that those specific, successful pathways would fire again. By mechanically formalizing trial-and-error learning, concepts Minsky later detailed in his Princeton dissertation, *\citetitle{minsky1954}* (\citeyear{minsky1954}), the SNARC proved that a decentralized network of McCulloch-Pitts cells could autonomously calculate behavioral adaptation.
blocks.section: The SNARC: The First Physical Neural Network (1951)

blocks.quote: A decade before Hopfield's 1982 paper re-introduced the field to recurrent attractor networks, and a quarter-century before it became standard textbook material, the British engineer \citeauthor{beurle1956wave} (\citeyear{beurle1956wave}) published in the *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society* one of the first proper *mathematical* theories of what happens in a *mass* of interconnected neurons, not one cell, but a continuum. Beurle's model treats the local density of active neurons as a continuous variable obeying a partial differential equation, the same formal structure used to describe chemical waves, flame fronts, and epidemics: a wave of excitation propagates outward from a focal site at finite velocity, and the tissue behind it falls into a refractory state. The result is a *travelling wave*: a coherent, self-sustaining pattern of activity that is not localised in any single cell but is a property of the population as a whole. Beurle showed that under the right conditions these waves can store and transmit information, and that the brain's *mass-action* dynamics, what he called the "mass of neurons acting together", is fundamentally different from, and computationally richer than, what any single neuron can do alone.
blocks.section: The SNARC: The First Physical Neural Network (1951)

blocks.quote: The 1956 paper is almost completely unknown outside specialist history-of-neuroscience circles; the standard Anglophone narrative of neural networks jumps from the McCulloch-Pitts 1943 logical neuron, through the Hebb 1949 learning rule, to the perceptron 1958 and the Amari 1972 / Hopfield 1982 attractor networks, with Beurle's wave-dynamics paper nowhere in the chain. That is a real loss.
blocks.section: The SNARC: The First Physical Neural Network (1951)

blocks.quote: Beurle's framework anticipates three things that the 1980s and 1990s connectionist revival would rediscover from a different direction. First, it anticipates the **continuum-field** model of cortical activity that modern neural-field theories (Amari 1977, Wilson-Cowan 1972/73, Jirsa-Kelso 2000) all descend from, and that today underpins whole-brain modelling frameworks like The Virtual Brain. Second, it anticipates the **wave-as-computation** view that connects neuroscience to the wider physics of excitable media, a connection now central to the study of cortical travelling waves during sleep, attention, and working memory.
blocks.section: The SNARC: The First Physical Neural Network (1951)

blocks.quote: Third, and most pointedly for this course, it anticipates the **attractor-network** intuition that *the brain's information is not in any single neuron but in a population-level pattern*, the same intuition Hopfield would repackage in 1982 as a content-addressable memory, and that today underpins every modern generative model that treats latent state as a population code. Beurle wrote it all down, in a Royal Society paper, twenty-six years earlier. The history of neural networks, as usually told, skips this chapter; the chapter is worth knowing about.
blocks.section: The SNARC: The First Physical Neural Network (1951)

blocks.quote: The Cyberneticians (1943-1953)
blocks.section: The Cyberneticians (1943-1953)

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{wienerphoto}, \citeyear{wienerphoto}
blocks.section: The Cyberneticians (1943-1953)

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{vonneumannphoto}, \citeyear{vonneumannphoto}
blocks.section: The Cyberneticians (1943-1953)

blocks.quote: Between the 1943 neuron papers and the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, a loose, deliberately cross-disciplinary group of mathematicians, neurophysiologists, engineers and anthropologists briefly gave the emerging field a different name: **\citealternativetitle{wiener1948cybernetics}**. The word is Greek: κυβερνήτης, *kybernētēs*, "the steersman". Steer a ship and you are running a feedback loop, turning the rudder in response to the effect it already had. \citeauthor{wiener1948cybernetics} and his circle coined it in the summer of 1947 for "control and communication in the animal and the machine", the one logic shared by a thermostat, a gun's fire-control, and a nervous system \cite{wiener1948cybernetics}.
blocks.section: The Cyberneticians (1943-1953)

blocks.quote: The word was not Wiener's invention. The French mathematician and physicist \citeauthor{ampere1843cybernetique}, better remembered for the *ampere* and for the right-hand rule of electromagnetism, proposed, in his unfinished *\citealternativetitle{ampere1843cybernetique}*, a classification of human knowledge in which he imagined two new political sciences, one of which he called **cybernétique**, after the same Greek root κυβερνήτης. The volume appeared only in \citeyear{ampere1843cybernetique}, seven years after his death in 1836. Ampère's *cybernétique* was the science of *how* a government steers the state, the science of public administration by means of feedback, the study of how a minister's orders propagate through the bureaucracy and how the resulting reports loop back to update policy. It was a political science, not a science of machines; but the underlying picture was exactly the one Wiener would later draw on the board at the Macy conferences: a chain of command is a feedback loop, a bureaucracy is a control system, and a nervous system is a more elaborate version of the same thing. The vocabulary waited more than a century for its subject matter to catch up. When Wiener finally used it in 1947, he knew he was reaching back to Ampère's term, and he kept the French ending, **cybernetics**, not **governology**, in part because Ampère had already done the work of naming the concept, leaving only the science to be done.
blocks.section: The Cyberneticians (1943-1953)

blocks.quote: The **Macy Conferences** (1946-1953), ten meetings funded by the Josiah Macy Jr. Foundation and chaired by **McCulloch**, gave the field its first regular meeting place; their stated aim was "a general science of the workings of the human mind" \cite{macyconferences} \cite{heims1991cyberneticsgroup}. In Britain the **Ratio Club** did the same thing over dinner in Cambridge \cite{ratioclub}. Its two founding papers both date to 1943: McCulloch-Pitts (above), and **Arturo Rosenblueth, Norbert Wiener and Julian Bigelow's** *Behavior, Purpose and Teleology*, which modelled purposeful action as negative feedback and asked what "purpose" even means when a machine acts \cite{behaviorpurpose1943}.
blocks.section: The Cyberneticians (1943-1953)

blocks.quote: Abraham and Heims both describe the Macy conferences as a social experiment as much as a scientific one. McCulloch was its architect and showman; Frank Fremont-Smith called the cybernetics group “the wildest” of his conference groups.
blocks.section: The Cyberneticians (1943-1953)

blocks.quote: The shared vocabulary (feedback, purpose, information, Gestalt) was deliberately ambiguous, a strategy Leah Ceccarelli calls strategic ambiguity: it let mathematicians, anthropologists and psychiatrists talk to one another, but it also made agreement hard. McCulloch recalled that when the word “Gestalt” came up, “five members of the group thought the other twenty were misusing it.” Robert Morison said he had the odd impression of being able to follow almost every sentence without understanding the paragraphs. By the last meeting in 1953 there was no unified science, only a set of rival programmes.
blocks.section: The Cyberneticians (1943-1953)

blocks.quote: Andrew Pickering's contrast is useful: the British cyberneticians around Ashby, Grey Walter and Pask were more playful and anti-disciplinary, while the American group around McCulloch and Wiener wanted a disciplined science with predictive laws (\cite{abraham2016rebelgenius, heims1991cyberneticsgroup, macyconferences}).
blocks.section: The Cyberneticians (1943-1953)

blocks.quote: McCulloch at MIT: reliability, probabilistic logic, and the reticular formation
blocks.section: McCulloch at MIT: reliability, probabilistic logic, and the reticular formation

blocks.quote: McCulloch left Illinois for MIT's Research Laboratory of Electronics in 1952, and the move changed what kind of scientist he was. At the RLE, in the open, defence-funded, multidisciplinary culture of Cold War MIT, he recast the brain as an information processor and himself as an engineer; the neuropsychiatrist became a modeller who spent his time on circuit theory, information theory and control. Abraham argues that this was not a late career change but the moment his transdisciplinary programme finally found an institutional home (\cite[Abraham, 2016, pp. 153-156]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
blocks.section: McCulloch at MIT: reliability, probabilistic logic, and the reticular formation

blocks.quote: One problem he took up there was reliability. If neurons are unreliable and their thresholds drift, how does a network keep working? With Manuel Blum, Jack Cowan and Leo Verbeek he designed circuits whose logic stayed stable under threshold shifts, and he moved from the Boolean logic of 1943 toward a probabilistic logic in which not only the truth value but the logical function itself has a probability. Blum remembered the motivating picture in McCulloch's own words: “When you drink coffee your thresholds go down; when you drink alcohol your thresholds all go up. And yet you can still walk, you can still talk, and you can still think.” The question was also a Cold War engineering question (the “reliability crisis” in defence electronics), and it is recognisably the same problem later connectionists faced when they asked how a network can degrade gracefully (\cite[Abraham, 2016, pp. 164-166]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
blocks.section: McCulloch at MIT: reliability, probabilistic logic, and the reticular formation

blocks.quote: A second project shows how far the engineering idiom went. After Moruzzi and Magoun's 1949 experiments made the brain-stem reticular formation look like the seat of consciousness, McCulloch took it up with Bill Kilmer and Blum and modelled it instead as a decision system that chooses behaviour. They treated neurons as nonlinear oscillators, built a computer simulation, and distinguished four modes of behaviour: a model of command and control, not of awareness. The reticular formation became a place where positive and negative feedback select an action, which is exactly the cybernetic picture of purpose applied to a concrete piece of anatomy (\cite[Abraham, 2016, pp. 166-167]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
blocks.section: McCulloch at MIT: reliability, probabilistic logic, and the reticular formation

blocks.quote: Ross Ashby and the Homeostat
blocks.section: Ross Ashby and the Homeostat

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{homeostatphoto}
blocks.section: Ross Ashby and the Homeostat

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{ashbyphoto}, \citeyear{ashbyphoto}
blocks.section: Ross Ashby and the Homeostat

blocks.quote: The most under-rated of the group, the psychiatrist \citeauthor{ashbyintrocybernetics1956}, built a machine to prove his ideas. His **Homeostat** (1948) wired four scrapped Royal-Air-Force bomb-control units into a maze of feedback; dropped into any state, it mechanically hunted its way back to equilibrium, a "self-organizing" machine that appeared to act with purpose \cite{ashbyhomeostat1948} \cite{ashbydesigndbrain1952}. \citeauthor{wienerhumaneuse1950} called the emergence of purposeful behaviour in it "one of the great philosophical contributions of the present day" \cite{wienerhumaneuse1950}. From the same insight came the **Law of Requisite Variety** (1956): a controller can cancel the variety (number of possible states) thrown at it only with its own variety: "only variety can destroy variety" \cite{ashbyintrocybernetics1956}. Conant and Ashby sharpened this in 1970 into the **Good Regulator Theorem**: every good regulator of a system must be a *model of that system* \cite{conantashby1970}, a prediction that a controller must resemble the thing it controls, made decades before deep learning rediscovered it.
blocks.section: Ross Ashby and the Homeostat

blocks.quote: Ashby kept a private notebook of ideas for 44 years: 25 volumes, 7,189 pages, now digitized as the W. Ross Ashby Digital Archive. He took correspondence courses in "Effective English and Personal Efficiency" before daring to write his first book, warning: "My fear is now that I may become conspicuous, for a book of mine is in the press." And in 1946 \citeauthor{turing1937} wrote to him suggesting he use the Automatic Computing Engine for his experiments instead of building his own machine.
blocks.section: Ross Ashby and the Homeostat

blocks.quote: Gregory Bateson: information as difference
blocks.section: Gregory Bateson: information as difference

blocks.quote: The anthropologist \citeauthor{batesonesteps1972} dragged the social and behavioural sciences into the group and rewired its vocabulary. For him a unit of information is simply "the difference which makes a difference", and a system learns when the *pattern* of differences around it changes \cite{batesonesteps1972}. With Jackson, Haley and Weakland he worked out the **double bind** (contradictory messages at different logical levels, with no way to step out), originally to explain schizophrenia \cite{batesondoublebind1956}. In the 1970s he turned the lens onto the observer and helped shape **second-order cybernetics**, "the cybernetics of cybernetics"; the term and programme are credited to Heinz von Foerster, with Margaret Mead's 1967 address as a defining moment (\cite{batesonesteps1972}; \cite{secondordercybernetics_wiki}).
blocks.section: Gregory Bateson: information as difference

blocks.quote: In World War II Bateson served in the OSS designing "black propaganda" radio broadcasts, using his theory of schismogenesis to drive rival enemy factions against each other. In 1973 he went further: only two events, he argued, were anthropologically important in the twentieth century: the Treaty of Versailles, and cybernetics.
blocks.section: Gregory Bateson: information as difference

blocks.quote: Shannon, chess and the rat
blocks.section: Shannon, chess and the rat

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{shannonphoto}, \citeyear{shannonphoto}
blocks.section: Shannon, chess and the rat

blocks.quote: Claude Shannon's Theseus maze (1952), the 25-square relay maze his mouse learned to navigate by trial and error (\cite[Theseus maze, MIT Museum]{theseus_maze_image}).
blocks.section: Shannon, chess and the rat

blocks.quote: Two years after he formalized \citealternativetitle{shannon1948communication}, \citeauthor{shannon1948communication} wrote the first real computer-chess program \cite{shannonchess1950}: a minimax search over a small board plus a ten-term evaluation function, the very template **Deep Blue** and, later, **AlphaGo** would scale up. At the Macy meetings he also showed **Shannon's rat**, a relay maze-solver that recalled its past paths to reach a goal, but which would sometimes loop forever, chasing its tail, until someone pulled the plug \cite{macyconferences}.
blocks.section: Shannon, chess and the rat

blocks.quote: Wiener had already asked "can it think?"
blocks.section: Wiener had already asked "can it think?"

blocks.quote: The group's horizon opened before Turing's: Wiener had already posed the question in *Cybernetics* (1948) and *The Human Use of Human Beings* (1950) (\cite{wiener1948cybernetics}; \cite{wienerhumaneuse1950}). In \citetitle{wienergodandgolem1964} (\citeyear{wienergodandgolem1964}), a slim monograph on where cybernetics impinges on religion, \citeauthor{wienergodandgolem1964} asked, in the guise of the biblical golem, whether a machine could think, and how to keep such a creation in its place: could the automaton ever rival the mind that made it? \cite{wienergodandgolem1964}
blocks.section: Wiener had already asked "can it think?"

blocks.quote: Abraham's verdict on McCulloch's second act is that his central legacy was not a particular model but a redistribution of the brain as a scientific object: he helped take brain research out of medicine and make it a problem for physics, engineering, mathematics and philosophy at once, and in doing so helped create the modern neurosciences. His clearest descendants, she argues, are computational neuroscientists rather than the symbolists or the connectionists: they share his interest in the wetware and his willingness to model it, even if they ask narrower “how” questions (\cite[Abraham, 2016, pp. 181-185]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
blocks.section: Wiener had already asked "can it think?"

blocks.quote: This transdisciplinary group is the direct parent of AI. When the field formalised in 1956 at \citealternativetitle{darthmouthartificialintelligence} \cite{darthmouthartificialintelligence}, it split off from cybernetics, and, as we will see, the neural-net wing was downplayed while symbolic AI took the funding.
blocks.section: Wiener had already asked "can it think?"

blocks.quote: The Imitation Game
blocks.section: The Imitation Game

blocks.quote: Before the term “Artificial Intelligence” even existed, **Alan Turing** laid the philosophical groundwork in \citeyear{turing1950computing} with his paper *\citetitle{turing1950computing}*.
blocks.section: The Imitation Game

blocks.quote: I propose to consider the question, 'Can machines think?'
blocks.section: The Imitation Game

blocks.quote: Turing argued that defining “thinking” was too ambiguous. Instead, he proposed the **Imitation Game** (now known as the Turing Test), an *operationalization*: a behavioral test designed to let the question “Can machines think?” be settled empirically rather than by philosophical argument \cite{hnfturing2020}. A computer would be considered intelligent if it could converse indistinguishably from a human. This shifted the goal of AI from replicating biological mechanics to replicating observable behavior.
blocks.section: The Imitation Game

blocks.quote: It is worth being clear, however, about what the test is and what it has come to mean. The test was never adopted as a formal scientific standard for measuring intelligence, and in modern AI research it is widely regarded as outdated: it probes the ability to *imitate* human conversation, which can be carried by surface fluency, small talk, and brief deceptions (the three classical objections of \citeauthor{levesque2014bestbehaviour} (\citeyear{levesque2014bestbehaviour}): **deception**: the machine must fabricate a human identity, which is not itself a component of intelligence; **conversation**: small talk and parlor tricks can carry a machine to a pass without real reasoning; and **evaluation**: human judges disagree and err), rather than by understanding, reasoning, or world knowledge. Its historical role is real (it shaped the field's first decades), but contemporary AI evaluation has largely moved to capability-specific benchmarks rather than open-ended mimicry.
blocks.section: The Imitation Game

blocks.quote: A detail in the paper is easy to miss. In Turing's sample dialogue the computer is asked to add 34,957 and 70,764 and answers **105,621**; the correct sum is **105,721**. Turing, a mathematician, almost certainly put the error there on purpose.
blocks.section: The Imitation Game

blocks.quote: Elsewhere in the paper he had suggested that a machine could be programmed to "deliberately introduce mistakes in a manner calculated to confuse the interrogator." A perfect calculator gives itself away; a machine that slips is easier to mistake for a person. The trick has a modern afterlife: **Eugene Goostman** (2014) was said to have passed a version of the test by playing a thirteen-year-old with English as a second language, and Google's **Duplex** (2018) inserted "umms" and "ahhs" into its speech. In both cases the imitation of fallibility did the work that understanding was supposed to do (\cite[Turing, 1950]{turing1950computing}).
blocks.section: The Imitation Game

blocks.quote: The term “Artificial Intelligence”
blocks.section: The term “Artificial Intelligence”

blocks.quote: The term “Artificial Intelligence” was coined in the 31 August 1955 proposal for the \citealternativetitle{darthmouthartificialintelligence}, when **John McCarthy**, along with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon, submitted it. The workshop itself took place in 1956, founded on the conjecture that “every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it,” marking the official birth of the field.
blocks.section: The term “Artificial Intelligence”

blocks.quote: The founding story is tidier than the event. Crevier, drawing on interviews with the participants, records that the summer project deeply disappointed its organizer: people came for different periods, no consensus emerged on what the field was or where it was going, and most participants returned to their own approaches. Herbert Simon later estimated that “Dartmouth got only half a dozen people active that weren't before.” Even the name was contested (Samuel thought “artificial” sounded phony, while Newell and Simon kept calling their work “complex information processing” for years), but McCarthy got “artificial intelligence” adopted, and with the label gave the discipline its public identity \cite{crevier1993ai}.
blocks.section: The term “Artificial Intelligence”

blocks.quote: John McCarthy, who coined “artificial intelligence” for the 1956 Dartmouth proposal. \cite{img_john_mccarthy}. [CC BY-SA 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/).
blocks.section: The term “Artificial Intelligence”

blocks.quote: Marvin Minsky, McCarthy's co-author on the Dartmouth proposal and later a leading critic of the perceptron. \cite{img_marvin_minsky}. [CC BY-SA 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/).
blocks.section: The term “Artificial Intelligence”

blocks.quote: Four ways to build a mind
blocks.section: Four ways to build a mind

blocks.quote: Naming the field was only the beginning. The harder question was *what an intelligent machine should be measured against*, and it splits the space into four targets. \citeauthor{russell2021aima} lay it out along two axes: should the system *think* or merely *act*, and should it be judged against *human behavior* or against *rational optimality* \cite{russell2021aima}:
blocks.section: Four ways to build a mind

blocks.quote: This taxonomy is the hidden fault line of the first winter. The Toosi review is explicit that the 1960s field mostly chased **thinking humanly** (replicating the *way* humans solve a problem rather than analyzing the problem's actual complexity), and that this choice, more than any single failed system, set up the over-promise the funding cuts then punished \cite{toosi2021history}. The programs that follow live in the top row of the grid: the **Logic Theorist** and **GPS** imitated human problem-solving, and the Perceptron was built to *behave* like a learner. The LLMs of the course's later chapters are, by contrast, largely **acting rationally**: not asked to think like us, only to do the task well.
blocks.section: Four ways to build a mind

blocks.quote: The First AI Programs (1956)
blocks.section: The First AI Programs (1956)

blocks.quote: The Dartmouth workshop catalyzed the first wave of AI programs. **Allen Newell**, **John Cliff Shaw**, and **Herbert A. Simon** presented the **Logic Theorist** (LT), a program that could prove symbolic logic theorems by searching a space of possible proof steps. LT successfully proved 38 of the first 52 theorems in the second chapter of Whitehead and Russell's *\citetitle{russell1910principia}* \cite{newell1956logictheorist}, and even discovered a proof for one theorem that was shorter than the one in the original text. Newell and Simon submitted that proof to the *Journal of Symbolic Logic* with the program listed as a co-author; the editor rejected it on the grounds that proving a theorem in the outmoded system of *Principia* was no accomplishment \cite{crevier1993ai}. This was the first program to deliberately separate human problem-solving into manipulable symbolic representations, establishing the “physical symbol system” hypothesis that would dominate AI for decades.
blocks.section: The First AI Programs (1956)

blocks.quote: Around the same time, **Arthur Samuel** at IBM developed a **checker-playing program** that learned through self-play using what we now recognize as **reinforcement learning**. The program evaluated board positions through a weighted sum of features (piece advantage, center control, etc.) and adjusted these weights based on game outcomes, improving over time until it could play at an intermediate level, better than its own creator \cite{samuel1959checkers}. Samuel's work demonstrated that a machine could improve its performance through experience, a foundational principle of modern machine learning.
blocks.section: The First AI Programs (1956)

blocks.quote: The Symbolic Path: Newell and Simon's General Problem Solver
blocks.section: The Symbolic Path: Newell and Simon's General Problem Solver

blocks.quote: Building on the Logic Theorist, Newell and Simon released the **General Problem Solver (GPS)** in 1957, designed to mimic the problem-solving protocols of the human brain through “means-ends analysis” \cite{newell1957gps}. GPS could solve a range of well-defined tasks, from proving logical theorems to solving puzzles, by recursively decomposing the difference between the current state and the goal state into subgoals. While limited to “toy” problems, GPS embodied the “thinking humanly” approach and remained influential for decades.
blocks.section: The Symbolic Path: Newell and Simon's General Problem Solver

blocks.quote: The first micro-worlds (1959-1972)
blocks.section: The first micro-worlds (1959-1972)

blocks.quote: Two programs from the years after Dartmouth showed that the Logic Theorist's search machinery could be pointed at more than logic. At IBM, **Herbert Gelernter**'s **Geometry Theorem Prover** (1959) proved theorems in Euclidean geometry by working backward from the goal, and, its real innovation, by consulting a coordinate description of the diagram to prune the search: what would have been a million candidate steps for a two-step proof collapsed to twenty-five, and the program could handle proofs up to ten steps. The program was the first demonstration of what AI would call **model referencing**, the ancestor of every system that reasons against an internal model of its problem \cite{crevier1993ai}.
blocks.section: The first micro-worlds (1959-1972)

blocks.quote: At MIT, **James Slagle**'s **SAINT** (1961) applied the same goal-directed search to symbolic integration. Tested on eighty-six problems, many of them from MIT freshman calculus exams, it solved eighty-four, and it was probably the first program to search an **and/or tree**: a goal that splits into subgoals that must *all* be solved, versus alternatives of which only one need be. Joel Moses later extended SAINT into SIN, which grew into the computer-algebra system MACSYMA \cite{crevier1993ai}.
blocks.section: The first micro-worlds (1959-1972)

blocks.quote: A \citeyear{poirier2025neat} historical study \cite{poirier2025neat} shows that the Symbolic AI program was never unified to begin with. From the 1960s through the 1990s, knowledge-representation researchers sorted themselves into two camps that Poirier traces back to a methodological, then an aesthetic, opposition. The **logicists** (“neats”) gathered around **McCarthy at Stanford** and traced their intellectual lineage to \citeauthor{frege1879}; Frege himself died in 1925 and was never at Stanford. They pursued McCarthy's program of expressing everyday knowledge in formal, declarative logic and drawing conclusions by predicate calculus.
blocks.section: The first micro-worlds (1959-1972)

blocks.quote: The **proceduralists** (“scruffies”) gathered around Minsky at MIT and were willing to tolerate paradox, hand-coded heuristics, and incomplete representations in exchange for systems that actually worked on messy problems. Patrick Hayes, interviewed by Poirier, summarizes the split bluntly: the classical line-up was Minsky versus McCarthy, and he adds that this is very much an oversimplification. Minsky's 1974 paper “A Framework for Representing Knowledge,” which introduced **frames** as stereotyped data structures, was the scruffy camp's counter-move to pure logic.
blocks.section: The first micro-worlds (1959-1972)

blocks.quote: By the 1990s most knowledge architects concluded both approaches were necessary, but by then the field had spent two decades unable to deliver commonsense reasoning, and the resulting loss of confidence, not the Perceptrons book alone, is what tipped AI into its first winter. The neat/scruffy split is also why the Minsky who co-authored the devastating critique of perceptrons was *not*, in this earlier frame, an enemy of neural networks; he was the champion of the *procedural* wing of symbolic AI against McCarthy's *logicist* wing.
blocks.section: The first micro-worlds (1959-1972)

blocks.quote: The Neural Network Revolution: From Hebb to Backpropagation (1943-1986)
blocks.section: The Neural Network Revolution: From Hebb to Backpropagation (1943-1986)

blocks.quote: Before the Perceptron: Associationism, Hebb, and the First Neural Nets (1943-1957)
blocks.section: Before the Perceptron: Associationism, Hebb, and the First Neural Nets (1943-1957)

blocks.quote: When an axon of cell A is near enough to excite a cell B and repeatedly or persistently takes part in firing it [...] some growth process or metabolic change takes place in one or both cells such that A's efficiency, as one of the cells firing B, is increased. What wires together, fires together
blocks.section: Before the Perceptron: Associationism, Hebb, and the First Neural Nets (1943-1957)

blocks.quote: In his \citeyear{bain} work \citetitle{bain}, \citeauthor{bain} proposed the concept of Neural Groupings (p. 89ff) to explain how the brain physically organizes complex thoughts and coordinated movements. Bain was a pioneer in “Association Psychology,” and he sought to bridge the gap between abstract mental associations and biological structures. He argued that when we learn a new skill or memorize a sequence, specific clusters of neurons, or “groupings”, become structurally linked through repeated stimulation. These groupings allow the brain to trigger a complex “aggregate” of actions or ideas through a single nervous impulse, essentially laying the groundwork for what modern neuroscience would eventually call **Hebbian Theory**.
blocks.section: Before the Perceptron: Associationism, Hebb, and the First Neural Nets (1943-1957)

blocks.quote: Farley and Clark: The Network That Came First (1954)
blocks.section: Farley and Clark: The Network That Came First (1954)

blocks.quote: Rosenblatt's perceptron gets the "first" in most histories of neural networks, but a 1961 doctoral thesis is unusually blunt about the real priority. Two researchers at the MIT Lincoln Laboratory, **\citeauthorlastnameand{farleyclark1954}** (\citeyear{farleyclark1954}), had already built a perceptron-like pattern-recognition device, and their small network, with its sensory input, non-linear decision elements and trial-and-error reinforcement, was the same basic skeleton that Rosenblatt later scaled up \cite{joseph1961perceptron}. Their names were forgotten for a simple reason: they ran a few experiments on a small machine and then stopped working on it, without a mathematical account of what the device could or could not do \cite{joseph1961perceptron}. Credit in this field went, as it often does, to whoever built the *theory* and kept going.
blocks.section: Farley and Clark: The Network That Came First (1954)

blocks.quote: The Perceptron: Rosenblatt's Brain Model (1957-1962)
blocks.section: The Perceptron: Rosenblatt's Brain Model (1957-1962)

blocks.quote: Frank Rosenblatt was born on July 11, 1928, in New Rochelle, New York. He graduated from the Bronx High School of Science in 1946, earned an A.B. from Cornell University in 1950, and stayed for a Ph.D. in psychology, completed in 1956. He spent the 1950s at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo, the university's contract-research arm, where he rose to head its cognitive systems section, and in 1959 he took a joint appointment as associate professor of psychology on Cornell's Ithaca campus. He drowned on July 11, 1971, his forty-third birthday, while sailing his sloop *Shearwater* on Chesapeake Bay (\cite[Lefkowitz, 2019]{lefkowitz2019perceptron}; \cite[Emlen et al., 1971]{rosenblattmemorial1971}).
blocks.section: The Perceptron: Rosenblatt's Brain Model (1957-1962)

blocks.quote: Based on the \citealternativetitle{hebb1949organizationofbehaviour}, idea of the canadian psychology professor \citeauthor{hebb1949organizationofbehaviour} published that neurons in the brain get a stronger connection to each other when they often fire together, which is often expressed as “neurons that fire together, wire together”, and the idea of neurons proposed by \citeauthorlastnameand{mccullochpitts1943}, in \citeyear{rosenblatt1958perceptron}, **\citeauthor{rosenblatt1958perceptron}** introduced the **Perceptron**, the biological-inspired ancestor of the modern neuron. Shifting away from rigid symbolic logic, he proposed a system that could “learn” by automatically adjusting its weights in response to errors. This marked a pivotal transition from hard-coded programming to the foundational principles of machine learning. The HNF blog's history of the McCulloch-Pitts paper follows their 1943 “logical calculus” from that first mathematical neuron to the networks that followed \cite{hnfmccullochpitts2023}.
blocks.section: The Perceptron: Rosenblatt's Brain Model (1957-1962)

blocks.quote: Frank Rosenblatt (\cite[Frank Rosenblatt, HNF]{rosenblatt_portrait})
blocks.section: The Perceptron: Rosenblatt's Brain Model (1957-1962)

blocks.quote: This project was funded by the *Office of Naval Research*, under the codename *Project Para*. Its first description was a 1957 Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory report, 85-460-1, and the simulations ran on an IBM 704 (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1957]{rosenblattperceptron}).
blocks.section: The Perceptron: Rosenblatt's Brain Model (1957-1962)

blocks.quote: \citetitle{mark_i_perceptron_manual}
blocks.section: The Perceptron: Rosenblatt's Brain Model (1957-1962)

blocks.quote: The Mark I Perceptron, the experimental letter-recognising machine built by Frank Rosenblatt's group and announced by the U.S. Navy. Photo: \cite[U.S. Navy]{perceptronimagedetection}, public domain.
blocks.section: The Perceptron: Rosenblatt's Brain Model (1957-1962)

blocks.quote: The Mark I and the First Hype (1958)
blocks.section: The Mark I and the First Hype (1958)

blocks.quote: The Mark I Perceptron, shown in Figure 2 of its operator's manual (\cite[Mark I Perceptron, operator's manual]{mark_i_perceptron_manual}).
blocks.section: The Mark I and the First Hype (1958)

blocks.quote: His physical implementation, the **Mark I Perceptron**, was a massive hardware system at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo. The perceptron was announced in 1958, but the Mark I itself was constructed between 1958 and 1960 and publicly demonstrated in 1960: a 20×20 grid of 400 photocells formed its retina, and electric motors turned the potentiometers that held the “weights” (\cite[Lefkowitz, 2019]{lefkowitz2019perceptron}; \cite[Jensen & Dunning, 2026]{jensen2026perceptron}). While limited to learning simple linear relationships, a constraint that eventually contributed to the first AI Winter, it established the fundamental architecture of weighted inputs and thresholds that powers every neural network today.
blocks.section: The Mark I and the First Hype (1958)

blocks.quote: The design was an **alpha-perceptron**: three layers, a pixel “retina”, a set of association units wired to random subsets of it, and one or more output units whose pattern of 1s and 0s named the category of the image. Perceptrons were never only about pictures, though: his follow-on machine, **Tobermory**, named after the cat in \citetitle{saki1911clovis}, was designed for *speech recognition* (\cite[Lefkowitz, 2019]{lefkowitz2019perceptron}).
blocks.section: The Mark I and the First Hype (1958)

blocks.quote: In 1959 he moved the work to Cornell University in Ithaca, where he became a professor of psychology and several Ph.D. students, including **George Nagy**, Carl Kessler, and R. D. Joseph, completed perceptron projects under him; in his last years he drifted further from hardware into the stranger territory of *chemical memory transfer* in flatworms and other animals, even publishing with Farrow and Rhine in 1966 on transferring learned behavior from trained rats to untrained ones by means of brain extracts. He died in a sailing accident in Chesapeake Bay in 1971, two years after Minsky and Papert's critique appeared (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
blocks.section: The Mark I and the First Hype (1958)

blocks.quote: \sideimage[float]{navy.png}{\citealternativetitle{newyorktimesperceptron}, \citeyear{newyorktimesperceptron}}
blocks.section: The Mark I and the First Hype (1958)

blocks.quote: When Frank Rosenblatt introduced the \citealternativetitle{rosenblattperceptron}, the press did not file it as one clever experiment among many; it treated it as the dawn of machine consciousness. At a 1958 United States Navy press conference, Rosenblatt's remarks opened a firestorm inside the fledgling AI community, and *The New York Times* seized on it, describing the Perceptron as “the embryo of an electronic computer that [the Navy] expects will be able to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence” (\cite[Kowitz, 2017]{ronkowitz2017perceptron}). That was the same framing the paper had already given it \cite{newyorktimesperceptron}: a machine that would eventually walk, talk, think, and even translate languages. What made the hype endure is that most of Rosenblatt's predictions were, in the end, surprisingly accurate. The coverage was even more literal than is usually remembered: it reported Perceptrons might one day be **fired to the planets as mechanical space explorers** \cite{newyorktimesperceptron}. Six decades later, on the Martian surface, that prediction was quietly realized, when NASA's Perseverance rover used autonomous target selection (**AEGIS**) and hazard-avoidant path planning (**ENav**) to choose which rocks to drill and how to steer around boulders without waiting for a human in Mission Control to tell it to (\cite{estlin2009aegis}; \cite{toupet2025enav}).
blocks.section: The Mark I and the First Hype (1958)

blocks.quote: Between the invention of the Perceptron in 1958 and the release of ChatGPT, were 64 years of development, until all Rosenblatt envisioned became true. As such, this is a case of a \citealternativetitle{sleepingbeauty} invention.
blocks.section: The Mark I and the First Hype (1958)

blocks.quote: What the Mark I Could Actually Do
blocks.section: What the Mark I Could Actually Do

blocks.quote: Rosenblatt's \cite[Mark I Perceptron]{perceptronresults} (p. 136) achieved up to 100% accuracy on binary classification tasks like shape and letter recognition using single-layer architectures of 500 to 1,000 neurons. Across various experiments, it processed training sets of 20 to 10,000 images, maintaining high performance (80% to 100%) despite variations in position and rotation (\cite{rosenblattperceptronresults}).
blocks.section: What the Mark I Could Actually Do

blocks.quote: A \citeyear{jensen2026perceptron} \cite{jensen2026perceptron} by the historian George Osborn Jensen and the Smithsonian curator David E. Dunning reconstructs the Mark I from the perspective of Thomas Osborn, a Cornell undergraduate hired as a “worker bee” at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo to solder its six-foot racks in the fall of 1959. The architecture mapped a 20×20 grid of photocell “S-units” onto **512** association units, whose connections were generated as genuinely random numbers on CAL's IBM 704 and then wired by hand.
blocks.section: What the Mark I Could Actually Do

blocks.quote: Each A-unit's output passed through a motor-driven potentiometer whose wiper voltage could swing continuously between −11 and +11 V, so “between zero and one there was any number in-between”: the “memory” of the machine was literally the angle of 512 little motors, updated automatically by the feedback loop. The single most striking finding from the testing phase was empirical: introducing a deliberate rate of **forgetting** (resistors allowed to decay slightly between iterations) dramatically sped up learning by preventing the network from overfitting idiosyncrasies of the first few examples, an early, hardware-level instance of what would later be formalized as weight decay.
blocks.section: What the Mark I Could Actually Do

blocks.quote: The Mark I never served its intended Pentagon mission of spotting Soviet missile sites from aerial photographs, but Osborn could train it to around 90 to 95% accuracy on letter recognition, and the team agreed it had done “what it said it was going to do.” After Osborn left Buffalo, “no one said one word to me about it”; he went on to become a quantum physicist at the University of Manitoba, a quiet reminder that landmark devices are also the product of anonymous assembly work.
blocks.section: What the Mark I Could Actually Do

blocks.quote: A \citeyear{lindquist2026weirdai} \cite{lindquist2026weirdai} in the same “Think Piece” department argues that midcentury neural-AI architects (Rosenblatt, then Rumelhart, Hinton, McClelland and the PDP group in the 1980s) deliberately engineered **nonrationality** into their machines rather than stumbling onto it. Lindquist reads the perceptron, and later PDP, as part of a Romantic countercurrent inside computing, a refusal to reduce thought to logical manipulation. In the original \citeyear{darthmouthartificialintelligence} proposal, IBM engineer **Nathaniel Rochester** himself argued that introducing randomness into neural networks could foster originality, comparing the effect to dreaming or intoxication. When Minsky and Papert wrote in \citetitle{minskyperceptrons} that perceptron work was “romantic,” they meant it as a *critique*; the PDP community later wore the label as a badge of pride. What we now dismiss as LLM “hallucinations,” Lindquist points out, is essentially the same property midcentury researchers deliberately prized: outputs landing in the thin tails of the probability distribution, the unreliability from which surprising new associations were supposed to emerge. Modern accounts that frame today's neural nets as a product of “big data and GPUs” alone miss that the original appeal of the architecture was never just pattern-matching; it was a wager that a machine which occasionally did the unexpected could be more useful than one which never did.
blocks.section: What the Mark I Could Actually Do

blocks.quote: The Geometry of a Neuron: Planes and Hyperplanes
blocks.section: The Geometry of a Neuron: Planes and Hyperplanes

blocks.quote: In algebra, such an equation defines a **plane**, a linear boundary, in the three-dimensional space of possible inputs: every input vector on one side of the plane makes the element fire, every vector on the other side leaves it silent. Training a perceptron is nothing more than moving and rotating that plane until the inputs that should fire and the inputs that should not end up on opposite sides. Changing the weights *rotates* the plane; changing the threshold *slides* it sideways, parallel to itself. Every step of the learning rule is a small rotation or slide of that plane. In more than three dimensions the same object is called a **hyperplane**: impossible to draw, mathematically identical, which is why a network trained on 784 pixel inputs is doing exactly this, just 784 dimensions at a time (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
blocks.section: The Geometry of a Neuron: Planes and Hyperplanes

blocks.quote: From Hebb's Rule to Error Correction
blocks.section: From Hebb's Rule to Error Correction

blocks.quote: The Perceptron learning rule $\Delta w = \eta \cdot (\text{target} - \text{output}) \cdot \text{input}$ is not a fundamentally new idea: it is Hebb's rule made precise by adding an error signal.
blocks.section: From Hebb's Rule to Error Correction

blocks.quote: Hebb's rule states: “Neurons that fire together, wire together.” The weight between two neurons increases when they activate simultaneously. This is an unsupervised, purely correlation-based rule, it strengthens connections regardless of whether the result is correct or not.
blocks.section: From Hebb's Rule to Error Correction

blocks.quote: Rosenblatt's Perceptron learning rule takes the same biological intuition but adds a critical component: **error correction**. When the output matches the target, $\Delta w = 0$, no change occurs, just as Hebb would predict (the firing pattern is consistent, so no adjustment is needed). But when there is an error, the weight changes in proportion to the input, scaled by the learning rate $\eta$:
blocks.section: From Hebb's Rule to Error Correction

blocks.quote: Rosenblatt did not invent a new biological principle; he gave Hebb's intuitive idea a mathematical error-correction mechanism.
blocks.section: From Hebb's Rule to Error Correction

blocks.quote: The central theoretical result was the **perceptron convergence theorem**: for any classification whose classes are linearly separable, the error-correction rule makes only finitely many mistakes and therefore reaches a correct weight setting. Proofs appeared in Rosenblatt's 1962 book and, independently, in work by H. D. Block and A. B. J. Novikoff in the same period (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1962]{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}; \cite[Block, 1962]{block1962perceptron}; \cite[Novikoff, 1963]{novikoff1963convergence}).
blocks.section: From Hebb's Rule to Error Correction

blocks.quote: The separability requirement was the theorem's sharp edge: a single adaptive layer can only represent linearly separable functions, and characterizing that limit became the substance of the Minsky-Papert critique.
blocks.section: From Hebb's Rule to Error Correction

blocks.quote: This connection foreshadows a deeper pattern in deep learning: nearly every major advance can be understood as taking a simple, intuitive principle (correlation, smoothness, sparsity) and making it differentiable. Hebb's correlation becomes the Perceptron; the smoothness prior becomes weight decay; sparsity becomes ReLU.
blocks.section: From Hebb's Rule to Error Correction

blocks.quote: These early neural networks were extremely limited by today's standards, but they introduced the core idea of learning from data rather than hard-coded rules. This is called *connectionist approach*, instead of the *symbolic approach*. In the *symbol approach*, like the *Rechenmaschine* by Leibniz, the rules are all set from the beginning on. In connectionist approaches, the rules are not set by humans, but trained on by data. Modern LLMs are connectionist rather than symbolic.
blocks.section: From Hebb's Rule to Error Correction

blocks.quote: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Rosenblatt's \citetitle{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics} (1962) is the book in which the scattered reports, proofs, and hardware results of the preceding five years were gathered into a single theory. He wrote it across the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo and Cornell University in Ithaca, both funded by the Office of Naval Research, and dated the preface 15 March 1961. Its four parts move from background and definitions, through the three-layer “minimal” perceptrons that had actually been analysed, to multi-layer and cross-coupled systems, and finally to back-coupled perceptrons and open problems (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1962]{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}). The aim was not a pattern-recognition gadget: “A perceptron is first and foremost a brain model, not an invention for pattern recognition,” Rosenblatt wrote, and its utility lay “in enabling us to determine the physical conditions for the emergence of various psychological properties” (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1962]{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}).
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: The surrounding papers fill in the formal and experimental edges: \citetitle{rosenblatt1959twotheorems} (1959) presented early separability results at the National Physical Laboratory symposium, \citetitle{rosenblatt1960simulation} (1960) reported the IBM 704 simulations, and \citetitle{rosenblatt1967recentwork} (1967) marks the later shift from pattern recognition to the biology of memory.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Part I is a history and defence of the brain-model programme, and it remains one of the clearest maps of the terrain the perceptron grew out of. Rosenblatt sorted the field into two strategies. **Monotypic** models begin with a specified psychological function and design a network to compute it; the McCulloch-Pitts logical neuron and the automata built on it are the canonical case, and Rosenblatt praised their analytic power while judging them overdetermined, biologically implausible, and unable to yield general laws of organization (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1962]{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}). **Genotypic** models begin instead with statistical rules for generating a whole class of networks and ask what such networks typically do. That was the road Rosenblatt took, and it is why probability theory rather than symbolic logic is the native language of perceptron theory \cite{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: The book is explicit about its debts, and they go well beyond McCulloch and Pitts. Rosenblatt names the theories of Hebb and Hayek and the experimental findings of Lashley as the main influences on his philosophical approach, and his probabilistic outlook as shared with Ashby, Uttley, Minsky, MacKay, and von Neumann \cite{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}. Hebb's \citetitle{hebb1949organizationofbehaviour} supplied the idea that repeatedly co-active neurons become linked into “cell assemblies” and “phase sequences”; Rosenblatt found it too programmatic and too loose in its definitions to test rigorously, yet close enough to a model that Rochester's IBM group could fill in the missing detail and run it (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1962]{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}). Hayek's \citetitle{hayek1952sensoryorder} treated recognition as a problem of classification, a framing that directly inspired Uttley's classifying automata; Rosenblatt placed Hebb and Hayek together, in the tradition of Mill and Helmholtz, as attempts to show how an organism builds perceptual capabilities through maturation and learning \cite{hayek1952sensoryorder, rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Lashley is the third leg of the tripod, and the one most often left out of later summaries. Rosenblatt says the perceptron began as an attempt to explain the “distributed memory” and “equipotentiality” that Lashley had found in rats with cortical lesions: memory did not sit in a single store but seemed spread across the cortex, with the size of the lesion mattering more than its location (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1962]{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}). In \citetitle{lashley1929brainmechanisms}, Lashley reported that ablation produced a general deficit proportional to the amount of cortex removed rather than wiping out specific memories, a result that shaped the genotypic picture of a brain whose fine wiring is statistical rather than a fixed blueprint \cite{lashley1929brainmechanisms, rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}. Rosenblatt notes that later work modified the extreme hypothesis of equipotentiality toward “relative localization”: strict for sensory projection areas, weak for association cortex, memory, and higher control \cite{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: The rest of Rosenblatt's list marks the probabilistic wing of mid-century brain theory. Ashby's \citetitle{ashbydesigndbrain1952} supplied two things Rosenblatt explicitly used.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Minsky's 1954 Princeton thesis on neural nets and the brain-model problem \cite{minsky1954} belongs to the same conversation, as do Uttley's conditional-probability machines, MacKay's work on the representation of perceptual information, and von Neumann's analyses of reliable computation from unreliable components (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1962]{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}). What united them was not a shared architecture but a shared wager: that the brain is not a conventional digital computer with statistics bolted on, and that a theory which leaves out probability and adaptation will fail to account for psychological performance.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Rosenblatt is remembered for machine learning, but in \citeyear{rosenblatt1971twocolor} he also published a paper in *Icarus* on how to detect planets around other stars \cite{rosenblatt1971twocolor}. A planet crossing a star's disk leaves a *color* signature, not merely a dip in brightness: because the stellar limb is darker and redder than the center, the transit first shifts the light slightly toward the blue as the planet crosses the limb, reddens it abnormally while the planet covers the central region, and shifts it toward the blue again near the far limb \cite{rosenblatt1971twocolor}. He estimated the chances of catching such transits, sketched the necessary instrumentation, and proposed three wide-field telescopes at well-separated sites, slaved to a central computer, each carrying a two-color photometer built around an image dissector that could switch rapidly between program stars without frequent resetting; once one telescope saw an unusual transient, all three would observe it as a coincidence detector (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1971]{rosenblatt1971twocolor}). The same man who tried to build a machine that could see also designed an instrument to watch other worlds.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: The idea was implemented long after his death: the French satellite CoRoT, launched in 2006, and NASA's Kepler and TESS missions turned transit photometry into a planet-hunting industry, and by the time the HNF blog published its portrait of Rosenblatt they had found more than 2,700 exoplanets \cite{hnfrosenblatt2019}.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Rosenblatt's interests were unusually broad even by the standards of a field that had not yet drawn its borders. His 1956 Cornell doctorate was in psychology, and his thesis work on multivariate analysis pushed him into building a custom computer, the **Electronic Profile Analyzing Computer (EPAC)**, to process survey data \cite{frankrosenblattwiki}. From 1966 he ran a second research programme on the transfer of learned behaviour between rats by injecting brain extracts; his later, more controlled comparison of two procedures found the effect unstable in the symmetric choice task and strongly dependent on dosage and test design \cite{rosenblatt1966transfer1, rosenblatt1966transfer2, rosenblatt1969behavior}. He gave an annual course on **Brain Mechanisms and Models** at Cornell \cite{rosenblattmemorial1971}. Outside the laboratory he composed music and was active in liberal politics, applying computer techniques to political statistics, working on Eugene McCarthy's 1968 primary campaigns and joining Vietnam War protests; at Cornell he helped channel the 1969 student upheavals into a Constituent Assembly and a University Senate \cite{rosenblattmemorial1971}.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Biographers James E. Dobson and Rena J. Mosteirin describe him as a psychologist, a computer engineer, a musician, an amateur astronomer, a sailor, and a poet, a “renaissance man” who kept crossing disciplinary lines \cite{dobson2025perceptron}.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Their open-access *Perceptron* (2025) uses letters, postcards, photographs, and invented poetic forms to recover the person behind the machine, and the Dartmouth Libraries' account describes it as a biography of a gay man \cite{dartmouthrosenblatt2026}. The recollections collected by the UMass computational-phonology blog are more cautious: Terry Koken, who worked for Rosenblatt and lived in his house, remembered him as “a confirmed bachelor” who showed no visible interest in the opposite sex, and said that whether he had any interest in the same sex was something his colleagues never speculated about \cite{koken2021remembering}. A woman who knew him recalls in the same comment thread that he proposed marriage to her in 1963-64 while saying he would not expect sex, and that he was deeply attached to a male student to whom he left his estate \cite{koken2021remembering}. The sources do not settle the question; what is clear is that his intimate life was private, and that he refused to “professionalize” his students, preferring to point them in several directions at once \cite{dartmouthrosenblatt2026}.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: The same Dartmouth account photographs him at home in “Chateau Rosenblatt,” a reminder that the man who tried to mechanize perception also had a life of music, love, and sailing outside the laboratory \cite{dartmouthrosenblatt2026}. Mosteirin's hope for readers is simple: “not to box yourself in and to keep dreaming and imagining and being weird” \cite{dartmouthrosenblatt2026}.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Donald Hebb took a long road to the neuron. He entered Dalhousie wanting to become a novelist, taught school in Nova Scotia, worked on a farm and as a labourer, and only then turned to psychology; his 1949 *The Organization of Behavior* gave the field the learning rule that still bears his name \cite{hebbwiki, hebb1949organizationofbehaviour}. His students included Brenda Milner, who became a pioneer of memory research, a reminder that the “Hebbian” idea was embedded in a living teaching tradition, not just a formula \cite{hebbwiki}.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert were an unlikely, formidable pair. Minsky built the SNARC from vacuum tubes and salvaged B-24 bomber gyropilots, invented an early confocal microscope and a head-mounted graphical display, and later wrote \citetitle{minsky1986society} (\cite{minskywiki}). Papert grew up in Pretoria, opposed apartheid as a student, worked with Piaget in Geneva, and came to MIT to build LOGO and the idea of constructionism: children learning mathematics by programming turtles \cite{hnfpapert2016}. Their 1969 \citetitle{minskyperceptrons} is often remembered as the book that ended the first perceptron boom, but it was written by two people who were themselves trying to understand how minds and machines learn.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: Joseph Weizenbaum was born in Berlin to Jewish parents and escaped Nazi Germany with his family in 1936; he served as a meteorologist during the war, worked on early computers, and in 1966 built ELIZA \cite{hnfweizenbaum2023}. What disturbed him was not the program but the people: users confided in it, and he spent the rest of his career asking what computers should not do \cite{weizenbaum1976computer}. His *Computer Power and Human Reason* remains one of the clearest moral voices from inside the field.
blocks.section: Principles of Neurodynamics (1962): The Brain-Model Manifesto

blocks.quote: The Wider Network Boom: Many Roads to Learning (1959-1968)
blocks.section: The Wider Network Boom: Many Roads to Learning (1959-1968)

blocks.quote: ADALINE: An Engineer's Neural Network (1959)
blocks.section: ADALINE: An Engineer's Neural Network (1959)

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{img_widrow_adaline} (Public Domain): \citeauthor{widrow1960adaline} with the ADALINE machine, 1963.
blocks.section: ADALINE: An Engineer's Neural Network (1959)

blocks.quote: While Rosenblatt was modeling the brain, a second tradition was building neural nets as *control instruments*. \citeauthor{widrow1960adaline}, an electrical engineer who had just joined Stanford after a Ph.D. in control theory at MIT, wanted neural networks for what he called **adaptive control**: a controller whose own parameters adjust themselves to the plant it regulates. His **ADALINE** (ADaptive LInear NEtwork) was a single neural element whose adjustable weights were implemented as switchable resistor circuits, and he and one of his students, **Marcian "Ted" Hoff Jr.** (who would a decade later invent the first microprocessor at Intel) built a "memistor" for the weights: a graphite rod on which a thin layer of copper could be electroplated or stripped off, varying its resistance. The training procedure they developed, the **Widrow-Hoff least-mean-squares (LMS) algorithm** \cite{widrow1960adaline}, is the direct ancestor of the delta rule. A stack of ADALINEs, a **MADALINE**, was trained by Stanford Ph.D. student William Ridgway (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}). Most of the work was simulation on an IBM 1620; the hardware was the argument that the idea was real.
blocks.section: ADALINE: An Engineer's Neural Network (1959)

blocks.quote: Roberts 1960: The First Multilayer Pattern Recognizer
blocks.section: Roberts 1960: The First Multilayer Pattern Recognizer

blocks.quote: The first publicly-documented working **multilayer feedforward pattern recognizer with adaptive weights** is \citeauthor{roberts1960perceptron}'s (\citeyear{roberts1960perceptron}) "Pattern Recognition with an Adaptive Network", a 1960 technical report from the **Aerospace Corporation** in El Segundo, California, the same \citeauthor{roberts1960perceptron} who, five years later, would draw the engineering sketch for **ARPANET** and earn a place in the canonical photograph of the ARPA principals. Roberts's report describes a small *two-layer* adaptive network (a *fixed* feature-extraction layer built of random feature detectors, followed by a *trained* classification layer built of adjustable threshold units) trained on hand-printed letters, and demonstrates that the network learns the classification task end-to-end. The training procedure was a perceptron-style error-correction rule, but the *architecture* (a non-trainable feature front-end feeding a trainable classifier) is the template that every modern convolutional network still uses, with the random-feature front-end replaced by learned convolutional filters.
blocks.section: Roberts 1960: The First Multilayer Pattern Recognizer

blocks.quote: The historical weight is two-fold. First, Roberts's report is the earliest known working *multi-layer* neural-network system: the *x*, *y* retinal coordinates of an image go through a bank of feature detectors (the *first* layer), then through a bank of threshold units with adjustable weights (the *second* layer), and the network as a whole is trained by adjusting only the second layer's weights. The pattern of *fixed* front-end, *trained* back-end is what the modern convolutional net inherits; the *fully* trainable version came later, with Ivakhnenko's GMDH (1965) and the modern backprop-trained ConvNets of the 1990s. Second, the report is a small, clean, working example of a *deep* system solving a real visual task at a moment when the field's leading lights were still arguing about whether one layer could solve XOR. The standard Anglophone narrative tells the multilayer story as if it begins with Ivakhnenko's GMDH or Fukushima's Neocognitron; in fact it begins here, with a 1960 technical report from an aerospace contractor that the standard history skipped.
blocks.section: Roberts 1960: The First Multilayer Pattern Recognizer

blocks.quote: Steinbuch 1961: The Learning Matrix: Hardware Associative Memory
blocks.section: Steinbuch 1961: The Learning Matrix: Hardware Associative Memory

blocks.quote: In January 1961, in the first issue of the new journal *Kybernetik*, the German communications engineer \citeauthor{steinbuch1961matrix} published "Die Lernmatrix", a circuit for learning Pavlovian "conditioned reflexes" out of wires and threshold elements rather than out of a stored program \cite{steinbuch1961matrix}. Steinbuch was professor at the Technische Hochschule Karlsruhe, where he directed the Institute for Information Processing and Communication; the work was funded largely by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, and the paper names the small team of engineers and physicists around him. The paper was not an isolated publication: on 13-14 April 1961, two days after Yuri Gagarin's flight, the TH Karlsruhe hosted a conference on learning automata organised by the Nachrichtentechnische Gesellschaft of the VDE, with the Lernmatrix as its centrepiece, probably the first German conference devoted to what would soon be called artificial intelligence \cite{hnflernendeautomaten2021}.
blocks.section: Steinbuch 1961: The Learning Matrix: Hardware Associative Memory

blocks.quote: The Lernmatrix is the missing link between the 1943 McCulloch-Pitts logical neuron and the 1982 Hopfield attractor network. Like the perceptron, it learns input-output associations from examples; unlike the perceptron, it has no error-correction rule, no convergence proof, and no gradient: it accumulates a coincidence statistic and thresholds it.
blocks.section: Steinbuch 1961: The Learning Matrix: Hardware Associative Memory

blocks.quote: The 1980s "discovery" of associative memory had a 1961 hardware ancestor, and the Anglophone narrative of neural networks usually skips it entirely: the German school of cybernetics around Steinbuch had its own journal (*Kybernetik*, founded in 1961), its own conferences, and its own industrial and public funding, and the Lernmatrix was its flagship contribution. The lesson is not that Steinbuch's matrix was "better" than the perceptron (for many tasks the perceptron's convergence guarantee was decisive), but that the *associative-memory* idea was already an engineering project in 1961, two decades before the cognitive-science revival made it famous.
blocks.section: Steinbuch 1961: The Learning Matrix: Hardware Associative Memory

blocks.quote: Joseph 1961: Putting the Perceptron on a Probabilistic Footing
blocks.section: Joseph 1961: Putting the Perceptron on a Probabilistic Footing

blocks.quote: The fullest primary snapshot of the field's state of play in 1961 is the Cornell PhD thesis of **\citeauthor{joseph1961perceptron}**, *\citetitle{joseph1961perceptron}* (\citeyear{joseph1961perceptron}) \cite{joseph1961perceptron}. Joseph was not a typical student: a self-taught mathematician who had been doing analyses of self-organizing systems at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, and who completed his doctorate while working in industry, first at the lab and then at Ford's Aeronutronic Division. His thesis advisor was the famous probabilist **\cite[Mark Kac]{markkac}**, which explains the heavily measure-theoretic style, and the work was funded by the Office of Naval Research and the Rome Air Development Center, the same Cold War military money that underwrote nearly all early neural-net research.
blocks.section: Joseph 1961: Putting the Perceptron on a Probabilistic Footing

blocks.quote: Joseph's central contribution was to take the perceptron results of the previous few years, which he judged to rest partly on heuristic arguments with inaccurate supporting formulae (though not incorrect conclusions), and to put them on a rigorous probabilistic footing \cite{joseph1961perceptron}. His most strikingly modern move was to stop asking about one hand-designed circuit and instead place a **probability distribution over an entire class of networks**: fix the retina, the number of association units, the threshold, a reinforcement rule and a measure over which sensory units feed each association unit, then ask what *fraction* of randomly wired members of the class meets a given performance standard. That is an early formal version of asking about the *typical* behavior of a random architecture, decades before such typical-case reasoning became standard. He contrasts the field's two research programs, a **statistical** one (analyze a randomly drawn member of a network class, what nearly all work up to about 1960 did) and an **optimality** one (find the best components and operating procedure under constraints), and his thesis makes the first rigorous while adding some of the second \cite{joseph1961perceptron}. It also already treats multi-layer (four-layer) perceptrons, bounded or saturating weights, and cross-coupled (recurrent) networks as first-class objects.
blocks.section: Joseph 1961: Putting the Perceptron on a Probabilistic Footing

blocks.quote: The Real History of the Perceptron Convergence Theorem
blocks.section: The Real History of the Perceptron Convergence Theorem

blocks.quote: Textbooks usually credit the "perceptron convergence theorem" to Rosenblatt (with Block and Novikoff), but Joseph's survey is a rare, candid record of how collaborative and messy the real provenance was \cite{joseph1961perceptron}. His account runs, roughly:
blocks.section: The Real History of the Perceptron Convergence Theorem

blocks.quote: The same survey records a related trick from the **Block, Knight and Rosenblatt** line: for a very large, nearly random network, or for one trained in extremely small steps, replace the *difference* equation governing the stored weights with a *differential* equation so the weights evolve monotonically and their limiting values can be read off. Joseph carefully labels this a *third* kind of analysis, neither statistical (a fraction of a class succeeds) nor exact (a single specified machine).
blocks.section: The Real History of the Perceptron Convergence Theorem

blocks.quote: Uhr & Vossler 1961: A Program That Invents Its Own Operators
blocks.section: Uhr & Vossler 1961: A Program That Invents Its Own Operators

blocks.quote: The deepest critique of the *hand-engineered feature* tradition in 1960s pattern recognition came from a programme, not a theory. In their paper "A Pattern-Recognition Program That Generates, Evaluates, and Adjusts Its Own Operators", \citeauthor{uhrvossler1961operators} (\citeyear{uhrvossler1961operators}) at the University of Wisconsin described a program that *learned* the feature operators end-to-end, rather than being told which ones to use. The Uhr-Vossler system started with a small, randomly-initialised pool of candidate operators (local feature extractors: dot-product masks, threshold comparisons, simple linear filters), combined them into longer composite operators, evaluated the *whole population* on the training task, retained the best-scoring variants, generated new variants by mutation-and-recombination, and iterated. The program was, in modern vocabulary, an *evolutionary* learner over a *symbolic-regression* space of feature operators, with the population-level evaluation serving as the fitness function.
blocks.section: Uhr & Vossler 1961: A Program That Invents Its Own Operators

blocks.quote: The paper anticipates three things that would not be rediscovered for decades. First, it anticipates **AutoML** and **neural architecture search**: the modern recognition that the *operators* the model uses are themselves a variable to be optimised, and that a search over operator space can outperform hand-designed operators once compute is available. Second, it anticipates the **genetic-programming** line of Koza in the 1980s and 1990s, in which the program *text* itself is the chromosome; Uhr and Vossler's composite operators are a small step away from Koza's full LISP programs, and the evolutionary loop is essentially the same. Third, and most strikingly for this course, it anticipates the modern **LLM-tool-discovery** line: where a modern agent learns to *use* tools (a calculator, a search engine, a code interpreter) as primitive operations whose compositions the model learns to drive, Uhr and Vossler's system learned to *use* feature operators as primitive operations whose compositions the program learned to drive. The same structural pattern (*a learner that picks which operator to invoke on which input, with the operators themselves partly plastic*) shows up in three fields (AutoML, GP, agents) sixty years apart, because it is genuinely the right way to delegate work that the programmer does not want to specify by hand.
blocks.section: Uhr & Vossler 1961: A Program That Invents Its Own Operators

blocks.quote: The Wider Field in 1961
blocks.section: The Wider Field in 1961

blocks.quote: The thesis's closing survey is a snapshot of how distributed the early-1960s scene already was. At the Aeronutronic/Ford group someone was building an adaptive neuron, the **MIND** element, on a square-loop magnetic core whose magnetic state encoded connection strength, analog weights in physical hardware. There were working groups on the limits of **majority logic** (the circuits a fully self-organized perceptron reduces to, Joseph notes), on **front-end feature extraction** (translating raw patterns into a form a classifier can use, the focus of Von Foerster's group at Illinois and of Sebestyen at Litton), and on military applications of the machinery. And at Stanford, **\citeauthor{widrow1960adaline}** and his student were analyzing the same adaptive systems with the tools of **servo theory**, the \citeyear{widrow1960adaline} *ADALINE* and LMS (delta-rule) line \cite{widrow1960adaline} that eventually leads, through backpropagation, to deep learning. Joseph's closing note is quietly proud and a little defensive: the field was attracting capable people from many directions, and although Cornell had benefited from all that outside activity, there was no reason to change the direction of the Cornell program in any fundamental way \cite{joseph1961perceptron}. At the same time, at Sandia Laboratories, **Woodrow Bledsoe** and **Iben Browning** were winning character-recognition work with a rival idea, the **N-tuple method**: project a character onto a 10×15 mosaic of photocells, sample 75 randomly chosen *pairs* of cells, and let the tally of which pairs light up vote for the letter, a statistical template scheme with no learned weights at all that rivaled the perceptron for a decade (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
blocks.section: The Wider Field in 1961

blocks.quote: MINOS: The SRI Learning Machines (1960s)
blocks.section: MINOS: The SRI Learning Machines (1960s)

blocks.quote: The same decade produced the most ambitious neural hardware after the Mark I: the **MINOS** systems at the Stanford Research Institute. (The name comes from Greek mythology: Minos, king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa, who after his death became one of the three judges of the underworld.) Charles A. Rosen, who was trying to etch microscopic vacuum tubes onto a solid-state substrate, had hired Frank Rosenblatt as a consultant, and Rosenblatt stayed in close contact with SRI because he hoped Brain's new magnetic weight devices could replace the Mark I's motor-driven potentiometers. Alfred "Ted" Brain's team then built a small network, MINOS, rather than simulating it, because on the IBM 1620 a simulation cycle took 21 microseconds and random-access memory held 60,000 digits. Funded by the U.S. Army Signal Corps from 1958 to 1967, the MINOS line aimed at a concrete military job: automatic recognition of symbols on maps. In MINOS II each input image was replicated 100 times through a 10×10 array of plastic lenses, each copy passed through its own optical feature mask, and the resulting 100 binary features fed 63 neural elements with 100 variable *magnetic* weights each; the 63 binary outputs addressed one of 64 equally distant prototype points in a 63-dimensional space, each prototype encoding one symbol category (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
blocks.section: MINOS: The SRI Learning Machines (1960s)

blocks.quote: By the mid-1960s the group, by then called the **Learning Machines Group**, had moved to **MINOS III**: the network's front end had grown to an array of 1,024 lenses, and the net now ran alongside an SDS 910, one of the first computers built with silicon transistors. Its most successful application, reading hand-printed FORTRAN coding sheets (led by John Munson, Peter Hart, and Richard Duda), achieved just over 98 percent accuracy on a large sample of material the system had never been trained on, and anticipated a design pattern that would dominate for a century: the net ranked the candidate letters for each character with a confidence score, and a **dynamic-programming** pass then chose, among all possible strings, the one with the highest total confidence that was also *legal FORTRAN*.
