The neural net proposed, the language vetoed, and search combined the two, the same division of labor a modern OCR pipeline still runs. The Learning Machines Group ultimately became the SRI Artificial Intelligence Center.
blocks.section: MINOS: The SRI Learning Machines (1960s)

blocks.quote: Ivakhnenko 1965: The First Deep Learning
blocks.section: Ivakhnenko 1965: The First Deep Learning

blocks.quote: In parallel with the Anglophone debate over the limitations of single-layer perceptrons, deep learning was being developed independently in the Soviet Union. In \citeyear{ivakhnenko1965}, \citeauthorlastnameand{ivakhnenko1965} published the first general, working learning algorithms for deep multi-layer perceptrons with arbitrarily many hidden layers. Their method, known as the **Group Method of Data Handling (GMDH)**, incrementally grew and trained layers using regression analysis, pruning superfluous units via regularization on a separate validation set. By \citeyear{ivakhnenko1971}, Ivakhnenko described a deep learning network with **8 layers**, trained when compute was millions of times more expensive than today. Their networks learned hierarchical, distributed internal representations of incoming data, two decades before the term “connectionism” became fashionable in the 1980s. The work remained highly cited and popular well into the new millennium, especially in Eastern Europe, and is surveyed in \citeauthor{schmidhuber2022deep}'s annotated history alongside the Anglophone deep-learning lineage.
blocks.section: Ivakhnenko 1965: The First Deep Learning

blocks.quote: Bongard 1966: Learning Visual Concepts from Examples
blocks.section: Bongard 1966: Learning Visual Concepts from Examples

blocks.quote: A year after Ivakhnenko's GMDH, the Moscow Institute for Information Transmission Problems (IITP, the Soviet Academy of Sciences' centre for cybernetics) produced a different *kind* of Soviet machine-vision contribution. \citeauthor{bongard1966pattern} (\citeyear{bongard1966pattern}), working alone at IITP, with no team, no GPU, no internet, published a thin monograph, \citetitle{bongard1966pattern}, that introduced what the field now calls the **Bongard problems**: visual analogy puzzles of the form "*here are six pictures that share a feature, here are six that share a different feature, which feature* differentiates them", and demonstrated a small program that learned to *solve* them. The program's input was a set of line drawings; its output was the *rule* that distinguished the positive from the negative examples; the test of competence was whether the program could recover the rule on a held-out problem without being told it. \citeauthor{bongard1966pattern}'s system used a hand-engineered vocabulary of shape features (closure, intersection, parallel-line counts, eccentricity) and a learned linear classifier to weight the features; the *learning* was a perceptron-style error-correction rule over the classifier weights. The system was, in modern vocabulary, a **weakly-supervised shape-analogy learner**: given only labels of which examples were positive and which were negative, it had to discover the visual concept that separated them.
blocks.section: Bongard 1966: Learning Visual Concepts from Examples

blocks.quote: The work is striking for two reasons. First, \citeauthor{bongard1966pattern}'s 1966 system is the earliest known example of *programmatic visual-concept learning from examples*, and the structural template it established (a fixed feature front-end, a learned classifier on top, an analogy-test for competence) is what every modern few-shot vision system (matching networks, prototypical networks, CLIP) still uses. Second, the **Bongard problems** themselves became a famous benchmark in AI: the original IITP monograph, translated into English in 1970, laid out a collection of 100 problems that became the canonical "Bongard-100" benchmark used to evaluate AI visual-reasoning systems in the 2010s. The story also fits a wider pattern in this section: deep learning was being developed in the Soviet Union (Ivakhnenko), pattern recognition was being engineered in the Soviet Union (Bongard), and statistical learning theory was being formalised in the Soviet Union (Vapnik and Chervonenkis, below). The Anglosphere had Rosenblatt, Minsky, Widrow, and Rumelhart; the Soviet bloc had Ivakhnenko, Bongard, and Vapnik. The two lines converged in the 1980s and 1990s, and most modern deep learning is built on contributions from *both*.
blocks.section: Bongard 1966: Learning Visual Concepts from Examples

blocks.quote: End-to-End Learning by Gradient Descent (1967-68)
blocks.section: End-to-End Learning by Gradient Descent (1967-68)

blocks.quote: Two years after Ivakhnenko's layer-by-layer approach (so around 1967), \citeauthor{adaptivepattern} proposed training multi-layer perceptrons with many layers in end-to-end fashion using stochastic gradient descent (SGD). His student Saito implemented this in a **five-layer MLP with two modifiable layers**, which learned internal representations to classify non-linearly separable pattern classes, demonstrating that hidden units could discover useful features without explicit human engineering. This was achieved when compute was billions of times more expensive than today, and predates the popularization of backpropagation by nearly two decades.
blocks.section: End-to-End Learning by Gradient Descent (1967-68)

blocks.quote: In 1967, Shunichi Amari made a foundational contribution to the theory of adaptive pattern classifiers in \citetitle{adaptivepattern}.
blocks.section: End-to-End Learning by Gradient Descent (1967-68)

blocks.quote: His work addressed the problem of determining the optimal weight vector of linear pattern classifiers under general, potentially non-separable pattern distributions. Amari proposed a “probabilistic-descent method,” in which a correction vector is associated with each misclassified pattern such that, on average, the correction moves the discriminant function toward the optimum, even though any individual trial may worsen it. He proved that the weight vector converges to the optimal solution and revealed an important tradeoff between the speed and accuracy of convergence: a larger learning constant accelerates convergence but reduces final accuracy, while a smaller one improves accuracy at the cost of slower learning. He further generalized the theory to multicategory classifiers, piecewise-linear discriminant functions, and general nonlinear classifiers, and even introduced an adaptive scheme for learning the learning rule itself.
blocks.section: End-to-End Learning by Gradient Descent (1967-68)

blocks.quote: Natural Language Processing Before LLMs (1947-1966)
blocks.section: Natural Language Processing Before LLMs (1947-1966)

blocks.quote: Machine Translation: The Longest-Running Bet
blocks.section: Machine Translation: The Longest-Running Bet

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{img_warren_weaver} (Public Domain, \citeauthor{img_warren_weaver}, \citeyear{img_warren_weaver}): seven years before his 1947 letter proposing machine translation.
blocks.section: Machine Translation: The Longest-Running Bet

blocks.quote: Machine translation was one of the first uses proposed for computers beyond numerical calculation: word dictionaries could be stored in memory, and a machine could look up English equivalents for foreign words. In 1947, the mathematician and science administrator **Warren Weaver** wrote to **Norbert Wiener** asking whether a digital computer might translate between natural languages; Wiener, who had spent the war predicting where aircraft would be, was unconvinced: the boundaries of words in different languages, he replied, are "too vague" and their connotations "too extensive" for any quasi-mechanical scheme to hope on. The New York Times got there first in print: on May 31, 1949, it reported that a new "electric brain" under construction at the National Bureau of Standards laboratory (Harry D. Huskey's team at the University of California's Institute of Numerical Analysis) would be "capable not only of performing complex mathematical problems but even of translating foreign languages," by holding the 60,000 words of the Webster Collegiate Dictionary with equivalents in as many as three foreign languages. The machine had not yet translated anything, and the next day's editorial doubted it could: how would it know whether French "pont" meant "bridge" or "deck"? By July 1949, Weaver had elaborated the idea into a memorandum, "Translation", which he sent to some 200 colleagues, and which is generally credited with initiating the field of **machine translation (MT)** (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
blocks.section: Machine Translation: The Longest-Running Bet

blocks.quote: The first demonstration came faster than the skeptics expected. On January 7, 1954, a collaboration between **IBM** and **Georgetown University**, running on the IBM 701, translated short Russian sentences into English for a press audience (\cite{georgetown_ibm_1954}): a woman who "didn't understand a word of the language of the Soviets" punched *Mi pyeryedayem mislyi posryedstvom ryechyi*, and the machine printed "We transmit thoughts by means of speech" at two and a half lines per second. The funding surge that followed ran for a decade before crashing against the wall **Yehoshua Bar-Hillel** had already identified: a translating machine needs *world knowledge*. His example was a child who finds his toy box, "the box was in the pen", and a machine that knows only the two dictionary senses of *pen* cannot tell a writing instrument from a playpen, unless it also knows the relative sizes of pens, toy boxes, and pens. He concluded that fully automatic high-quality translation was infeasible "not only in the near future but altogether", and called the prospect of equipping computers with the required encyclopedic knowledge "utterly chimerical" (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
blocks.section: Machine Translation: The Longest-Running Bet

blocks.quote: The field's first winter was bureaucratic rather than mathematical: the US **ALPAC** report concluded that there was "no immediate or predictable prospect of useful machine translation", and large-scale funding vanished, leaving what MT's historian W. John Hutchins called the **"quiet decade"** (1967-1976). The American exception was **Systran**, built by **Petr Toma**, a Hungarian-born scientist from the Georgetown team: he founded Latsec in La Jolla in 1968, took a U.S. Air Force contract, and tested the system at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in 1969, where it "continues to provide Russian-English translations", its promoters claimed, for the Air Force's Foreign Technology Division to this day. By Margaret Boden's reckoning, Systran's intelligibility rose from 45% (1976) to 78% (1978), against 98-99% for human translators, and post-editing a page of its output took twenty minutes where a human translation took an hour. Machine translation, in other words, never died: it learned to survive as a tool for post-editors, until statistics and then neural networks carried it across the finish line.
blocks.section: Machine Translation: The Longest-Running Bet

blocks.quote: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years
blocks.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

blocks.quote: The Pāṇinian line of structural linguistics reaches its otherworldly culmination in a single short book, \citetitle{tesniere1959deps} (\citeyear{tesniere1959deps}), written by the French linguist \citeauthor{tesniere1959deps} (\citeyear{tesniere1959deps}) and published posthumously five years after his death. Tesnière's central claim is that the basic unit of syntactic description is not the **phrase** (as in Pāṇini's phrase-structure rules and in Chomsky's later constituent-structure trees) but the **dependency relation**: a directed link from a *governor* word to a *dependent* word. A sentence is, on this view, a **stemma**: a tree of word-to-word dependencies, with the main verb at the root and each word hanging directly off the word whose meaning it modifies, with no intermediate phrasal nodes. A simple sentence like "the cat sat on the mat" is one verb (*sat*) with three dependents (*the cat*, its subject; *on the mat*, its prepositional complement), each of which carries its own dependents (*the* on *cat*, *the* on *mat*).
blocks.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

blocks.quote: What is striking about Tesnière's framework is how much modern NLP silently inherits from it. Constituent-structure trees dominated the syntactic theory of the 1960s-80s and underlie most formal grammars, but the dependency view turned out to be a better match for the kinds of *local* relations that matter in practice (who is the subject of which verb, which noun does a pronoun refer to, which preposition links which argument), and modern dependency parsers now dominate the field. The Stanford, Universal Dependencies, spaCy, and Stanza parsers all produce exactly Tesnière's dependency trees, with typed governor→dependent relations like `nsubj`, `dobj`, `amod`, `prep`; Universal Dependencies' 200+ typologically diverse languages are precisely the kind of cross-linguistic coverage Tesnière would have wanted. The two are also formally equivalent in a precise sense: a constituent-structure tree can be derived from a dependency tree (by collapsing chains of head-dependent relations into phrasal nodes), and a *projective* dependency tree can be derived from a constituent-structure tree (by reading off the head of each constituent). The difference is not in *what can be expressed*; it is in *what is taken as primitive*, and on that question, the modern NLP field has voted for Tesnière.
blocks.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

blocks.quote: The deeper lesson is methodological. Tesnière's book appeared in 1959, only two years after Chomsky's *Syntactic Structures* (1957) and before Chomsky's constituent-structure frame had become dominant in generative linguistics, but the dependency idea was not new with him; it had been sketched by the Sanskrit grammarians, by the Roman *modistae*, and by Lucien Tesnière's own predecessors. The reason the framework is taking *forty years* to mature in NLP is partly that the computational tools needed to parse at scale (transition-based parsers, neural parsers, large dependency-banks) only became available in the 2000s, and partly that the *training data* (sentences annotated with dependency relations) only became widely available in 2014 with the Universal Dependencies project. The progress curve of dependency parsing looks, on the chart, much like the progress curve of every other old AI idea: the framework existed for decades; the right *representation* and *learning algorithm* took decades more; the moment it became usable, every system quietly switched to it.
blocks.section: Tesnière 1959: Dependency Grammar: French, Predates Modern NLP by 40 Years

blocks.quote: The Illusion of Empathy: The ELIZA-Effect
blocks.section: The Illusion of Empathy: The ELIZA-Effect

blocks.quote: I had not realized ... that extremely short exposures to a relatively simple computer program could induce powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people.
blocks.section: The Illusion of Empathy: The ELIZA-Effect

blocks.quote: In the era of Symbolic AI, before machines played chess at a master level, they attempted conversation. In 1966, **\citeauthor{weizenbaum1976computer}** created **ELIZA**, a program designed to parody a Rogerian psychotherapist \cite{hnfweizenbaum2023}.
blocks.section: The Illusion of Empathy: The ELIZA-Effect

blocks.quote: Unlike modern LLMs which calculate probabilities, ELIZA relied on simple pattern matching and substitution scripts. If a user typed “My mother hates me,” ELIZA might use a decomposition rule to transform “My X Y me” into “Who else in your family Y you?”
blocks.section: The Illusion of Empathy: The ELIZA-Effect

blocks.quote: Despite having no understanding of the world, users, including Weizenbaum's own secretary, attributed genuine human emotions and wisdom to the machine. Weizenbaum was so disturbed by this tendency of humans to project humanity onto code that he wrote \citealternativetitle{weizenbaum1976computer} to warn against the reliance on “deciding” machines over “choosing” humans.
blocks.section: The Illusion of Empathy: The ELIZA-Effect

blocks.quote: A \citeyear{lane2025eliza} \cite{lane2025eliza} reveals a surprising fact about ELIZA's history: the original program is not the version most historians have been writing about. Weizenbaum wrote ELIZA in MAD-SLIP at MIT's Project MAC, but the Lisp clone made soon after by Bernie Cosell at BBN, distributed through the ARPANet, supplanted the original within a few years; the BASIC re-implementation by Jeff Shrager in 1977 was what the wider public ever met. For decades the original MAD-SLIP source was assumed lost.
blocks.section: The Illusion of Empathy: The ELIZA-Effect

blocks.quote: In 2021, Shrager (coincidentally the same Jeff Shrager who wrote the 1977 BASIC version) and the MIT archivist Myles Crowley located a fan-fold printout of the original ELIZA, an early DOCTOR script, and substantial parts of MAD-SLIP itself in Weizenbaum's papers at the MIT Institute Archives. The rediscovered code differs in informative ways from the 1966 CACM paper: the preliminary “PRE” reassembly pattern is missing, the keyword stack and “NEWKEY” rule are not implemented, and reassembly-level calls between rules are not supported. A team led by Rupert Lane, David Berry, Anthony Hay, Arthur Schwarz and Shrager hand-transcribed the roughly 2600 lines of MAD and Fortran Assembly Program, brought up CTSS on an emulator of the IBM 7094 (the same 36-bit, 32 K-word, ~450 kHz machine Weizenbaum had used), debugged a single-character typo deep in the FAP, and on 21 December 2024 at 10:54 GMT got ELIZA running again after nearly sixty years.
blocks.section: The Illusion of Empathy: The ELIZA-Effect

blocks.quote: The reconstructed system nearly exactly reproduces the famous “Men are all alike” conversation from the original paper; the entire stack is open source, so any Unix user can now run the world's earliest chatbot on its original timesharing system. This means the “ELIZA” cited in most AI textbooks is, strictly speaking, Cosell's Lisp clone; Weizenbaum's own program is now the better-documented of the two.
blocks.section: The Illusion of Empathy: The ELIZA-Effect

blocks.quote: Computer-Generated Text: Early Examples
blocks.section: Computer-Generated Text: Early Examples

blocks.quote: More than iron, more than lead, more than gold I need electricity. I need it more than I need lamb or pork or lettuce or cucumber. I need it for my dreams.
blocks.section: Computer-Generated Text: Early Examples

blocks.quote: However, Racter was not the first instance of computer-generated text. Earlier examples include **Christopher Strachey's** \citetitle{strachey1952} (\citeyear{strachey1952}), which ran on the Manchester Mark I computer and used templates to produce randomized romantic letters, arguably the earliest known computer-generated literary text.
blocks.section: Computer-Generated Text: Early Examples

blocks.quote: A later example is **Theo Lutz** (1932-2010), a German computer scientist, student of the philosopher-cyberneticist **Max Bense**, and one of the pioneers of what is now called *digital poetry* \cite{lutzobituary}. His \citetitle{lutz1959} (\citeyear{lutz1959}) ran on a Zuse Z22 at the TH Stuttgart computer center and recombined words from Kafka's *The Castle* according to probabilistic rules, producing what he explicitly called “stochastic texts”:
blocks.section: Computer-Generated Text: Early Examples

blocks.quote: Nicht jeder Blick ist nah. Kein Dorf ist spät. Ein Schloss ist frei und jeder Bauer ist fern. Not every look is near. No village is late. A castle is free and every farmer is far.
blocks.section: Computer-Generated Text: Early Examples

blocks.quote: Remarkably, Lutz even sketched how such a program could learn: by raising the transition probabilities between subject and predicate whenever a generated sentence was judged “meaningful”, \cite[“the machine has 'learned' in a certain way”]{lutz1959}, preferring certain word combinations over time, essentially a trainable n-gram-style language model proposed in 1959. These experiments predate Racter by decades and sit at the intersection of combinatorics and language that traces back through \cite[Shannon's]{shannon1948communication} information-theoretic treatment of English as a stochastic process.
blocks.section: Computer-Generated Text: Early Examples

blocks.section: The Foundations: From Silicon to the Bitter Lesson

blocks.quote: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory: The Soviet Cold-War Secret
blocks.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory: The Soviet Cold-War Secret

blocks.quote: The theory became an engineering tool when Vapnik, by then at Bell Labs, and **Corinna Cortes** turned it into the **support vector machine** (1995): instead of minimising training error, the SVM finds the maximum-margin separating hyperplane, so only the few **support vectors** near the boundary determine the classifier, and the **kernel trick** lifts the same geometry into a high-dimensional feature space without ever constructing it (\cite{cortes1995svm}; \cite{boser1992svm}). For a decade before deep learning, the SVM was the default strong baseline on small and medium-sized datasets.
blocks.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory: The Soviet Cold-War Secret

blocks.quote: The Anglo-American ML community did not learn of the result for nearly twenty-five years. The Russian-language paper sat in a Soviet journal behind a language barrier and a Cold-War travel barrier; the related 1974 monograph (*The Theory of Pattern Recognition*, in Russian) reached only those who read Russian. By the time the result crossed the Iron Curtain, in the late 1970s and 1980s (through personal contacts, translations by Vapnik's collaborators, and the slow internationalisation of the field), the connectionist community was already fully invested in *empirical* "generalisation is just running on a held-out set" approaches, and the *theoretical* community was absorbed with PAC-learning, Bayesian model comparison, and statistical-decision theory. It took Vapnik's move to Bell Labs in 1990, his joint work with Cortes on the **support vector machine** (1995), and the publication of *The Nature of Statistical Learning Theory* (1995, English) to make VC theory *the* theoretical backbone of kernel methods, regularisation theory, and modern generalisation bounds. From the late 1990s onward, VC theory became standard textbook material (*Understanding Machine Learning* by Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, Bishop's *Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning*, Mohri's *Foundations of Machine Learning*), but the original contribution, published in 1971, sat for a generation unread in the West.
blocks.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory: The Soviet Cold-War Secret

blocks.quote: The Cold-War provenance matters for this chapter's deeper story. The 1960s and 1970s Soviet AI tradition was not a *single* programme; it was *three* parallel programmes, one in each of the three subfields this chapter traces. In **deep learning**, \citeauthor{vapnik1964vc}'s colleagues \citeauthor{ivakhnenko1965} and his collaborators in Kyiv were building GMDH networks. In **pattern recognition**, \citeauthor{bongard1966pattern} at the Moscow IITP was solving Bongard problems. In **statistical learning theory**, \citeauthor{vapnik1964vc} in Moscow was formalising the generalisation bound.
blocks.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory: The Soviet Cold-War Secret

blocks.quote: All three programmes were funded, conducted, and published in Russian; all three were *unknown* to the Anglophone AI community for one or two decades; all three were *rediscovered* and integrated into mainstream ML between 1985 and 2010. The Anglosphere's contribution (Rosenblatt's perceptron, Widrow's ADALINE, Rumelhart's backpropagation, LeCun's ConvNets, Hinton's deep belief nets, Sutskever's sequence-to-sequence) is more *visible* in the standard history because the network effects of English-language publication were enormous, but it is not *larger* in mathematical content. The Soviet trio (Ivakhnenko, Bongard, Vapnik) produced the three pieces of the modern ML stack the Anglophone tradition did *not* independently produce, and the 1990s integration of all three lines is the moment "machine learning" became a single field.
blocks.section: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: VC Theory: The Soviet Cold-War Secret

blocks.quote: Traditional methods for finding optimal flight paths relied on complex differential equations (**Euler-Lagrange**) that were nearly impossible to solve for real-world missions. They often failed to satisfy “two-point boundary conditions”, meaning you couldn't easily force the math to start at Point A and end exactly at Point B.

blocks.section: The Solution: Method of Gradients

blocks.quote: 2. **Find the Gradient:** Calculate the direction of steepest improvement (e.g., less time/fuel).

blocks.quote: Relation to Modern AI (Neural Networks)
blocks.section: Relation to Modern AI (Neural Networks)

blocks.quote: This paper is a foundational application of **Gradient Descent**, the engine of modern AI:
blocks.section: Relation to Modern AI (Neural Networks)

blocks.quote: This paper is now recognized as a direct **precursor of backpropagation**. Kelley's method backpropagated derivative information through standard Jacobian matrix calculations from one “stage” to the previous one, anticipating the core logic of the algorithm that would later be generalized by \citeauthor{linnainmaa1970} in \citeyear{linnainmaa1970} and eventually become the foundation of all modern deep learning. See also the related early 1960s work of Stuart Dreyfus and Arthur E. Bryson in control theory.
blocks.section: Relation to Modern AI (Neural Networks)

blocks.quote: The Silicon Engine: Moore's Law
blocks.section: The Silicon Engine: Moore's Law

blocks.quote: While AI research suffered through funding winters, the physical substrate of computing was undergoing an explosion. \citealternativetitle{mooreslaw} describes the observation made by Gordon Moore that the number of transistors in a dense integrated circuit doubles about every two years.
blocks.section: The Silicon Engine: Moore's Law

blocks.quote: This relentless exponential growth meant that while algorithms remained largely unchanged for decades, the machinery running them became millions of times more powerful. This “free” improvement in performance is the engine behind \citetitle{sutton2019bitter}: methods that scale with computation (like neural networks) were destined to eventually overtake methods that relied on human cleverness, simply because the hardware kept getting faster.
blocks.section: The Silicon Engine: Moore's Law

blocks.quote: Automatic Differentiation (1970)
blocks.section: Automatic Differentiation (1970)

blocks.quote: While the popularization of backpropagation is often credited to the 1980s, its mathematical genesis lies in the 1970 master's thesis of \citeauthor{linnainmaa1970}. He developed the “automatic differentiation” method, specifically the *reverse mode*, originally to efficiently manage rounding errors in complex computer calculations. Without explicitly intending it for neural networks, Linnainmaa created the highly efficient algorithm required to calculate gradients in nested functions. This work serves as the invisible mathematical backbone of modern Deep Learning, allowing error signals to be propagated backward through billions of parameters with minimal computational overhead.
blocks.section: Automatic Differentiation (1970)

blocks.quote: NASA Spaceflight Computers: Real-Time Reliability in Orbit (1965-1989)
blocks.section: NASA Spaceflight Computers: Real-Time Reliability in Orbit (1965-1989)

blocks.quote: Long before neural networks, a different kind of computing was pushing the hardware forward: the computers that flew. A spacecraft computer could not crash, could not be powered off, and could not be handed to a technician who walked over and pressed *reset*, so NASA's spaceflight programs forced the industry into **real-time, fault-tolerant** design decades before it became mainstream. \citeauthor{tomayko1988spaceflight} documents the full arc in \citetitle{tomayko1988spaceflight} (\citeyear{tomayko1988spaceflight}).
blocks.section: NASA Spaceflight Computers: Real-Time Reliability in Orbit (1965-1989)

blocks.quote: NASA had no choice but to become a leader in the development of real-time systems [...] it is in this field of computing that NASA has had its greatest impact.
blocks.section: NASA Spaceflight Computers: Real-Time Reliability in Orbit (1965-1989)

blocks.quote: The Apollo 11 landing alarms
blocks.section: The Apollo 11 landing alarms

blocks.quote: During the lunar descent of Apollo 11 the AGC began throwing **1201 and 1202 program alarms**: the docking radar was flooding it with interrupt requests and eating about 15% of the machine's resources. Instead of aborting, the computer's **restart software** gracefully shed the overload, kept the guidance functions alive, and let Armstrong land \cite{tomayko1988spaceflight}. Sixty years on this is still the textbook example of **fault-tolerant real-time computing**, a property modern autonomous and ML systems quietly depend on.
blocks.section: The Apollo 11 landing alarms

blocks.quote: Computer synchronization proved to be the most difficult task in producing the Shuttle's avionics.
blocks.section: The Apollo 11 landing alarms

blocks.quote: To stop a single common software bug from taking down all four at once, a fifth **Backup Flight System** ran independently developed code \cite{tomayko1988spaceflight}. The high-level language NASA commissioned for the Shuttle, **HAL/S**, introduced real-time statements like `SCHEDULE`, `TERMINATE`, `WAIT` and `PRIORITY` with priority-based task scheduling, ideas that carried straight into **Ada**, the language later adopted for the Space Station \cite{tomayko1988spaceflight}.
blocks.section: The Apollo 11 landing alarms

blocks.quote: The Personal Computer: Ed Roberts and the Altair 8800 (1974-1975)
blocks.section: The Personal Computer: Ed Roberts and the Altair 8800 (1974-1975)

blocks.quote: While MIT, Bell Labs, and IBM were building million-dollar mainframes, an Air Force veteran named **Henry Edward “Ed” Roberts** (\citeauthor{edroberts}, 1941-2010), running a small kit company called **MITS** out of Albuquerque, was rebuilding his calculator business after a brutal price war with Texas Instruments had driven it into 300,000 US Dollar of debt. The result, the **\citealternativetitle{altair8800}** (\citeyear{altair8800}), was the first commercially successful personal computer: a 397 US Dollar mail-order kit based on the new Intel 8080 microprocessor, featured on the cover of the January 1975 issue of *Popular Electronics* \cite{edroberts}. Roberts is most often remembered as “the father of the personal computer” \cite{edroberts_bbc}.
blocks.section: The Personal Computer: Ed Roberts and the Altair 8800 (1974-1975)

blocks.quote: What the Altair lacked (no keyboard, no display, no operating system, programs entered by toggle switches) was less important than what it started: an industry. \citeauthor{historyofpc} documents how the Altair spawned the **S-100 bus clone industry** (including the IMSAI 8080), the **Homebrew Computer Club**, and ultimately the founding of **Microsoft** when **Bill Gates** and **Paul Allen** wrote **Altair BASIC** \cite{historyofpc} as the company's first product.
blocks.section: The Personal Computer: Ed Roberts and the Altair 8800 (1974-1975)

blocks.quote: For competing claims to the title “father of the personal computer,” \citeauthor{historyofpc} lists:
blocks.section: The Personal Computer: Ed Roberts and the Altair 8800 (1974-1975)

blocks.quote: VisiCalc and the Killer App (1979)
blocks.section: VisiCalc and the Killer App (1979)

blocks.quote: In 1979, **Dan Bricklin** watched a Harvard Business School professor erase and redraw an entire spreadsheet on the blackboard after changing a single number. Bricklin's \citealternativetitle{visicalc} (\citeyear{visicalc}) automated exactly that: a “killer app” that, by being Apple-II-exclusive for its first year, is credited with single-handedly selling the Apple II to the business market \cite{visicalc} \cite{historyofpc}. It is widely considered the first “killer application” in computer history.
blocks.section: VisiCalc and the Killer App (1979)

blocks.quote: The IBM PC (1981)
blocks.section: The IBM PC (1981)

blocks.quote: Released August 12, 1981, the **IBM PC** used the Intel 8088 CPU and Microsoft-supplied **PC-DOS** (later **MS-DOS**), since IBM's negotiations with Digital Research for CP/M had failed \cite{ibmpc} \cite{historyofpc}. IBM copyrighted the BIOS rather than licensing it; Compaq's clean-room reimplementation of the BIOS made possible the clone industry that ultimately overwhelmed IBM itself, establishing the Wintel architecture as the dominant PC standard for decades.
blocks.section: The IBM PC (1981)

blocks.quote: The First AI Winter and the Connectionist Revival (1969-1986)
blocks.section: The First AI Winter and the Connectionist Revival (1969-1986)

blocks.quote: The Critique and the First AI Winter (1969-1980)
blocks.section: The Critique and the First AI Winter (1969-1980)

blocks.quote: Minsky and Papert's Critique (1969)
blocks.section: Minsky and Papert's Critique (1969)

blocks.quote: Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published their book \citetitle{minskyperceptrons}, which provided a mathematical proof of the architecture's limitations. They demonstrated that a single-layer perceptron could not solve the **XOR (Exclusive OR)** problem because it was not “linearly separable.”
blocks.section: Minsky and Papert's Critique (1969)

blocks.quote: To understand why the XOR problem was so significant, we first need to look at how a computer processes logic. We can represent logical gates as functions that take an input matrix (representing all possible combinations of two inputs) and map them to an output vector.
blocks.section: Minsky and Papert's Critique (1969)

blocks.quote: In these examples:
blocks.section: Minsky and Papert's Critique (1969)

blocks.quote: The OR Gate
blocks.section: The OR Gate

blocks.quote: The **OR** gate is “True” if at least one input is “True.”
blocks.section: The OR Gate

blocks.quote: The XOR Gate (Exclusive OR)
blocks.section: The XOR Gate (Exclusive OR)

blocks.quote: The **XOR** gate is “True” *only* if the inputs are different.
blocks.section: The XOR Gate (Exclusive OR)

blocks.quote: Minsky and Papert demonstrated that while a single-layer perceptron can draw a line to separate the results of an OR gate, it is mathematically impossible to do so for XOR because the “True” and “False” results are not **linearly separable**.
blocks.section: The XOR Gate (Exclusive OR)

blocks.quote: Even though Minsky realized that having a Multi-Layer-Perceptron with non-linear activation functions would be able to solve this problem, there was no way to efficiently train those until in \citeyear{rumelhart1986} Rumelhart et al. popularized \citealternativetitle{rumelhart1986}, which reignited interest in connectionist models and paved the way for modern deep learning.
blocks.section: The XOR Gate (Exclusive OR)

blocks.quote: The neurons Rosenblatt studied only had discrete outputs, as suggested by \citeauthorlastnameand{mccullochpitts1943}, a Heaviside-style step function that emits $0$ or $1$. The deeper problem for gradient-based learning is not just that the derivative is $0$ almost everywhere; the step function is **discontinuous at the threshold** and therefore *not differentiable there at all*. The chain rule needs a derivative at every point along the signal path; a single non-differentiable step is enough to break backpropagation. The introduction of continuous, differentiable activations (first the sigmoid and tanh, then the piecewise-linear ReLU) is what made the chain-rule gradient flow mathematically well-defined and the backpropagation algorithm practical. He suggested the term 'back-propagating errors' already in \citeyear{rosenblattbackprop}, but didn't know how to implement it.
blocks.section: The XOR Gate (Exclusive OR)

blocks.quote: Since early Perceptrons could only classify linearly separable data, they could not solve XOR. This limitation contributed to the **First AI Winter**. Multi-layer networks and **Backpropagation** later overcame this.
blocks.section: The XOR Gate (Exclusive OR)

blocks.quote: An important nuance: **Minsky and Papert knew multi-layer networks could solve XOR.** They said so in \citetitle{minskyperceptrons}. Their argument was not that neural networks were fundamentally flawed, but that **no one knew how to train multi-layer networks efficiently**. Backpropagation was already being developed by \citeauthor{linnainmaa1970} (\citeyear{linnainmaa1970}), but it took two decades to be rediscovered and popularized.
blocks.section: The XOR Gate (Exclusive OR)

blocks.quote: There is a second, less repeated nuance, and it comes from an insider. Some have claimed that the Minsky-Papert book caused the fading interest in neural-network research, but Nilsson, who watched the shift from the inside, doubts it: Rosenblatt himself had already begun concentrating on other topics well before 1969, and the success of heuristic (symbolic) programming methods had shifted the field's attention, including his own, away from neural networks during the mid-1960s (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}). The book did not kill a healthy field; it stamped a verdict on one that was already in retreat. Papert himself later rejected the single-book reading, framing the conflict as one between research paradigms rather than the work of one volume (\cite[Papert, 1988]{papert1988oneai}), and the sociologist Mikel Olazaran's study of the controversy concluded that the funding shifts reflected institutional competition and the machines' genuine limitations as much as any critique (\cite[Olazaran, 1996]{olazaran1996sociological}; see also the oral histories in \cite[Anderson & Rosenfeld, 2000]{anderson2000talkingnets}).
blocks.section: The XOR Gate (Exclusive OR)

blocks.quote: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: In no part of the field have the discoveries made so far produced the major impact that was then promised.
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{lighthillreport}, published in the UK, was a devastating critique that shattered confidence in AI research. It led to a “deep freeze” in the field known as the **First AI Winter**.
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: The realization that simple neural networks couldn't handle basic logic gates, combined with the \citealternativetitle{lighthillreport} in the UK, shattered confidence in the field.
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: This “AI Winter” was primarily an **Anglosphere phenomenon**. Deep learning research remained alive and productive throughout the 1960s and 70s outside the English-speaking world, particularly in the Soviet Union (Ivakhnenko), Japan (Amari, Fukushima), and continental Europe, where funding for such “blue skies” mathematical research continued.
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: The Lighthill debate had a specific date and venue: on **9 May 1973**, at the **Royal Institution** in London, the BBC broadcast a 90-minute televised debate in which Lighthill faced off against **Donald Michie** (Edinburgh), **John McCarthy** (Stanford) and the psychologist **Richard Gregory** (Bristol). The transcripts show the AI researchers struggling to rebut Lighthill's central claim that **Category B** (his name for robotics and integrated common-sense reasoning) had produced nothing of substance; McCarthy in particular was put on the defensive about his own laboratory's modest progress. The audience poll, taken before and after the debate, shifted decisively against AI. Within a year, the British Science Research Council had moved to cut AI funding in most UK universities, giving the Anglosphere winter its sharpest edge.
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: The American side of the winter was legislative. Responding to Congressional pressure that Defense Department research be relevant to military needs, on **November 19, 1969**, Congress passed the **Mansfield Amendment**, which required the Defense Department to restrict its support of basic research to projects "with a direct and apparent relationship to a specific military function or operation"; on March 23, 1972, the Advanced Research Projects Agency was renamed the **Defense** Research Advanced Projects Agency (DARPA) to reflect that emphasis (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}). And yet the field was still institutionalizing right up until the freeze: the first large conference devoted exclusively to AI, the **International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI)**, was held in Washington, DC, in May 1969, organized by Donald E. Walker of MITRE and Alistair Holden of the University of Washington, sponsored by sixteen technical societies, with about 600 attendees and 63 papers from nine countries.
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: In Edinburgh, the cost was human: **Donald Michie**, who had run the invitation-only Machine Intelligence workshops there since 1965, later said of the Lighthill report that "work of excellence by talented young people was stigmatised as bad science and the experiment killed in mid-trajectory. This destruction of a co-operative human mechanism and of the careful craft of many hands is elsewhere described as a mishap. But to speak plainly, it was an outrage." His FREDDY robot and other Edinburgh AI work were among its casualties (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}).
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: The field only recovered in the 1980s with the popularization of \citealternativetitle{rumelhart1986}, which allowed multi-layer networks to finally solve the XOR problem.
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: Long before Lighthill's report, a Heideggerian philosopher at Berkeley had been telling AI researchers that their entire program was misconceived. \citeauthor{dreyfus1972what}'s 1972 \citetitle{dreyfus1972what} attacked symbolic AI from the side of phenomenology: expert skill, Dreyfus argued, is not a collection of rules the expert could in principle articulate, but a holistic, situated, often pre-reflective responsiveness to context. The 1960s AI optimism that “thinking” could be formalized as symbol manipulation therefore missed what thinking actually is, a position he sharpened in seminars at Berkeley that AI faculty and graduate students were essentially required to attend, since Dreyfus taught in the Philosophy Department next door. The AI community's classical counter (that AI would succeed once enough rules were collected) looks, in retrospect, like the precise pattern Sutton would later diagnose as the loser in the bitter lesson. Dreyfus's 1992 *What Computers Still Can't Do*, written after the second AI winter, was widely read as a vindication.
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: Harmon's "artificial eye" was less a single device than a research programme: machine recognition of faces, profiles and print, and the use of degraded images to find out what human vision needs (\cite{harmonwiki}). He was also one of the field's sharpest internal critics. In a 1981 *Christian Science Monitor* essay, "Artificial intelligence: accent is on artificial," he wrote that "most artificial-intelligence (AI) systems do trivial things impressively": chess, face recognition, constrained dialogue and medical diagnosis worked because their domains had been sharply restricted, while generalization, semantics, autonomy and creativity remained out of reach. The essay is a useful corrective to the usual winter narrative: the skepticism did not come only from philosophers and funding agencies, but from a vision researcher who had built some of the demos himself (\cite[Harmon, 1981]{harmon1981ai}).
blocks.section: The Lighthill Report (1973) and the Collapse (1974-1980)

blocks.quote: The Road Back: Neocognitron, Backpropagation, and the Deep-Learning Revival (1980-1986)
blocks.section: The Road Back: Neocognitron, Backpropagation, and the Deep-Learning Revival (1980-1986)

blocks.quote: Fukushima's Neocognitron (1980)
blocks.section: Fukushima's Neocognitron (1980)

blocks.quote: Before LeCun perfected the CNN, the architectural blueprints were drawn by **Kunihiko Fukushima** (who, in turn, based his work in the work of \citeauthorlastnameand{hubelwiesel}, who researched the cat's visual cortex), in \citeyear{neocognitron}, he developed the **\citealternativetitle{neocognitron}**, a hierarchical network inspired by the visual cortex. It introduced the two key layers of modern vision AI: “S-cells” (simple) for feature extraction and “C-cells” (complex) for pooling, which allowed the machine to recognize objects even if they were shifted in position.
blocks.section: Fukushima's Neocognitron (1980)

blocks.quote: Backpropagation Before Backpropagation: Rosenblatt's 1961 Report
blocks.section: Backpropagation Before Backpropagation: Rosenblatt's 1961 Report

blocks.quote: The full argument sits in Rosenblatt's 1961 Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory report, \citetitle{rosenblattbackprop} (16 March 1961), a book-length synthesis of the perceptron program that runs from the biological motivation through three-layer series-coupled systems to multi-layer, cross-coupled and speculative models. Its §13.3 is the "back-propagating error correction procedure": the error of the response units is assigned back to the association units by a probabilistic rule, and the connections are then corrected exactly as in the elementary perceptron. It is not backpropagation as modern deep learning knows it (there is no gradient, no chain rule, and the credit assignment is stochastic), but the name and the central intuition that an output error can be pushed back into earlier layers are already there. Chapter 13 of the 1962 book added layer-wise learning rates, bypass connections, and multimodal variants; the heuristics did not work reliably because the step nonlinearity inherited from the threshold neuron had no usable gradient (\cite[Rosenblatt, 1962]{rosenblatt1962neurodynamics}). The Defense Technical Information Center's scan is available in full at the Internet Archive.
blocks.section: Backpropagation Before Backpropagation: Rosenblatt's 1961 Report

blocks.quote: Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams (1986)
blocks.section: Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams (1986)

blocks.quote: However, these deep structures were difficult to train until the popularization of **Backpropagation** by \citeauthor{rumelhart1986} in \citeyear{rumelhart1986}. This mathematical technique allowed the “error” of a network to be sent backward through the layers, adjusting the weights with precision. The combination of Fukushima's architecture and Rumelhart's training algorithm set the stage for the deep learning revolution.
blocks.section: Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams (1986)

blocks.quote: The Expert-System Boom and the Second Winter (1970s-1990s)
blocks.section: The Expert-System Boom and the Second Winter (1970s-1990s)

blocks.quote: While the connectionists rebuilt, symbolic AI found its commercial peak in **expert systems**. At Stanford, **Edward Feigenbaum**, Bruce Buchanan and Joshua Lederberg built **DENDRAL**, which inferred molecular structures from mass spectra and cut the search from more than eleven million candidates to about twenty-two thousand; **MYCIN**, built by Edward Shortliffe with Buchanan and Feigenbaum, diagnosed blood infections from a few hundred IF-THEN rules, separated its rules from its inference engine to become the first expert-system shell (EMYCIN), and in a blind test prescribed antibiotics as well as, or better than, nine clinicians. **John McDermott's XCON** configured VAX computers at Digital Equipment Corporation, growing from about three hundred rules in 1979 to more than three thousand by 1984. Feigenbaum called the activity **knowledge engineering**, and it became the commercial face of AI in the 1980s (\cite[Feigenbaum et al., 1969]{feigenbaum1965dendral}; \cite[Shortliffe & Buchanan, 1976]{shortliffe1976mycin}; \cite[Feigenbaum, 1984]{feigenbaum1984expert}; \cite{crevier1993ai}).
blocks.section: The Expert-System Boom and the Second Winter (1970s-1990s)

blocks.quote: The European counterpole to LISP was **Prolog**, the logic-programming language built by **Alain Colmerauer** and Philippe Roussel in Marseille around 1972, after **Robert Kowalski** showed that predicate logic could be read as a programming language: a program is a set of Horn clauses, and a query is a proof search (\cite{colmerauer1973prolog}; \cite{kowalski1974prolog}). Japan bet its industrial policy on that idea: the **Fifth Generation Computer Systems** project, launched by MITI in 1982 and run through the ICOT institute under Kazuhiro Fuchi, spent roughly 400 million dollars on parallel inference machines and logic-based AI, and ended in 1994 without the promised breakthrough (\cite{hnffifthgen2023}).
blocks.section: The Expert-System Boom and the Second Winter (1970s-1990s)

blocks.quote: The bust that followed (brittle systems, unmaintainable rule bases, and the collapse of the LISP-machine market) produced the **second AI winter** in the early 1990s \cite{toosi2021history}. The lesson repeated the first: the demonstration worked in the narrow domain, and the promise outran the engineering.
blocks.section: The Expert-System Boom and the Second Winter (1970s-1990s)

blocks.quote: The Road to Deep Learning: CNNs, LSTM, and the Neural Turn (1989-2003)
blocks.section: The Road to Deep Learning: CNNs, LSTM, and the Neural Turn (1989-2003)

blocks.quote: Convolutional Neural Networks and LeNet-5 (1989-1998)
blocks.section: Convolutional Neural Networks and LeNet-5 (1989-1998)

blocks.quote: While early neural networks were limited, **Yann LeCun et al** revolutionized computer vision by developing the first practical **Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)**. In \citeyear{lecun1989backpropagation}, LeCun combined convolutions with backpropagation to recognize handwritten ZIP codes for the U.S. Postal Service, an early influential demonstration of a backprop-trained convolutional network. In \citeyear{lecun1998gradientbased}, he introduced **LeNet-5**, the refined architecture for recognizing handwritten digits (and, later, bank checks). Unlike standard networks, CNNs use small, learnable filters to automatically extract spatial features like edges and shapes. This proved that biological inspiration, mimicking the visual cortex, could solve complex pattern recognition tasks that traditional logic-based AI could not.
blocks.section: Convolutional Neural Networks and LeNet-5 (1989-1998)

blocks.quote: The popular attribution of the CNN to LeCun overlooks substantial earlier work, which \citeauthor{schmidhuber2025cnn} documents in detail. **Kunihiko Fukushima** introduced a rectified linear activation in \citeyear{fukushima1969relu}, a direct precursor of the ReLU that powers essentially every modern Transformer, and the basic **Neocognitron** architecture with alternating convolutional and downsampling layers in \citeyear{neocognitron}, inspired by Hubel and Wiesel's cat visual-cortex work. **Alex Waibel**, a German researcher in Japan, trained supervised one-dimensional convolutional NNs with weight-sharing (TDNNs) on Linnainmaa's 1970 backpropagation in \citeyear{waibel1987tdnn} for speech recognition, and introduced the term *convolution* into NNs. **Wei Zhang** at Osaka then built the first *modern* two-dimensional CNN trained by backpropagation in \citeyear{zhang1988cnn}, applied to character recognition, one year *before* LeCun's 1989 Bell Labs paper, and LeCun's widely read 1998 survey does not cite it.
blocks.section: Convolutional Neural Networks and LeNet-5 (1989-1998)

blocks.quote: LeCun's contribution was nevertheless substantial. His 1989 Bell Labs work combined backpropagation with convolutions on handwritten ZIP codes for the U.S. Postal Service, a research prototype that showed the approach could work end-to-end. His 1998 **LeNet-5** refined the architecture for bank-check recognition and was the first robust, end-to-end backprop-trained system deployed on a real commercial OCR problem at scale. The lineage runs from Fukushima's biological inspiration, through Zhang's and Waibel's first end-to-end CNNs, to LeCun's production-grade system; each step added something the earlier work had not.
blocks.section: Convolutional Neural Networks and LeNet-5 (1989-1998)

blocks.quote: Jürgen Schmidhuber's \citetitle{schmidhuber2022deep} documents a striking concentration of foundational ideas at his lab at TU Munich in the twelve months from early 1990 to mid 1991, a window worth knowing about in its own right. In it the group published the principles for what we now call **generative adversarial networks** (a controller network in a zero-sum game with a predictor, February 1990); the first **subgoal-generating** networks for hierarchical reinforcement learning; and in 1991 a *fast-weight programmer* in which one neural network learns to slowly modify the weights of another, an abstraction Schmidhuber's group has connected to the learned key-query-value projections of the modern **Transformer**. The same window saw unsupervised **pre-training** of deep neural networks; **knowledge distillation**, in which a small network is trained to mimic a larger one (the technique that underpins DeepSeek's compression of much larger frontier models); the formal identification of the **vanishing/exploding gradient** problem in Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis; and the **Long Short-Term Memory** architecture, gated recurrent residual connections that have since become one of the most cited AI papers ever published. Several foundational ideas of modern deep learning (gated residual connections, fast-weight programmers, the GAN principle) can be traced to papers from this single window at a Bavarian technical university. Schmidhuber has argued that the standard Anglophone narrative under-credits this European and Japanese work; other researchers in the field read the priorities more cautiously, and several of the cited innovations were independently rediscovered in different communities at different times. Whatever position one takes on the priority disputes, the technical lineage itself is documented in the original papers and useful to know, because every modern AI system stands on at least some of these ideas.
blocks.section: Convolutional Neural Networks and LeNet-5 (1989-1998)

blocks.quote: Bridging the Gap: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
blocks.section: Bridging the Gap: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)

blocks.quote: The “Vanishing Gradient” Problem (1991)
blocks.section: The “Vanishing Gradient” Problem (1991)

blocks.quote: The Fundamental Deep Learning Problem was identified and analyzed in \citeyear{hochreiter1991vanishing} by \citeauthor{hochreiter1991vanishing} in his diploma thesis supervised by Jürgen Schmidhuber. He showed that in typical deep or recurrent networks, back-propagated error signals either shrink rapidly (vanish) or grow out of bounds (explode), making learning impossible for long sequences. Crucially, Hochreiter derived from first principles the concept of a **recurrent residual connection**: a neural unit with the identity activation function connected to itself with weight 1.0, ensuring constant error flow across arbitrarily many time steps.
blocks.section: The “Vanishing Gradient” Problem (1991)

blocks.quote: The Architecture (1995-2000)
blocks.section: The Architecture (1995-2000)

blocks.quote: Building on this analysis, **Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber** developed the **Long Short-Term Memory** architecture; Schmidhuber coined the term in a 1995 tech report, and the main peer-reviewed publication of \citeyear{lstm} by \citeauthorlastnameand{lstm} is often described as the most cited AI paper of the 20th century. A critical milestone was the **“vanilla LSTM” architecture with forget gates** (\citeyear{lstm_vanilla}), the variant that everybody uses today (e.g., in Google's TensorFlow). It features gated recurrent residual connections whose gates are initially open (1.0), allowing the network to start with plain residual connections.
blocks.section: The Architecture (1995-2000)

blocks.quote: CTC and the Speech Revolution (2006-2015)
blocks.section: CTC and the Speech Revolution (2006-2015)

blocks.quote: In \citeyear{ctc2006}, **Alex Graves** and colleagues introduced **Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC)**, a loss that trains a recurrent network to label unsegmented sequences (no pre-segmented frames and no post-hoc alignment), which made end-to-end speech recognition practical. CTC-trained LSTM was successfully applied to speech in 2007 and became the first superior end-to-end neural speech recognizer. In 2015, this CTC-LSTM combination **dramatically improved Google's speech recognition** on Android smartphones. Google Translate (2016), whose technical paper mentions LSTM over 50 times, was based on two connected LSTMs. By 2017, LSTM also powered Facebook's machine translation (over 30 billion translations per week), Apple's Quicktype on roughly 1 billion iPhones, and the voice of Amazon's Alexa.
blocks.section: CTC and the Speech Revolution (2006-2015)

blocks.quote: The Bridge to Modern AI
blocks.section: The Bridge to Modern AI

blocks.quote: LSTMs were the “workhorse” of AI for two decades (approx. 1997-2017). Without the LSTM, the second AI Winter (early 1990s, triggered by the expert-systems bust) likely would have dragged neural NLP along with it for much longer. It proved that connectionist models could handle the sequential, complex nature of human speech by implementing a form of persistent memory. The most widely used neural language models of that era were based on LSTM as well, the transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) in the modern sense arrived with the GPT series (2018-2020). A hands-on, visual tour of that two-decade workhorse (the loops, the gates, the vanishing gradients) lives in the [Networks with Memory chapter](recurrent_networks.php).
blocks.section: The Bridge to Modern AI

blocks.quote: The Triumph of Symbolic AI
blocks.section: The Triumph of Symbolic AI

blocks.quote: While Perceptrons attempted to mimic the brain's structure, a different approach focused on logic and brute-force search. This “Symbolic AI” reached its zenith in May 1997, when **Deep Blue** won the six-game rematch against Kasparov; it had lost the 1996 match (\cite{deepblue}).
blocks.section: The Triumph of Symbolic AI

blocks.quote: In a historic six-game rematch, IBM's Deep Blue defeated the reigning world chess champion, **Garry Kasparov**. Unlike the learning-based Perceptron, Deep Blue relied on massive parallel processing capable of evaluating 200 million positions per second. It proved that for well-defined logical problems, a machine could exceed human capability not through intuition, but through sheer computational calculation. The match was broadcast live, and the win struck hard enough that IBM's share price briefly touched an all-time high \cite{toosi2021history}.
blocks.section: The Triumph of Symbolic AI

blocks.quote: However, Deep Blue's victory represented the pinnacle of specific, hand-crafted logic rather than general intelligence. While effective for the rigid rules of chess, relying on human-designed strategies proved to be a bottleneck for more complex, unstructured problems. This realization leads directly to a fundamental, and somewhat painful, observation about the trajectory of AI progress.
blocks.section: The Triumph of Symbolic AI

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{shrdlu_image} (CC BY-SA 4.0, \citeauthor{shrdlu_image}) shows Terry Winograd's SHRDLU (1972), which answered typed questions about a virtual world of blocks, the canonical demonstration that natural-language reasoning over a small world was possible \cite{winograd1972understanding}.
blocks.section: The Triumph of Symbolic AI

blocks.quote: A Deep Blue-class IBM chess machine at the Computer History Museum, from \citealternativetitle{deep_blue_image} ([CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/), \citeauthor{deep_blue_image}). The Commons description notes that the computer shown is similar to, not identical with, the machine that beat Kasparov in 1997.
blocks.section: The Triumph of Symbolic AI

blocks.quote: The Neural Turn
blocks.section: The Neural Turn

blocks.quote: In 2003, **“\citetitle{neuralprobabilistic}”** by **Yoshua Bengio** and co-authors revived backpropagation for language modeling. Their model replaced sparse n-gram tables with dense **word embeddings** \cite[first formalized in]{rumelhart1986pdp}, mapping semantic relationships into a continuous vector space.
blocks.section: The Neural Turn

blocks.quote: The Democratization of ML Research
blocks.section: The Democratization of ML Research

blocks.quote: Frameworks like **\cite[Torch]{collobert2002}**, **\cite[TensorFlow]{tensorflow2016}** and **\cite[PyTorch]{pytorch}** abstracted away manual differentiation and GPU memory management, allowing researchers to focus on architecture rather than implementation.
blocks.section: The Democratization of ML Research

blocks.quote: The Bitter Lesson: Scale over Strategy
blocks.section: The Bitter Lesson: Scale over Strategy

blocks.quote: The biggest lesson that can be read from 70 years of AI research is that general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, and by a large margin [...] We have to learn the bitter lesson that building in how we think we think does not work in the long run.
blocks.section: The Bitter Lesson: Scale over Strategy

blocks.quote: The **Bitter Lesson** (\citeauthor{sutton2019bitter}) argues that for decades, AI researchers tried to teach computers human rules (chess strategies, grammar). History shows this approach usually fails: **compute** and **data** almost always beat human-designed cleverness.
blocks.section: The Bitter Lesson: Scale over Strategy

blocks.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{jelinek}'s aphorism **“Every time I fire a linguist, the performance of the speech recognizer goes up”** captures the same principle: general-purpose algorithms at scale outperform hand-crafted knowledge.
blocks.section: The Bitter Lesson: Scale over Strategy

blocks.quote: Sutton writes from the perspective of a research director surveying decades of failed research programs. The view from inside the lab, on any given afternoon, is much messier. \citeauthor{karpathy2019recipe}'s 2019 \citetitle{karpathy2019recipe}, written by an OpenAI co-founder and former Tesla AI head, describes the everyday experience of trying to make a neural network work, and it is surprisingly downbeat. Two facts dominate, he says.
blocks.section: The Bitter Lesson: Scale over Strategy

blocks.quote: First, **neural net training is a leaky abstraction**: frameworks advertise 30-line plug-and-play miracles, but backprop + SGD does not in fact magically make a network converge. Second, **neural net training fails silently**: a mislabeled augmentation, an off-by-one in an autoregressive model, a learning-rate decay secretly driving the rate to zero before convergence; none of these produces an exception. The network trains happily, only worse.
blocks.section: The Bitter Lesson: Scale over Strategy

blocks.quote: Karpathy's counter-recipe is to spend hours simply looking at the data before touching code, build a tiny model first, overfit one batch to confirm the pipeline is wired correctly, and only then add complexity one ingredient at a time. *“The qualities that correlate most strongly with success in deep learning,”* he writes, *“are patience and attention to detail.”* His favourite anecdote: he once accidentally left a model training over the winter break and returned in January to a new state of the art. The bitter lesson is true in the long run; getting there is mostly debugging.
blocks.section: The Bitter Lesson: Scale over Strategy

blocks.quote: The Deep Learning Revival (2010s)
blocks.section: The Deep Learning Revival (2010s)

blocks.quote: From CPU to GPU: The Realization of the “Bitter Lesson”
blocks.section: From CPU to GPU: The Realization of the “Bitter Lesson”

blocks.quote: The shift from the Central Processing Unit (CPU) to the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) represents the most significant hardware pivot in AI history. While the CPU is designed for deep, sequential logic, a direct descendant of the von Neumann architecture, the GPU utilizes thousands of simple cores to perform matrix multiplications simultaneously. This hardware shift validates the core thesis of \citetitle{sutton2019bitter}: that methods leveraging massive computation eventually outcompete those relying on human-centric heuristics. By abstracting away complex conditional logic in favor of “brute-force” parallel math, the GPU provided the raw power necessary to turn neural networks from theoretical models into dominant technologies.
blocks.section: From CPU to GPU: The Realization of the “Bitter Lesson”

blocks.quote: The Hardware Lottery: How Gamers Saved AI
blocks.section: The Hardware Lottery: How Gamers Saved AI

blocks.quote: We tend to view the progress of AI as a purely mathematical evolution. However, \citeauthor{hooker2020} reminds us of a grounded reality in \citetitle{hooker2020}: the success of an algorithm is often dictated by available hardware rather than intellectual superiority.
blocks.section: The Hardware Lottery: How Gamers Saved AI

blocks.quote: Ideas win when they are “hardware-friendly.” Because GPUs were optimized for parallel matrix multiplication (due to the gaming industry), models that relied on these operations, like Deep Learning and Transformers, surpassed their rivals. Highly efficient but difficult-to-parallelize approaches were relegated to the “researcher's graveyard.” We conduct our research in the shadow of the computing architectures we happened to inherit.
blocks.section: The Hardware Lottery: How Gamers Saved AI

blocks.quote: While the theoretical foundations of deep learning were laid in the 1980s, the field remained dormant largely due to a lack of computing power. The solution came from an unlikely source: the video game industry.
blocks.section: The Hardware Lottery: How Gamers Saved AI

blocks.quote: In the mid-2000s, researchers began to realize that the mathematical operations required to render 3D video games, specifically, the manipulation of massive matrices of pixels, were mathematically identical to the operations required to train neural networks.
blocks.section: The Hardware Lottery: How Gamers Saved AI

blocks.quote: The “Why”: SIMD vs. MIMD
blocks.section: The “Why”: SIMD vs. MIMD

blocks.quote: The fundamental difference lies in architecture. A **CPU** (Central Processing Unit) is designed for **latency**: it has a few powerful cores optimized to do complex, sequential logic (MIMD: Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data). It is like a professor who can solve difficult calculus problems one by one.
blocks.section: The “Why”: SIMD vs. MIMD

blocks.quote: A **GPU** (Graphics Processing Unit), conversely, is designed for **throughput**: it has thousands of smaller, simpler cores designed to perform the same instruction on massive amounts of data simultaneously (SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data). It is like a thousand elementary school students who can all perform simple addition at the exact same time.
blocks.section: The “Why”: SIMD vs. MIMD

blocks.quote: Since training a neural network involves multiplying billions of floating-point numbers (weights) by billions of other numbers (inputs), the GPU's architecture allowed for speedups of **70x to 100x** over CPUs.
blocks.section: The “Why”: SIMD vs. MIMD

blocks.quote: The Discovery
blocks.section: The Discovery

blocks.quote: While early attempts to use GPUs for neural networks date back to **Oh & Jung** in \citeyear{oh2004gpu}, the breakthrough required a bridge between hardware and code. This arrived with NVIDIA's release of **CUDA** in 2006, which allowed researchers to program GPUs without translating everything into “graphics” language.
blocks.section: The Discovery

blocks.quote: This hardware lottery, the fact that AI researchers could piggyback on the massive R&D budget of the gaming industry, is likely the single most important factor in the 21st-century AI boom.
blocks.section: The Discovery

blocks.quote: The “Hardware Lottery” describes how the success of an idea depends less on its brilliance and more on whether it fits existing technology. This is perfectly illustrated by **\citeauthor{weatherfactory}'s** **“\citealternativetitle{weatherfactory}”** (\citeyear{weatherfactory}). Richardson envisioned a massive theater filled with 64,000 humans performing manual calculations (then called “computers”) in parallel to predict global weather. While mathematically sound, it was a practical failure because human “hardware” was too slow and expensive to outpace the actual weather.
blocks.section: The Discovery

blocks.quote: Just as Richardson's vision remained a “researcher's graveyard” until electronic computers arrived, **Deep Learning** remained relatively dormant in the 1980s. The breakthrough wasn't mainly a new mathematical discovery, but the realization that **GPUs**, built for the gaming industry, were essentially Richardson's “Weather Factory” on a chip. By using **SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data)** architecture, a single GPU could perform the work of thousands of sequential processors simultaneously. This shifted AI from the slow, logical processing of a CPU to the massive throughput required for modern **LLMs**, finally providing the “hardware-friendly” environment Richardson's numerical methods always required.
blocks.section: The Discovery

blocks.quote: CUDA
blocks.section: CUDA

blocks.quote: The Dream of Structure: Recursive Neural Networks
blocks.section: The Dream of Structure: Recursive Neural Networks

blocks.quote: For decades, it was considered an axiom that language possesses an inherent hierarchical architecture. In \citeyear{socher2011}, Richard Socher et al. argued that neural networks must explicitly map this structure to succeed. Rather than treating words as beads on a string, these models used parsers to combine semantic vectors within a tree-like hierarchy.
blocks.section: The Dream of Structure: Recursive Neural Networks

blocks.quote: This represents a pivotal moment in the intellectual history of LLMs: the eventual departure from the idea that we must impose human syntax on the machine. The Transformer did not prevail because it possessed “better” linguistics, but because it ignored rigid structure in favor of patterns learned implicitly through massive scaling.
blocks.section: The Dream of Structure: Recursive Neural Networks

blocks.quote: The Deep Learning Revolution (2012)
blocks.section: The Deep Learning Revolution (2012)

blocks.quote: After the second AI winter, the field shifted back to connectionism. In \citeyear{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, a team in Geoffrey Hinton's group at the University of Toronto, led by Alex Krizhevsky, demonstrated that deep convolutional neural networks, when powered by **GPUs** and massive datasets like ImageNet, could outperform all traditional methods \cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}. The network, **AlexNet** (named after its leading author), was decisive not only for its depth but for a stack of then-unfashionable tricks: rectified-linear-unit (ReLU) activations and **dropout**, which together let it train far more layers end-to-end on raw pixels, with no hand-crafted features at all \cite{toosi2021history}. The result was the birth of the third AI boom \cite{toosi2021history}, and it validated the \citealternativetitle{sutton2019bitter}: scale and computation ultimately triumph over hand-coded human intuition. The connectionist revival was formally recognized in 2018, when the Turing Award went to Bengio, Hinton and LeCun for their pioneering work on deep learning \cite{toosi2021history}.
blocks.section: The Deep Learning Revolution (2012)

blocks.quote: Supervised classification was only half the revival. In 2014 **Ian Goodfellow** and colleagues introduced the **generative adversarial network (GAN)**: a generator that produces samples and a discriminator that tries to tell them from real data, trained as a minimax game in which the generator learns to make the discriminator's mistake probability high (\cite{goodfellow2014gan}). GANs produced the first sharp, high-resolution synthetic images and made generative modelling a mainstream research programme before diffusion models displaced them for most image work.
blocks.section: The Deep Learning Revolution (2012)

blocks.quote: Breaking the Bottleneck: The Birth of Attention
blocks.section: Breaking the Bottleneck: The Birth of Attention

blocks.quote: Before the modern Transformer, neural networks suffered from a “representational bottleneck.” Systems like the LSTM attempted to compress the entire meaning of a long sentence into a single, fixed-length vector, a task as impossible as summarizing a complex novel into a single word without losing the nuance. The philosopher-engineer *\cite[Dzmitry Bahdanau]{bahdanau2014}* shattered this constraint by introducing the **Attention Mechanism**. Instead of forcing the model to remember everything at once, Bahdanau proposed a system that allows the decoder to “look back” at the input sequence and selectively focus on the most relevant words for each step of the translation. This shift from static compression to dynamic alignment was the pivotal moment that allowed machines to handle long-range dependencies. Without this breakthrough, the later “Self-Attention” of the Transformer would have had no foundation; Bahdanau taught the machine to observe what matters.
blocks.section: Breaking the Bottleneck: The Birth of Attention

blocks.quote: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: While LSTM had made recurrent networks very deep through residual connections since the 1990s, feedforward networks remained limited to roughly 20-30 layers until 2015. In May 2015, \citeauthorlastnameand{highway2015} published **Highway Networks**, the first working, truly deep gradient-based feedforward neural networks with **hundreds of layers**, over ten times deeper than any previous feedforward network. They achieved this by transferring the 1999 LSTM principle of gated residual connections (gates initially open at 1.0) from recurrent to feedforward architectures. Seven months later, in December 2015, Microsoft's **ResNet** won the ImageNet competition.
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: ResNet can be described as a Highway Network variant whose gates are always open (i.e., an open-gated Highway Net), a framing most strongly associated with the Schmidhuber group, though He et al. developed ResNet independently and their contribution is broader than this reduction suggests: it combined open-gated residual connections with a deeper empirical exploration (training a 152-layer network end-to-end on ImageNet), a specific initialization scheme, and a bottleneck block design that made the architecture practical at scale. Both descriptions are accurate; neither is the whole story. The Highway Net principle, constant error flow through residual connections, is now the core of virtually all modern deep learning architectures.
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: The architectural lineage from LSTM to ResNet can be traced as a clear sequence of innovations transferring the same core principle, constant error flow through residual connections:
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: - **1991:** Hochreiter's recurrent residual connections solve the vanishing gradient problem
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: - **1997:** LSTM introduces plain recurrent residual connections (weight 1.0)
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: - **1999-2000:** Vanilla LSTM adds gated recurrent residual connections (gates initially open at 1.0)
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: - **2005:** Unfolding LSTM leads from recurrent to feedforward residual NNs
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: - **May 2015:** Highway Networks apply gated feedforward residual connections (initially 1.0)
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: - **Dec 2015:** ResNet adopts the principle as an open-gated Highway Net
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: This timeline demonstrates that the most cited neural network of the 21st century (ResNet) is a direct descendant of the most cited neural network of the 20th century (LSTM), connected through the Highway Network.
blocks.section: Highway Networks: The First Very Deep Feedforward NNs (2015)

blocks.quote: The Transformer and Attention (2017)
blocks.section: The Transformer and Attention (2017)

blocks.quote: Then came another breakthrough, the \citealternativetitle{vaswani2017attention}. By utilizing a mechanism called **Self-Attention**, models could process entire sequences of data in parallel rather than word-by-word. This mitigated the vanishing-gradient and long-range-dependency problems that had limited recurrent networks, and let models handle long context in text. The further text will lead you through every step you need to understand this Self-Attention-Mechanism on a basic level. The original goal of the Attention paper was not to build a chatbot, but to improve translation systems by a lot.
blocks.section: The Transformer and Attention (2017)

blocks.quote: In this context, “attention” is a mathematical mechanism for weighting information, not a form of awareness or intent.
blocks.section: The Transformer and Attention (2017)
