blocks.quote: There is a second, quiet invention inside the same paper that is just as load-bearing, and it is easily overlooked. Pure self-attention is **insensitive to word order**: it weighs every pair of tokens against every other, so a layer that has seen "the dog bites the man" and "the man bites the dog" sees, at its input, the same two clouds of tokens arranged differently, and would happily map both to the same output. Language would collapse into a bag of words. The authors solved this by adding **positional encodings** to every token: a deterministic pattern of sine and cosine waves overlaid on the embeddings so that each position in the sequence carries its own signature \cite{vaswani2017attention}. Its descendants (learned position vectors, and later **rotary** embeddings (RoPE), which rotate pairs of embedding coordinates by an angle proportional to the position) remain inside every modern LLM. Attention supplies the *what-goes-with-what*; positional encoding supplies the *where-it-was*, and both are needed, because neither order nor association alone is language.
blocks.section: The Transformer and Attention (2017)

blocks.quote: The Attention Mechanism will be explained in detail later on.
blocks.section: The Transformer and Attention (2017)

blocks.quote: The Age of Large Language Models
blocks.section: The Age of Large Language Models

blocks.quote: From Language Models to LLMs
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: The idea of modeling language statistically predates computers themselves. At the end of the 1940s and the start of the 1950s, \citeauthor{shannon1948communication} applied information theory to English text, treating language as a stochastic process and asking how predictable the next symbol is. His 1948 paper laid the mathematical foundation, and his 1951 paper on the entropy of printed English made the prediction view explicit: **n-gram models**, which predict the next word from the previous *n* words, could capture statistical regularities in language (\cite{shannon1948communication}; \cite{shannon1951communication}). Through the 1980s and 1990s, n-gram-based statistical language models dominated speech recognition and machine translation, championed by researchers like Frederick Jelinek at IBM. Meanwhile, **ELIZA** (1966), created by \citeauthorlastnameand{weizenbaum1976computer}, demonstrated early natural language interaction through simple pattern matching, but had no statistical understanding of language whatsoever.
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: Long before Shannon counted letters, so did the code-breakers. The great Arab polymath \citeauthor{alkindi_cryptanalysis} (c. 801-873), in his *Manuscript on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages*, invented **frequency analysis** \cite{historyofmath_wikipedia} \cite{alkindi_cryptanalysis}: count how often each symbol occurs in an intercepted message, compare the tallies against the known letter-frequencies of the language, and the ciphertext begins to crack itself. That is a *statistical model of language*: the very insight Shannon's n-grams would formalize a thousand years later, and, ultimately, the one on which "predict the next word" rests: language carries measurable statistical structure, and that structure alone suffices to do useful work. Frequency analysis is, in a real sense, the ninth-century great-grandparent of the language model, the point where the *counter* (al-Kindi) first out-performed the *rule-book* (Pāṇini).
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: The neural revolution in language modeling began with Bengio et al.'s \citeyear{neuralprobabilistic} paper \citetitle{neuralprobabilistic}, which replaced sparse n-gram tables with dense, continuous **word embeddings**, learned vector representations capturing semantic similarity. This was supercharged in 2013 by \citealternativetitle{mikolov2013word2vec}, which efficiently trained embeddings on large corpora and revealed striking algebraic properties of language (e.g., $\text{king} - \text{man} + \text{woman} \approx \text{queen}$). In \citeyear{elmo}, \citealternativetitle{elmo} introduced **contextualized embeddings** that changed depending on surrounding context, finally addressing polysemy, ie. the idea that one word can have multiple meanings.
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: The concept of a neural probabilistic text model was first published by \citeauthorlastnameand{schmidhuber1996nplm} in \citeyear{schmidhuber1996nplm}, who used a neural network to predict the next character in a text sequence for the purpose of text compression, effectively creating the first neural language model. The basic concepts of this approach were later reused and extended in the more widely known 2003 work by Bengio et al.
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: The real inflection point came with the \citealternativetitle{vaswani2017attention}, which replaced sequential processing with parallelizable **self-attention**. Two competing branches emerged almost simultaneously. \citealternativetitle{bert} used the Transformer's *encoder* with **Masked Language Modeling**, hiding random words and predicting them from both directions, to produce deeply bidirectional representations. A single pre-trained BERT model, fine-tuned with minimal data, shattered nearly every NLP benchmark overnight and popularized the **pre-train then fine-tune** paradigm.
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: In parallel, OpenAI pursued the *decoder-only* path: \citealternativetitle{firstgpt} showed that autoregressive next-token prediction over a large Transformer could learn powerful representations, and that fine-tuning those representations on each target task (with the task's inputs rewritten as one token sequence) beat task-specific architectures. The 2018 model was a 12-layer decoder with roughly 117 million parameters, pretrained on BooksCorpus, a collection of more than 7,000 unpublished books; with only a small linear output layer and delimiter embeddings added, it set the state of the art on 9 of the 12 benchmarks it was tested on.
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{gpt2} then scaled the recipe roughly tenfold, to 1.5 billion parameters, and trained it on **WebText**, a corpus assembled from outbound Reddit links that had earned at least three karma and filtered down to about 40 GB of text. The striking result was not a better benchmark score but a change in method: without any fine-tuning, the model could answer reading-comprehension questions, translate, summarize, and perform other tasks when the task was demonstrated or named in its prompt. The paper called this **unsupervised multitask learning**; the field soon called it prompting. \citealternativetitle{brown2020gpt3}, with 175 billion parameters, turned the observation into a programme by showing that few-shot in-context learning improves smoothly with scale.
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: GPT-2 was also the first model whose *release* became part of the story. OpenAI announced it in February 2019 but withheld the largest version, citing concerns about synthetic text; it published the smaller models in stages and released the full 1.5B weights only in November 2019, alongside a report on misuse monitoring (\cite[OpenAI, 2019]{openai2019betterlms}; \cite[OpenAI, 2019]{openai2019gpt2release}). Critics saw publicity-driven security theatre that broke open-publication norms; defenders saw the first serious experiment in staged release for a capable model. The argument rehearsed nearly every later open-weights debate, from Llama licensing to the GPT-OSS release. Underneath the release question sits a larger one that the \cite[Nooscope]{joler2020nooscope} names *knowledge extractivism*: the model is a compressed map of text that millions of people wrote, and the debate over weights is also a debate over who owns and can inspect that map.
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: The recipe was assembled in stages. **ULMFiT** (\cite[Howard & Ruder, 2018]{howard2018ulmfit}) supplied the three-step template that every later system follows: pretrain a language model on general text, fine-tune it on the target domain, then fine-tune it on the task, with *discriminative* learning rates and *gradual unfreezing* so that the pretrained knowledge survives. **RoBERTa** (\cite[Liu et al., 2019]{liu2019roberta}) was a replication study that found BERT significantly undertrained: removing the next-sentence-prediction task, resampling masks dynamically, and training longer on more data set new records with the same architecture. **ELECTRA** (\cite[Clark et al., 2020]{clark2020electra}) changed the objective from filling in blanks to *detecting* replaced tokens, reaching BERT-class quality at a fraction of the compute because every position, not just the masked ones, supplies a training signal. And **T5** (\cite[Raffel et al., 2020]{raffel2020t5}) unified everything into one text-to-text format: translation, summarization, classification, and question answering all became “given this string, generate that string,” with span corruption as the pretraining objective. The modern pretrain-then-post-train pipeline is the consolidation of these four ideas.
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: A crucial refinement came with the **Chinchilla scaling laws** (\citeauthor{hoffmann2022chinchilla}, \citeyear{hoffmann2022chinchilla}), which showed that most large models were undertrained: for a given compute budget, the optimal strategy is to train a smaller model on far more data. This insight directly influenced the design of models like LLaMA (\citeauthor{touvron2023llama}, \citeyear{touvron2023llama}), which deliberately used more tokens (1.0 to 1.4 trillion) with a moderately sized 7B to 65B parameter architecture, instead of pushing raw parameter counts higher. LLaMA's release was a pivotal moment for the democratization of AI: by showing that smaller, efficiently trained models could compete with GPT-3, it made advanced language modeling accessible to the broader research community, enabling fine-tuning on consumer hardware and sparking the open-source LLM movement. Meta's **LLaMA** family, developed at its FAIR lab and championed by **Yann LeCun**, and later **DeepSeek's** open-weight V3 and R1 models (V3 trained for 2.788 million H800 GPU-hours, R1 trained largely by reinforcement learning) turned that movement into a market: the frontier was no longer defined only by closed APIs, but by how quickly open weights could close the gap (\cite{touvron2023llama}; \cite{llama3herd2024}; \cite{deepseek2024v3}; \cite{guo2025deepseekr1}; \cite{lecun2022path}).
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: The institutions mattered as much as the architectures. **Ilya Sutskever**, co-inventor of sequence-to-sequence learning, co-founded OpenAI and served as its chief scientist through the GPT and ChatGPT era; **Dario Amodei**, co-author of the original RLHF study and of *Concrete Problems in AI Safety*, left OpenAI to co-found **Anthropic** in 2021, which made safety its organising principle and built the Claude line (\cite{sutskever2014seq2seq}; \cite{sutskever_bio}; \cite{amodei2016concrete}; \cite{anthropic_bio}; \cite{amodei2024machines}).
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: Combined with \citetitle[Deep-Reinforcement-Learning]{christiano2017rlhf}, as described in the \citealternativetitle{ouyang2022instructgpt} paper, this lineage culminated in **ChatGPT** in November 2022, the moment large language models crossed from research artifact into mainstream cultural phenomenon \cite{hnfchatgpt2023}.
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: The trajectory from Shannon's n-grams to ChatGPT vindicates a consistent theme: each generation traded hand-crafted linguistic knowledge for greater scale and more general learning, raw computation and data, given the right architecture, eventually surpassing human-designed heuristics, again proving the \citealternativetitle{sutton2019bitter}.
blocks.section: From Language Models to LLMs

blocks.quote: The Machine's Alphabet: Tokens
blocks.section: The Machine's Alphabet: Tokens

blocks.quote: There is a step in the previous story that is easy to miss, because it happens before any model is trained, yet without it, *none* of the "next-word prediction" above would even be defined: an LLM does not read words, and it does not read letters. It reads **tokens**, small fragments of text chosen in advance, and every one of its trillion predictions is a probability over that fixed token table. Tokenization is the invisible alphabet of the age \cite{sennrich2016subword}.
blocks.section: The Machine's Alphabet: Tokens

blocks.quote: How did the alphabet form? Each of the three candidate granularities fails alone:
blocks.section: The Machine's Alphabet: Tokens

blocks.quote: In the modern decoding path, "predicting the next word" is literally "predicting the next *token ID*", a number in a fixed table, looked up through the embedding matrix described in the [Embeddings](embeddinglab) chapter. You can watch a byte-pair vocabulary grow in the [Tokenizer Lab](tokenizerlab). And the historical irony is worth stating plainly: the machine that "thinks" is doing it over an alphabet that a 1994 file-compressor forged out of byte counts: the same statistical instinct that made al-Kindi's ninth-century frequency analysis work, now baked into the very units of thought.
blocks.section: The Machine's Alphabet: Tokens

blocks.quote: Scaling Laws: From Encyclopedias to the Digital Ocean
blocks.section: Scaling Laws: From Encyclopedias to the Digital Ocean

blocks.quote: The breakthrough of modern AI was predicated on a shift in data philosophy: moving from “quality” (hand-curated expert knowledge) to “quantity” (the total sum of digital footprints). Early AI failed because the world was not yet sufficiently digitized. The current era of 2020s AI only became possible once the internet provided a large enough corpus, petabytes of text, code, and images, to allow models to internalize the latent structures of human logic. In this context, data is the “terrain” that the machine's “wheels” must traverse; without a world-scale digital ocean, the abstraction of thought would have had nothing to grip.
blocks.section: Scaling Laws: From Encyclopedias to the Digital Ocean

blocks.quote: Taming the Stochastic Parrot: The Alignment Era
blocks.section: Taming the Stochastic Parrot: The Alignment Era

blocks.quote: The final layer of abstraction in the history of LLMs is not mathematical, but teleological. As explored in \citetitle{ouyang2022instructgpt}, the raw statistical power of a base model often results in “hallucinations” or unhelpful outputs because the machine is merely predicting the next likely word, not the user's intent. The key idea came from **Paul Christiano** and colleagues in 2017: learn a reward model from pairwise human preferences, then optimise a policy against it (\cite{christiano2017rlhf}). By introducing **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)**, researchers moved beyond the “Black Box” of raw data ingestion into the realm of social alignment. This process essentially acts as a cultural filter, rewarding the model for being helpful, honest, and harmless. This represents the moment where the machine ceased to be a mere calculator of probabilities and began to function as a conversational agent, transitioning from a mirror of the internet's chaos to a tool that respects the subjective constraints of human interaction.
blocks.section: Taming the Stochastic Parrot: The Alignment Era

blocks.quote: The “stochastic parrot” framing reopens the oldest wound in the philosophy of AI. In 1980, \citeauthor{searle1980minds} had proposed the **Chinese Room** thought experiment: imagine a person locked in a room who follows an English rule-book to shuffle incoming Chinese characters into outgoing Chinese characters. From outside, the room behaves indistinguishably from a fluent Chinese speaker. Yet the person inside understands nothing.
blocks.section: Taming the Stochastic Parrot: The Alignment Era

blocks.quote: By Searle's argument, no amount of clever symbol-shuffling is sufficient for *understanding*; minds require specific biological machinery, what he calls *biological naturalism*. The standard rebuttals in the AI literature (the *systems reply*: the room-plus-rules understands; the *robot reply*: grounding in a body fixes the problem; the *connectionist reply*: a neural net would not have the problem) all attempt to push the “understanding” somewhere outside the formal manipulation.
blocks.section: Taming the Stochastic Parrot: The Alignment Era

blocks.quote: \citeauthor{russell2021aima} point out that Searle's argument is *not* an argument against AI as a field: even if no digital computer literally understands Chinese, AI systems can still be made to behave as if they do, and that behaviour is what the field optimises for. The question the Chinese Room leaves unresolved is whether there is a meaningful difference between these two outcomes, and whether the distinction, if it exists, can be settled empirically at all. LLMs in 2026 have not answered it; they have only made the question louder.
blocks.section: Taming the Stochastic Parrot: The Alignment Era

blocks.quote: The Rise of Generative AI
blocks.section: The Rise of Generative AI

blocks.quote: Today, the focus has shifted to **Large Language Models (LLMs)** like GPT (first introduced by the paper \citetitle{firstgpt} in \citeyear{firstgpt}). These models are “pre-trained” on nearly the entire internet to predict the next token in a sequence. By scaling these architectures to billions of parameters, AI has moved from simple classification to generating human-like text, code, and reasoning and even video and music.
blocks.section: The Rise of Generative AI

blocks.quote: What changed since the early days was not the basic ideas, but the availability of data, computing power, and practical training techniques.
blocks.section: The Rise of Generative AI

blocks.quote: The Great Convergence: From Syllogisms to Silicon
blocks.section: The Great Convergence: From Syllogisms to Silicon

blocks.quote: The emergence of ChatGPT represents the “Great Convergence” of a multi-millennial effort to decouple human thought from biology and translate it into formal abstraction. This journey began with **Aristotle's** syllogisms and was radicalized by **Llull's** mechanical knowledge wheels and **Leibniz's** binary alphabet, the idea that all reasoning could be reduced to a series of calculations. From **Babbage and Lovelace's** “algebraic patterns” to **McCulloch and Pitts'** mathematical neurons, the lineage of AI has always sought to treat thought as a formal calculus.
blocks.section: The Great Convergence: From Syllogisms to Silicon

blocks.quote: However, the final transition required more than logic; it required a physical substrate of sufficient scale. As noted in \citetitle{sutton2019bitter}, the “Bitter Lesson” of AI history is that raw computation eventually outpaces human intuition. This was made possible by Moore's Law \cite[Moore's Law]{mooreslaw} and the revolutionary discovery that the massive-parallel SIMD architecture of GPUs, originally forged for the sensory demands of video games, provided the perfect engine for neural matrix operations, as demonstrated by \cite[Oh et al.]{oh2004gpu} and \cite[Raina et al.]{raina2009large}.
blocks.section: The Great Convergence: From Syllogisms to Silicon

blocks.quote: Today's models are the ultimate synthesis: the combinatorial logic of the ancients finally meeting the brute-force scaling of the modern era. We have reached a point where the machine “weaves” language by calculating billions of vectors across silicon clusters, proving that when enough compute meets enough abstraction, the machine does not just mimic thought, it executes it.
blocks.section: The Great Convergence: From Syllogisms to Silicon

blocks.quote: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: The history of AI, viewed through a wider lens, reveals a pattern of repeated boom-and-bust cycles \cite{toosi2021history}. The first summer (1956-1969) was fueled by the Dartmouth workshop and Rosenblatt's Perceptron, producing early milestones: **Arthur Samuel's** checker player (1959), the first reinforcement-learning-based AI program; **Newell and Simon's Logic Theorist** (1956), which proved theorems from *Principia Mathematica*; McCarthy's **LISP** language (1958); the **Unimate** industrial robot (1961); the **ELIZA** chatbot (1966); and the **Shakey** mobile robot (1966), the first omni-purpose platform with environment reasoning. The HNF blog's 70-year retrospective places the Dartmouth workshop in a much longer lineage running back to Kempelen's chess Turk, Torres Quevedo's endgame machine and Shannon's chess program \cite{hnfki70jahre2026}; its essay on Shakey reconstructs the SRI robot's television camera, planner and computer link \cite{hnfshakey2019}.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: The first winter had several independent causes that compounded, and putting them in chronological order helps to see which were technical, which were bureaucratic, and which were legislative \cite{toosi2021history}. The **ALPAC report** (1966) had already documented machine translation's failure to deliver useful military output and triggered the first wave of DARPA defunding. The **Mansfield Amendment** of November 1969 then required the Defense Department to restrict basic research to projects "with a direct and apparent relationship to a specific military function or operation", explicitly cutting the long-horizon funding that had supported symbolic AI and the perceptron program (\cite[Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence]{nilsson1984qai}). The mathematical **Minsky-Papert critique** of the single-layer Perceptron (1969) was a contributing factor in the academic credibility of connectionism, not a funding cause in itself: the funding had already started moving, and the field had been retreating from perceptrons since the mid-1960s.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: The UK **Lighthill report** (1973), a written document, convinced the British Science Research Council to cut AI funding in most UK universities within a year; the BBC broadcast a debate about it on 9 May 1973, not the report itself (\cite{lighthillreport}). The American legislative lever (Mansfield, ALPAC) and the British scientific-audit lever (Lighthill) thus hit roughly simultaneously; the technical critique rode alongside them but did not, on its own, redirect money.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: The lesson Toosi et al. draw is that exaggerated claims and failure to appreciate computational complexity have repeatedly triggered downturns, a warning relevant to today's AI boom \cite{toosi2021history}. The revived expert systems era (1980s) created a second summer, but unfulfilled promises led to a second winter by the early 1990s.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: The Japanese Fifth Generation project (1982-1994) is the canonical case: a state-funded bet on parallel AI hardware that ended without the promised breakthrough \cite{hnffifthgen2023}. The emerging **neuro-symbolic AI** paradigm \cite{toosi2021history} aims to bridge the historic divide between connectionist and symbolic approaches, combining the trainability of neural networks with the explainability of symbolic systems.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: Toosi et al. frame the whole arc as a recipe for the next crash, because the same over-promise that built each summer is what the subsequent funding freeze punished \cite{toosi2021history}. Their review of where the field stands now shows how high the third summer has climbed, which is precisely what makes a fourth winter expensive: global venture investment in AI startups grew from roughly $1.3 billion in 2010 to more than $40 billion in 2020, while corporate investment in AI alone reached nearly $70 billion that year, the number of peer-reviewed AI articles per year multiplied roughly twelve-fold between 2000 and 2020, and NeurIPS attendance grew tenfold since 2012 \cite{toosi2021history}. When the stakes are that large, the difference between a field that matures and one that crashes is how well it disciplines its own hype.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: Their proposed guardrails therefore read like a checklist for the present moment. Be sober about what counts as intelligence and avoid claims that machines have “become” human; resist extrapolating from toy problems to the general case on the assumption that faster hardware will absorb the difference; define the terms “AI”, “machine learning” and “deep learning” precisely, since their ambiguity has already become a cover for marketing; and treat the field's methodological lapses (confusing explanation with speculation, misattributing where performance gains come from, and misleading use of mathematics) as systemic risks rather than isolated slips \cite{toosi2021history}. Two of these deserve to outlive the rest. The **AI effect** is the field's moving target: a technique is only called “AI” while it is still unsolved, and the moment it is cracked it graduates into an ordinary engineering discipline, and the excitement moves to the next frontier \cite{toosi2021history}. And the **black box** is the standing objection to deep learning: the model often cannot say how it reached a decision, which is tolerable for a game but not for medicine, transport, or finance, where a wrong judgment has a human cost and regulation increasingly demands that it be retraced \cite{toosi2021history}. The interpretability chapters of this course are the direct answer to that demand.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: The HNF blog is especially good on the German strand of this story. Its portrait of \cite[Karl Steinbuch]{hnfsteinbuch2017} follows him from the Lernmatrix and the first German transistor computer to his later right-wing politics; its account of the \cite[1975 Bonn meeting]{hnfbonn2020} marks the organisational birth of West German AI research; and its \cite[survey of women in AI]{hnfki_frauen2023} recovers researchers the standard narrative tends to leave out.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: As hardware matured from relays to vacuum tubes and finally to silicon, the bottleneck shifted from physical construction to the management of “Software.” To handle the growing complexity of these systems, computer science adopted a strategy of increasing abstraction.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: This evolution moved from:
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: 1. **Machine Logic:** Managing individual bits and relays (Zuse).
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: 2. **Operating Systems:** Managing hardware resources so the human doesn't have to.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: 3. **High-Level Frameworks:** Tools like **TensorFlow** or **Keras** that allow researchers to treat complex neural operations as “simple boxes.”
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: 4. **Graphical User Interfaces:** They move the abstraction even further away from what the hardware is doing when the user can, for example, just speak to control the computer.
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: 5. **AI**: Abstracting away the non-human interaction part of using computers by simulating *meaning* (as in transformers do, for example).
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters

blocks.quote: Today, a developer can invoke a convolutional layer with a single command, such as `model.conv2d`. Under the hood, the system manages millions of matrix multiplications, a level of complexity that would have been impossible for a human to track manually, but which fulfills the trajectory started by Lovelace: reducing the mechanics of thought to a manageable, symbolic architecture. Operating Systems, later frameworks, growing complexity on the system side to reduce complexity on the human side, until progress could be made by just moving simple boxes like in asanAI or TensorFlow like model.Dense or model.conv2d. Very important to think that level of abstraction
blocks.section: The Cycles of AI: Learning from the Winters
